Part II · Constructing the arithmetic inputs›Ch. 5 · Lattices and the arithmetic main term›§5.1 The lattices that carry the comparison

A local valuation gain becomes a positive multiple of log p after taking a lattice height. Each word in the theta construction carries an auxiliary prime level. A lower bound on the logarithm of that prime enters the lattice comparison. Expanding the bound cancels the period and auxiliary-prime terms and identifies the main term to subtract from the arithmetic prime sum.

The count of minor lists by size bounds the diagonal error for each word. The dimension estimate combines this bound with the row and column counts and the correlations between different words. It gives the rank needed in the slope inequality.

5.1The lattices that carry the comparison

Over a number field K, an arithmetic lattice in a finite-dimensional K-vector space V is a finitely generated module over the ring of integers of K spanning V. To measure it one also needs norms at the infinite places. A basis of V and a matrix Xv at each such place give these frames. Each frame must have nonzero determinant. For such a lattice A of positive rank r over a totally complex number field, its mean slope is −(2/[K : ℚ]) log(ht(A))/r. Here ht is the lattice height in the chosen metric. The factor 2/[K : ℚ] averages over the complex places. A smaller height at fixed rank raises the mean slope. The proof obtains positivity of ht and uses [K : ℚ] = 2 times the number of infinite places.

For each choice of translation and each word u in a finite nonempty set W, the construction has a lattice Nu, a height allowance hu, and a linear map from the ambient space of Nu to the dual of the ambient space of a common lattice R. This dual consists of linear forms on that space. Its integral lattice consists of the forms taking integral values on R. The global hypotheses include an upper bound by hu for the height of each nonzero map.

Write μ for the mean slope, μmax for the maximum sublattice slope, and μmin for the minimum quotient slope. The comparison takes a mean weighted by the positive ranks ru of the word lattices. Set

s = ∑u ru(μ(Nu) − hu)/∑u ru,   bF = maxu(μmax(Nu) − hu) − s.

The latter quantity is nonnegative. For each word, its adjusted mean slope is bounded above by that word's adjusted maximum and hence by their common maximum. Averaging gives the assertion. The symbols s and bF in this chapter are real quantities at a fixed translation.

5.2What the counting bound contributes

Fix this translation. Let m be the number of successive lifts, f the positive number of place indices, and at ≥ 0 a weight at index t in the finite top set. Put A = ∑tat. Each stage j and place ρ has positive weight wjρ. Let v > 0 be the host normalization, and ℓg the logarithm of the product of the two auxiliary primes used for the host. A word has an associated prime Tu. The uniform counting estimate uses a nonnegative constant Cc, scale parameters k > 0, L and La, and the following quantities.

Ec = CcLa(1 + m²/k),   λ = ∑j (1/f) ∑ρ log(wjρv/π) + mℓg − Ec.

For every word u, the word count gives λ ≤ log Tu ≤ CcmL. It also gives |log Tu − log Tu′| ≤ Cc log k between any two words at this translation. The first inequality supplies the counting floor used in the main term. The other two control fluctuations in the slope estimate. Scalar La is log of the product of the master scale a and the root discriminant of the field E.

5.3The cancellation in the main term

Write γ for Euler's constant and d for the real logarithmic derivative at 1 of the distinguished quadratic character in this comparison. Set Ωlog = γ + log(π/v) − d. The local divisibility inequality contributes the term SD − A log Tu, where

SD = m∑t[at log at − at − atΩlog].

At zero we interpret a log a by its continuous value zero. Since A ≥ 0, subtracting A log Tu is bounded above by subtracting Aλ. The local exponent comparison contributes mAℓg with an explicit error bound. We can now calculate exactly which deterministic quantity lies under those bounds.

First expand the logarithm inside λ. Each place contributes log wjρ + log(v/π). The second summand is independent of ρ, so the mean over f places reproduces it once per stage. Thus −Aλ contributes −mA log(v/π), −mAℓg, and +AEc, as well as the weighted logarithms of w. The period term inside SD contributes +mA log(v/π), exactly cancelling the first of those terms. Adding the exponent main term +mAℓg cancels the second. Distributing A = ∑tat in the remaining place sum yields

SD − Aλ + mAℓg = M + AEc,
M = ∑j,t at[log at − 1 − γ + d − (1/f) ∑ρ log wjρ].

The plus sign of d comes from subtracting Ωlog. At m = f = 1 with a single top index and w = 1, the main term reduces to a(log a − 1 − γ + d). Doubling v adds a log 2 to SD and subtracts the same amount through −Aλ. This illustrates why a change of metric normalization in only one term would leave a linear error.

A check with two different place weights. Specialize the displayed identity to one stage, top weights 1 and 3, and place weights 2 and 8. Then A = 4 and the mean of the place logarithms is log 4. To track the cancellations, set v = 2π and write ℓg = log 15. These are values for checking the algebra. The formula for λ gives log 8 + log 15 − Ec. The period in SD contributes +4 log 2. Substitution gives

SD − 4λ + 4 log 15 = 3 log 3 − 4 − 4γ + 4d − 4 log 4 + 4Ec.

The coefficient of log 15 is zero. The surviving −4 log 4 comes from the geometric mean √(2·8) of the place weights. The count error enters with a plus sign, scaled by the total top weight 4. These three features persist for arbitrary finite sets of places and top weights.

The identification with the prime-sum expression uses specific bijections and equalities. The top indices correspond to the finite arithmetic sample, the f place indices to the chosen half of the finite group, the respective weights agree, γ agrees, and d equals the real part of the coefficient of the distinguished sign character. With these correspondences, reindex the two finite sums and take real parts. The final identification equates the weighted arithmetic prime sum to the sum over the sampled top indices and stages. Subtracting the matched main term M on both sides identifies the residual in the balance calculation.

5.4Where the slope inequality enters

Fix an upper bound H > 0 for s − μmin(R∨). Let 0 ≤ δ < 1 be the rank-deficit parameter, η ≥ 0 a frame-error parameter and 0 ≤ e ≤ 1/4 the second error parameter. The slope bound to be proved is

s − log |W| − [4bF log(1 + H/bF) + (η + 4√e)H]/(1 − δ) ≤ μ(R∨).

If bF = 0 the first product inside the brackets is zero, also its limit from positive bF. This inequality places the same dual-lattice slope appearing in the divisibility inequality on the opposite side. Combining its lower bound with divisibility's upper bound, the rank mean comparison, and the counting inequalities bounds the finite-place gain by M plus errors. The construction supplies an additional ceiling H ≤ xCHb, where x is the arithmetic scale and b its weight scale. It also supplies bounds for the error parameters, so large values of H can be multiplied by small η and √e.

5.5Eliminating the two auxiliary lattice quantities

Write G for the weighted finite-place gain, F for the separate finite-place correction, Eu for the word’s exponent sum, and μR for μ(R∨). At a fixed translation and word, write Qu for its source-lattice mean, Lu for its explicit loss, and Derr for the divisibility error. The two inequalities entering the proof are

μ(Nu) ≥ Qu + G + F − Eu − Lu,   μR + hu − F ≤ SD − A log Tu + Derr.

Solve the second inequality for F and insert its lower bound in the first. The word height then cancels upon passing to μ(Nu) − hu. Average with the word ranks. Using log Tu ≥ λ, the exponent upper bound and the lower bound on Qu gives s ≥ G + μR − M − errors. Now rearrange the slope inequality above as s ≤ μR + log |W| + frame error. Comparing eliminates μR, leaving G ≤ M + errors. This explains both the sign of the finite-place correction and the need to bound the same dual lattice from both sides. The word-independent error is exactly the sum of AEc, Derr, the exponent error mCEB₀, and the source-slope error Cslope|Top|aLa(1+m/k). The rank-averaged word losses and the frame error still appear separately.

5.6Why the slope bound contains a logarithm

Think of a lattice through its finite list of Harder–Narasimhan slopes, each repeated according to rank. A step in its filtration contains the directions whose slopes meet a given threshold. For a slope λ of the underlying real lattice the arithmetic normalization is 2λ + cK, with the same field constant for all words and the target. The resulting list has arithmetic mean equal to the lattice's mean slope. For the source lattices subtract each height allowance and concatenate the lists over all words. Their mean is s and every entry is at most s + bF. If a fraction p lies below s − τ, for τ ≥ 0, then the mean is at most p(s − τ) + (1 − p)(s + bF). Rearranging gives p ≤ bF/(bF + τ) when the denominator is positive. If both quantities vanish, all slopes equal s and the strict lower tail is empty. This bounds the rank lost when we discard low-slope steps in the source.

At a fixed infinite place, let Ai be the word maps on all D rows, with each positive frame weight absorbed into its map by multiplying by the square root of the weight. Write r for the sum of their source dimensions, after the ramified restriction and before the slope cutoff. Both r and D are positive. The retained source step for word i spans a complex subspace Ui. Its codimension di counts the discarded source slopes for that word, so ∑i di = pr. The rank estimate from the minors and the choice of frame errors give the following hypotheses on the maps before this cutoff. Put Ki = Ai∗Ai and Q = ∑i AiAi∗.

∑i ‖Ki − I‖HS² ≤ er,   D tr(Q²) ≤ (1 + η)(tr Q)²,   0 ≤ e ≤ 1/4,   η ≥ 0.

Rank bound for the selected subspaces. Let S = ∑i Ai(Ui). Its missing fraction x = codim(S)/D is at most η + 4p + 4√e. For one identity map and a retained subspace of codimension k, the errors vanish and the missing fraction is exactly p = k/D. This example exhibits the linear dependence on the discarded dimension.

Why the discarded dimensions bound the missing rows

Let P project orthogonally onto S⊥ and let Pi project onto Ui⊥. Write t = tr Q. Applying Hilbert–Schmidt Cauchy–Schwarz to ∑i tr(Ki − I) gives |t − r| ≤ √r √(er). Indeed, the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of each identity is its source dimension. Thus t ≥ r(1 − √e) ≥ r/2.

Only discarded directions can contribute to the trace on the missing rows. Each PAi vanishes on Ui, and orthogonal projection decreases lengths. Hence tr(PQ) = ∑i ‖PAiPi‖HS² ≤ ∑i tr(PiKi). Splitting each Ki into I and its error gives a main term ∑i di = pr. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the remaining term by √(pr) √(er), since ‖Pi‖HS² = di.

For a lower bound on the same trace, subtract the mean eigenvalue from Q. The second trace hypothesis gives ‖Q − (t/D)I‖HS² = tr(Q²) − t²/D ≤ ηt²/D. As tr P = ‖P‖HS² = Dx, Cauchy–Schwarz gives

t(x − √(ηx)) ≤ tr(PQ) ≤ r(p + √(pe)).

Divide by t and use r/t ≤ 2 and 2√(ηx) ≤ η + x. Rearranging gives x ≤ η + 4p + 4√(pe). Since 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, this implies the stated bound.

Now project S onto the Dar arithmetic rows. This projection loses at most D − Dar independent directions, so its image has codimension at most Dx among the arithmetic rows. At the chosen place each source basis change carries its retained subspace to the corresponding arithmetic filtration step. All words use the same target basis change. It therefore carries the sum of their projected images into the complex span of the arithmetic images. The nonzero scalar attached to each word preserves its image subspace. The slope inequality and the height allowance for each word put its retained image in the target filtration step at s − τ. The count of target slopes strictly below that threshold is the codimension of this step. Divide by Dar ≥ (1 − δ)D, where 0 ≤ δ < 1, and substitute the source bound on p. The resulting upper bound for the fraction is

ω(τ) = [η + 4bF/(bF + τ) + 4√e]/(1 − δ).

At bF = τ = 0, use zero for the source fraction because the strict source tail is empty.

Let ν run through the normalized target slopes with multiplicity. The lower-slope bound says ν ≥ s − H. Consequently the interval of τ in [0, H] for which ν < s − τ has length max(s − ν, 0). Average these lengths over the finite list. Their integral representation, followed by the bound above, gives

s − mean(ν) ≤ mean[max(s − ν, 0)] = ∫0H fraction{ν < s − τ} dτ ≤ ∫0H ω(τ) dτ.

For example, set s = 4 and take the three numbers 1, 3, 5 with H = 3. Two lie below 4 − τ for 0 ≤ τ < 1, and one lies below it for 1 ≤ τ < 3. The integral of the fraction is (2/3)·1 + (1/3)·2 = 4/3. This equals the average of the positive deficits 3, 1, 0. The signed mean deficit is only 1, since the last value exceeds 4. This finite list illustrates the integration step.

For bF > 0, integrating bF/(bF + τ) gives bF log(1 + H/bF). For bF = 0 this contribution vanishes. The two constant terms in ω integrate to (η + 4√e)H/(1 − δ). Since mean(ν) = μ(R∨), the calculation actually proves the bound without subtracting log |W|. The later theorem uses the displayed weaker version by subtracting the nonnegative logarithm of the number of words.

5.7What supplies the inequalities?

Here is how the number 6 enters the uniform frame bound. Put σ = x−CH. For sufficiently large x, σ ≤ 1/20. The dimension calculation below explains the loss in the rank. The real-frame input provides error caps de and ē in [0, 1/4], with (3√de + 4√ē)xCH ≤ 1. The trace estimate for the retained columns gives η = 5σ + 3√de and e = 2e0 ≤ ē, where e0 is the matrix deviation for the selected family member. Multiplying η + 4√ē by xCH gives a constant term 5 and a remainder bounded by 1. This proves the common cap 6 for every index at that scale.

Three different constructions enter the family assembly. The divisibility estimate is uniform in all sufficiently large x and all family indices. Its pointwise inequality already involves μ(R∨), map height and the signed finite-place term F. The estimate weights a place w through 2 log N(w)/[K : ℚ] times its ramification index. The family assembly applies this pointwise inequality to each member and replaces its error constant C by max(C,0) using nonnegativity of the two error factors.

For counting, a torus-pair bound, a Vandermonde variation bound, scale and rank identifications, and a bound on the logarithm of an auxiliary factor supply the three inequalities with counting constant max(C,0) + 2. The family theorem arranges a single such bound before the scale varies. For the slope, the frame estimates first give a common threshold and then, at each scale, two caps η̄ and ē satisfying (η̄ + 4√ē)xCH ≤ 6. At each family index a frame supplies admissible η and e under those caps. The assembled estimate feeds exactly these local values into the displayed slope inequality.

The proof chooses its constants and a common threshold before the scale x or the family index varies. The every-character theorem uses two constructions here. Its divisibility estimate comes from rows, admissibility and the finite-place data, including the inert coefficient calculation. The period calculation below supplies the archimedean mean for the kernel column heights. For the separate global estimate, the proof derives counting and real-frame rank bounds from the real-place and mass conditions. At the chosen family, the divisibility inequality and the slope consequence derived from it enter this global estimate together.

5.8How many columns survive the ramification conditions?

For a word u, write T for its prime level, f for the number of selected places over T, dfull for the dimension at level zero and dram for the dimension left after imposing the local conditions. The real-frame estimate needs to know how much of the source it loses. The proof computes that loss exactly, orbit by orbit. The three counting inequalities measure a different quantity, the size and variation of log Tu. Both enter the selected global theorem.

5.9Why each orbit is a product of residue groups

At each selected place the residue field has T elements. Its unit group H has T − 1 elements. The level-zero forms admit a model as complex functions on a finite set X. An element of H in one coordinate acts by a local dilation, also called a diamond operator. The operator Nv sums all these dilations in the coordinate v. Under the model, its kernel consists of functions whose sum along that coordinate is zero at every point. The ramified subspace is the intersection of these kernels.

Freeness uses arithmetic. Suppose a tuple of local multipliers fixes a level class. Represent it by an adelic element δ, whose components at the two auxiliary type primes are the identity. The power δT−1 belongs to the level subgroup, since the residues of all its multipliers have that power equal to 1. The diamond operator normalizes the level, so the same power of δκ belongs to the level for every level element κ. Fixing the class supplies a rational element γ from the double-coset relation. The admissible stabilizer gives γT−1 = 1. At each of the two distinct auxiliary primes p, the local reduction calculation kills every power of γ of order coprime to p. To see the force of having two primes, write T − 1 = pam with p ∤ m. The first condition kills γpa, whose order divides m. Now γ has order dividing pa, which is coprime to the second prime. Hence γ = 1 and δ itself lies in the level subgroup. Each local multiplier fixes a nonzero level functional killed by T. A multiplier c must therefore satisfy c ≡ 1 mod T. The tuple is the identity.

Choosing orbit representatives now identifies X with Q × Hf, where Q indexes the orbits of the function model. Its size includes the multiplicity of the value space. On each orbit a function has (T − 1)f entries before imposing any sums.

5.10Counting the independent values

Keep only the entries indexed by tuples with every coordinate different from the identity. They determine a function with vanishing line sums uniquely. To recover an entry with an identity coordinate, it must be the negative of the sum of the other entries on that line. Each of those entries has one fewer identity coordinate, so induction recovers the full table. Conversely, to extend a unit value at such a tuple a, use the product over coordinates v of (1hv=av − 1hv=1). It sums to zero along every coordinate and restricts to the unit value at a and zero at every other retained tuple. Taking linear combinations extends arbitrary data. Thus there are (T − 2)f independent values on each orbit.

dfull = |Q| (T − 1)f,   dram = |Q| (T − 2)f.

A four-by-four check. Take one orbit, T = 5 and f = 2. Order the four residues in both coordinates as 2, 3, 4, 1. Put ones on the diagonal of the first three-by-three block, zeros in its other six entries. Zero row sums force the first three entries of the last column to be −1. Zero column sums force the first three entries of the last row to be −1. Both conditions put 3 in the final corner. The nine free entries determine all sixteen. The eight row and column equations have one redundancy because summing all rows also sums all columns. The lost fraction is 7/16.

5.11From an exact count to a uniform error

For a nonzero full space and T ≥ 3, Bernoulli’s inequality gives

1 − dram/dfull = 1 − (1 − 1/(T − 1))f ≤ f/(T − 1) ≤ 2f/T.

The scale conditions give T ≥ bm/2 ≥ b, with b = exp(xε), b ≥ 3 and m ≥ 2. Thus dfull − dram ≤ de dfull for de = 2f/b. The undivided inequality also holds if the full space is zero. For each fixed family with ε > 0, one threshold works for every later x and every family index. The number f can depend on that index, but the same de works for all its words. Eventually f ≤ k ≤ x5, 2f ≤ exp(xε/2), and xε ≥ 4xε/8. Consequently √de ≤ exp(−xε/4) ≤ exp(−xε/8). Put Ex = exp(−xε/8). To obtain a bound common to all indices at this x, the proof enlarges the rank-loss cap to Ex² and the separate matrix-error cap to 2Ex². The rank term in the frame error 5σ + 3Ex now has the same value at every index. The common frame calculation supplies the diagonal and off-diagonal bounds on the full period matrices.

5.12What controls the variation of the prime level?

The comparison of two word counts uses a Vandermonde product V(z) = ∏a<b(za − zb) in the decreasing real parameters at a place. Its logarithm is a sum over pairs. For the first row a = 0 the two compared gaps are each at least 4kΔ and change by at most Δ. The variation of each logarithm is at most 1/(4k). For a ≥ 1 the gaps are at least 3(b − a)Δ and change by at most 2Δ, giving 2/[3(b − a)] per pair. Both bounds follow by integrating 1/t between the gaps. A harmonic sum over b bounds the logarithmic variation at a place by 1/4 + (2/3)k(1 + log k). Summing over f places and applying the factor 1/(fk) in the level parameter leaves variation of order log k. The shared auxiliary factor cancels when the two word windows are compared. The absolute bounds for each word also use a torus-pair estimate involving the mass, volume and formal degree.

5.13How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame?

Two periods can each preserve lengths and still take their values on the same line. A slope estimate that uses many words therefore needs two measurements. For a fixed family member let Pu carry the full complex space of word u, of dimension du, into one Hilbert space. Normalize by the real number cu, the product of its two unfolding volumes divided by the product of its column representation dimensions over the infinite places. The operator from the space of v to the space of u is

Kuv = (cucv)−1/2 Pu∗Pv,   Q(A) = ∑j ‖Aej‖².

Here the ej run through an orthonormal basis of the domain. For u = v we measure Q(Kuu − I). For distinct words we measure Q(Kuv), which adds the squared absolute values of all correlations between the two normalized families of columns. The estimates are for the full word dimension. The arithmetic lattice retained at the ramified level can have fewer columns. To see why correlations influence rank, collect any set of nonzero retained columns in a matrix A and put G = A*A. If its positive eigenvalues are λ₁,…,λᵣ, then (∑λᵢ)² ≤ r∑λᵢ² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus rank(A) ≥ (tr G)²/tr(G²). For two unit columns the numerator is 4. Identical columns give denominator 4 and rank one. Orthogonal columns give denominator 2 and rank two. The estimates below control the corresponding diagonal and cross terms for the selected arithmetic spaces.

5.14Separating the nonidentity terms with zero Gram label

The geometric expansion of Kuv converges absolutely. Write Buv for its subseries of terms with Gram label zero and with the identity excluded. Set D∗ equal to the positive reference size for the target dimension and ξ = exp(−kf log k). The proof uses four estimates. On different words the subseries vanishes, and the remaining squared norm is at most (1 + b−6)dudv/D∗. On the diagonal it gives

Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu,   Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗.

The four estimates have different suppliers. Local types kill the unwanted off-diagonal terms. A positive-kernel estimate controls their diagonal subseries. The selected different-word estimate controls the rest off the diagonal. On the diagonal a geometric row estimate controls what is left after subtracting the identity. Absolute convergence permits these subtractions.

Why can a pair of words have a zero orbital term?

Fix two distinct words u and v in the selected family. Their local unitary representations have different weight parameters at every infinite place. Examine a single nonidentity term with Gram label zero in Buv. It compares a flag with a translate of the other flag. Call the pair relevant when the differentials of their two characters agree on every common infinitesimal unipotent direction. There are two ways for its orbital integral P to vanish.

If relevance fails, one direction gives unequal phases. In fact the proof rescales that direction so that, with N infinite places, the difference in the two character exponents is πi/N at each place. The product of the first character with the conjugate of the second therefore takes the value exp(πi) = −1. This character is trivial on the rational lattice. Averaging over its compact quotient in the common unipotent group gives zero, since translating the character average by that element changes its sign. The orbital integrand transforms by exactly this character, so the orbital integral vanishes.

For a relevant pair with Gram label zero, the geometric normal form gives a positive orthonormal frame perpendicular to both flag subspaces at each infinite place. Write its columns as W and the ambient Hermitian form as J, so W∗JW = I. Every M ∈ U(k) extends to a symmetry fixing those subspaces pointwise. Indeed, put

H = I + W(M − I)W∗J.   HW = WM,   Hy = y whenever W∗Jy = 0.

On the frame this map preserves the inner product because M is unitary, and on its orthogonal complement it is the identity. The other flag sees the action as CMC∗ for a fixed unitary matrix C at that place. Invariance of the orbital integral under the pointwise stabilizer gives covariance between these two actions. This uses the existence of the fundamental domain and integrability of the orbital kernel.

Choose one infinite place and let M vary only there. Fix arbitrary vectors in every other tensor factor on each side. Let Su and Sv insert a local vector into those fixed tensors. For A = Su∗PSv, covariance reads

πu(M)A = Aπv(CMC∗),   πu(M)R = Rπv(M),   R = Aπv(C).

A nonzero R would be an isomorphism. Its kernel and image are invariant, and the two finite-dimensional representations are irreducible. An isomorphism preserves the weights of the diagonal torus, including the distinguished extremal weight that determines each type. The unequal parameters rule this out. Hence R = 0 and A = 0. Varying the fixed tensors shows that every matrix coefficient of P between pure tensors vanishes. They span both spaces.

Can a scalar unitary distinguish these two types of U(2)?

On the determinant line and on Sym²(ℂ²), the scalar zI acts by z². Suppose an intertwiner sends a generator of the determinant line to a quadratic tensor w. Every diag(z,z−1) with |z| = 1 fixes w. In the basis e₁², e₁e₂, e₂², the three eigenvalues are z², 1 and z−2. Thus w is a multiple of e₁e₂. Swapping the basis vectors fixes that monomial and multiplies the determinant by −1. Equivariance gives w = −w, so w = 0.

Both cases kill each selected term individually, so their sum Buv is zero. The other terms still contribute to Kuv. The separate different-word estimate bounds the squared norm of Kuv − Buv, and substituting zero gives the bound for the full block.

How large can the surviving part of a different-word block be?

Fix distinct words u and v and put Δ = dudv/D∗. The preceding argument removes the nonidentity terms whose geometric Gram label is zero. The remaining sum, called K₀, contains the identity part and two groups of terms with nonzero label. The identity part also vanishes for this calculation. The two groups can point in the same direction in the Hilbert space of operators. The proof bounds the squared norm of each group before adding them.

Call the two groups G (generic) and N (nongeneric). Genericity tests a pair of lattice flags. Their integral span has a saturation, obtained by intersecting its field span with the ambient lattice. At primes away from the level, genericity requires that the original span already give the saturation locally. At primes dividing the level, one admissible matrix must supply the saturation using the corrected frame differences divided by the level. A term is generic when a representative passes these tests.

Each term t contributes a vector vt supported on one pair of lattices. Its row records those lattices and a finite index i. For either group S, form ai by summing its vectors with index i. In the square of that sum, terms with the same index but different lattice pairs have disjoint support. Absolute convergence permits regrouping, so only ordered pairs in the same row contribute. With Γ₁ the positive Gram normalization, the resulting energy is

Φ(S) = Γ₁ ∑i ‖ai‖² = Γ₁ ∑s,t ∈ S, same row Re ⟨vs, vt⟩.

Individual inner products can have either sign. To bound the sum, the proof groups pairs by their corank s₀ = k − dim Θ, where Θ consists of first components of vector pairs compatible with the two flags and their comparison map. On a common row with both Gram labels nonzero, s₀ ≥ 1. Among generic pairs of corank one, the scalar pairs preserve the two coefficients of the distinguished flag vectors under comparison.

The large-corank estimate bounds the sum of absolute inner products over all same-row pairs of nonzero-label terms of corank at least two by εΔ, including the factor Γ₁. Thus each group can use this bound on its own subset. In G, the nonscalar corank-one pairs cost at most another εΔ in absolute value. The signed sum of the scalar pairs is at most AΔ. In N, one signed bound ε′Δ covers all corank-one pairs. These are the only cases, giving

Φ(G) ≤ (A + 2ε)Δ,   Φ(N) ≤ (ε + ε′)Δ.

The common Gram matrix converts each energy to an upper bound on the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of its operator sum, with a factor P. The triangle inequality then gives the retained block bound

‖K₀‖² ≤ (√[P(A + 2ε)] + √[P(ε + ε′)])² Δ ≤ (1 + b−6)Δ.

Why take the square roots? Consider two contributions along one unit vector, with coefficients 1 and 1/10. Their squared norms are 1 and 1/100, but their sum has squared norm 121/100. That example illustrates only the last addition. On the selected route the kernel expansion identifies the surviving block with the full block after the zero subseries is removed. Its Hilbert–Schmidt squared norm therefore obeys the same bound used in the frame estimate.

Why does the Gram matrix cost only P, and where does b−6 come from?

For each group the squared norm is Re ∑ij Mij⟨ai, aj⟩. The supplied matrix bound says that PΓ₁I − M is positive semidefinite. Factor it as a sum of outer products wℓwℓ∗. Substituting in the difference between PΦ(S) and the squared norm gives ∑ℓ ‖∑i wℓi ai‖² ≥ 0.

Set h = b−7. Under the selected size hypotheses, b ≥ 16, the two level primes satisfy gi ≥ (kb)⁸, and k ≥ 70 log b. The full rank and density inequalities give ε, ε′ ≤ h² and A ≤ (1 + h)exp(h²). For f infinite places, the Gram factor P = (1 + 3/g₁)f(1 + 3/g₂)f is at most exp(6h). Using h ≤ 1/1000, the two radicands are at most 1 + 11h and 3h². Their square roots sum to at most 1 + 11h/2 + 7h/4. Its square is at most 1 + 16h ≤ 1 + b−6. The remaining arithmetic inputs are the absolute bounds from counting loops, the nongeneric corank-one estimate, and the main scalar-row estimate from the lattice and mass calculation.

How many flags can have the same Gram data?

Fix a row in the common frame and one Gram class Z. To count generic flags in this row, keep the part of a flag visible in the definite orthogonal space. It is a sublattice P of a fixed lattice L₀ of ambient dimension k. Its rank is k − 1. The frame determinant formula gives a bound G depending on the prescribed data. Write B for the fixed-witness bound on the number of flag classes supported by any one such P. Each contributing flag has a witness P. Summing over possible witnesses gives an upper bound even when two witnesses count the same class.

The difficulty is that P can have large index in the integral points of its own span. Set M = L₀ ∩ spanK(P), where K is the CM field. This saturation has the same field span and rank as P. It is primitive in L₀, meaning it contains every point of L₀ in that span. With the normalized determinant (the square root of the order of the dual quotient in the span), write d = det(M) and j = #(M/P). The integral, positive definite lattice and the standing CM norm hypotheses give an integer d ≥ 1. The index formula gives det(P) = j d. Hence the determinant budget G leaves room for indices only up to G/d.

For a fixed saturation let α = k + log₂[K ∶ ℚ]. The projective-module counting bound supplies at most jα submodules of index j. For x ≥ 1 there are at most ⌊x⌋ indices through x, each contributing at most xα. This accounts for the extra power in the estimate. If Cprim(L₀,n,d) counts primitive sublattices of rank n and determinant d, the total number of eligible witnesses satisfies

#{P ⊆ L₀ ∣ rank P = n, det(P) ≤ G} ≤ ∑1 ≤ d ≤ ⌊G⌋ Cprim(L₀,n,d) (G/d)α + 1.

For G < 1 there are no witnesses. For the single generic flag take n = k − 1 and multiply by B. The row weights are nonnegative, so summing first over rows or first over d yields the same upper bound. The remaining arithmetic estimate concerns the mean of the primitive counts.

Count the eight rank-one sublattices of determinant at most two by hand

Take the standard Hermitian lattice ℤ[i]². A nonzero rank-one submodule has a generator (a,b), unique up to the four units, because ℤ[i] is a principal ideal domain. The Gram entry is h = |a|² + |b|². Its dual in its own line is obtained by dividing the generator by h. The quotient has h² elements, hence the normalized determinant is h. At h = 1 the two coordinate axes are the only possibilities. At h = 2 both coordinates can be units, giving the four primitive lines generated by (1,u), u ∈ {1,−1,i,−i}. Otherwise one coordinate vanishes and the other is a unit times 1 + i. These last two submodules have index two in the coordinate axes. This lists 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 submodules. In this concrete model the primitive counts are 2 and 4, and α + 1 = 4. The general counting expression gives 2·2⁴ + 4·1⁴ = 36. Its slack comes from bounding every index by the same power.

Why a pair costs two flag counts. A loop term carries two flags and a comparison isometry. For fixed Gram classes, positive corank s and a determinant cutoff, the two flags admit a common witness P of rank k − s. Under the level and admissibility hypotheses, moving each flag by its allowed integral unipotent transformation carries the comparison isometry to the one for the new pair, by uniqueness on the orthogonal quotient. Thus the two flag classes determine the triple class. If each flag set at P has at most J classes, the ordered pair has at most J² choices. Multiply the displayed witness bound by J² and average the primitive counts in the relevant genus. The fixed-witness estimates and the primitive genus estimates enter separately in the uniform row bounds.

How many flag classes can one fixed sublattice support?

Fix a base flag, a row lattice Λ and a Gram class Z in the common frame. Let r be its isotropic rank, k the dimension of its definite complement, f the number of conjugate pairs of embeddings of the CM field E, and N = T(u)f for the base word u. Fix P inside the definite row lattice L₀, of rank k−s over E after taking its span, with 1 ≤ s ≤ k. A term flag belongs to this count if it satisfies the row and frame conditions, its cross-Gram matrix is equivalent to Z by integral triangular changes with diagonal one, and its visible lattice contains P. Count classes under the integral unipotent transformations and allowed frame changes.

The uniform theorem assumes the standing and numerical conditions on the two words, a standard base flag, an admissible row, a relevant Gram cell and Cℓ ≥ 1. For a sufficiently large height parameter C, write HZ for the prescribed height of Z. Choose Δ ≥ 1 and H with det P ≤ Δ, HZ ≤ H and Δ ≤ H³. Saturation in L₀ gives [sat(P)∶P] ≤ Δ since the saturated lattice has determinant at least one. If the flag set is nonempty, an actual term proves the Gram invariant is nonzero. The cell supplies a nonzero maximal minor of the first r rows. The proof uses Z itself as its bounded representative. The common budget Q = HZ² bounds the absolute norm of that minor, the product of the absolute values of the Gram invariant over the selected complex embeddings, and the specified different-ideal norm.

How many ways can P lift? An isometry fixing the base frame puts the row in split form and preserves the definite lattice. Every original class has a representative with exact cross-Gram matrix Z in the split calculation. A lift of P there has the form p ↦ p + φ(p), with φ valued in the isotropic lattice and the graph orthogonal to the moving frame. In one isotropic coordinate a linear form on P costs at most [sat(P)∶P] representatives beyond the restrictions of forms on its saturation. Forms on the primitive saturation contribute at most N² modulo pairings with L₀. Taking all r coordinates gives at most (N²Δ)r lift representatives. Frame-fixing integral unipotents move each graph into this list. Summing over the list gives an upper bound even if a class admits more than one graph.

What remains once the lift is fixed? Put S₀ = L₀ ∩ P⊥, a definite lattice of rank s. A nonzero ideal I of norm at most M = Δ²N² satisfies I S₀∨ ⊆ S₀, where the dual is taken in its span. Let Y be the top r rows of the exact Gram matrix and let a be its chosen nonzero maximal minor. The moving frame gives a tuple of perpendicular components w₀,…,wᵣ in S₀∨. Write y for their linear combination with the signed maximal minors of Y as coefficients. Its squared length satisfies T(u)⟨y,y⟩ = G, the fixed nonzero Gram invariant. For a nonzero difference in the dual lattice, integrality after multiplication by I bounds the product of its embedded squared lengths below by 1/N(I). Packing points separated in this way gives at most 9sf(MQ)s possible y. For a fixed y, the difference of two tuples has cofactor combination zero. The adjugate of the chosen submatrix expresses this difference as a combination of the rows of Y with coefficients in ((a)I)−1S₀. Reducing those r coefficients modulo S₀ costs at most (MQ)sr. The integral changes are realized by unipotents preserving the lifted graph.

With the perpendicular tuple fixed, the remaining difference is an r × (r+1) matrix x in the isotropic coordinates satisfying x*Y + Y*x = 0, where * denotes conjugate transpose. The centre acts by x ↦ x + cY for integral skew-Hermitian c. Clearing denominators with the minor a and the r-th power of the extended different bounds the number of residual representatives by Q2r². Every flag class occurs in the image of the perpendicular and isotropic representative sets. Multiplying their sizes is therefore sufficient.

A rank-one coordinate calculation over the Gaussian integers

Take S₀ = ℤ[i] with its usual norm, r = s = 1, Y = (t,0) for an integer t ≥ 1, and impose |t w₁|² = t². There are four choices for w₁, the Gaussian units. Row translations add tv to w₀, so its real and imaginary parts each give one residue modulo t. This yields exactly 4t² perpendicular classes. For integral isotropic corrections the skew equation forces x = (ij,0) with j ∈ ℤ. Integral skew scalars act by adding (itℓ,0), leaving t classes. At t = 2 this gives 16 perpendicular representatives and 2 isotropic representatives. The 32 ordered pairs describe the two coordinate equations in this model. To obtain an admissible flag one would also have to realize the pair in a single integral row with the prescribed base, Gram matrix and level.

The bound used in the row sum. Combining the graph count and the two residual counts first gives the following upper bound on the number of classes over P.

(N²Δ)r · 9sf(Δ²N²Q)s+sr · Q2r².

The standing height estimate gives N² ≤ HZ ≤ H. Since Δ ≤ H³ and Q ≤ H², the middle base is at most H6+1+2 = H⁹. The last factor is at most H4r². With H ≥ 1 one may enlarge this last exponent to 16r², obtaining

Bₛ = N2r Δr 9sf H9s + 9sr + 16r².

The generic row uses s = 1, Δ = max(G,1) for its determinant cutoff G, and H = HZ. The paired row uses a common determinant allowance and height for the two Gram classes. It applies Bₛ to each flag at the same P, then uses Bₛ² before summing over witnesses. The primitive genus mean then counts candidate witnesses of corank one. The ordered-pair estimate uses a mean allowing higher corank.

How often does a primitive hyperplane occur across the rows?

The fixed-witness estimate bounds the number of flags once their witness lattice is given. To average this bound we also need to count witnesses. After saturation the arithmetic input for one generic flag concerns primitive hyperplanes of exact determinant. Fix the frame and the word in the standing unramified CM datum. Its prime Tu is at least three and splits completely in the CM field E. The definite complement has dimension k ≥ 3. Write j = k−1 and f = [E∶ℚ]/2. For a row lattice L and an integer d ≥ 1, count the E-hyperplanes U for which the restriction to P = L ∩ U has |P∨/P| = d². Call this count Nd(L). Intersecting with the whole field hyperplane is what makes P primitive. Submodules of finite index in P have already been accounted for at saturation.

Why average over a genus? A genus collects lattices that are isometric at every completion. The count above is invariant under isometries. For a nonempty set of row representatives choose one complement lattice L₀. In its genus take one representative L per isometry class, and write a(L) = 1/|Aut(L)| and m = ∑ a(L). Apply the row-to-genus comparison first with the observable Nd, then with the constant observable one. The common row multiplicity cancels. With wΛ the row weights, the exact identity is

m ∑Λ wΛNd(LΛ) = (∑Λ wΛ) ∑[L] a(L)Nd(L).

Count the marked pairs in the other order. For a fixed lattice its finite automorphism group permutes the marked hyperplanes. Each orbit contributes its size divided by |Aut(L)|, which is the reciprocal order of the subgroup fixing the pair. This lets us first choose a rational isometry class of hyperplanes and then count the lattices meeting that hyperplane with the prescribed discriminant. The proof covers all possible marked pairs by its subspace representatives, so this second operation yields an upper bound.

Check both counts in one Gaussian lattice

Take the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]³. A primitive normal vector v determines U = v⊥, and four unit multiples give the same hyperplane. Put d = ⟨v,v⟩. Primitivity gives a vector w pairing to one with v. A basis of P followed by w is a basis of the full lattice. The squared length of the projection of w onto the normal line is 1/d. Factoring the Gram determinant of that basis thus gives 1 = det Gram(P)/d. The Gaussian index of the dual quotient, counted as a finite abelian group, is the absolute norm of this determinant, namely d².

At d = 3 the three coordinate norms are 1,1,1 or 0,1,2 up to permutation. In the first case the four phases per coordinate give 4³/4 = 16 hyperplanes. In the second there are 6 orders, four phases for the norm-one entry and four for the norm-two entry, giving 6·4²/4 = 24. Every integral isometry permutes the three coordinate axes and assigns a Gaussian unit to each, so the group has order 6·4³ = 384. The two stabilizers have orders 24 and 16. Counting marks at the lattice gives 40/384. Counting by orbits gives 1/24 + 1/16, the same 5/48. This example checks the change of order for one ambient lattice.

What is left when a hyperplane is fixed? Split the space orthogonally into U and a line. A lattice L gives a pair of intersections, one in each factor. Put t = Tuf. In this genus the ambient discriminant module is isomorphic over 𝒪E to 𝒪E/(Tu). One generator suffices over that ring. As an additive group it has t² elements and Tu kills every element. The hyperplane intersection has discriminant order d². The line intersection has discriminant order between 1 and d²t². For fixed intersections the one-generator gluing estimate permits at most t²d² ambient lattices. The count therefore uses the product of two masses, one for each factor, multiplied by this gluing allowance.

Where does the determinant gain enter? Let Mj and M₁ be the standard lattice masses of ranks j and one, and set b = log₂ f. Using the sum over rational hyperplanes and the mass on the perpendicular line, the unnormalized marked mass is at most the following product. Its last factors come respectively from the subspace estimate, the gluing allowance and the summed line masses.

MjM₁ · dj+2+b · t²d² · (dt)2+b.

At the split prime the ambient genus mass is Mk(1 + Tu + ⋯ + Tuk−1)f. Keeping the last summand gives the lower bound Mktj. Dividing accounts for the factor (d/t)j in the row mean. The consecutive-rank mass comparison bounds Mj/Mk, and the rank-one bound contributes at most hE2f, where hE is the class number. Take a height H ≥ max(d,t). The remaining powers satisfy d4+bt²(dt)2+b ≤ H10+3b. Since H ≥ 1 the caller may use its stated exponent 11+3b. With rd(E) the root discriminant and v = rd(E)/2, the row-weighted sum is at most the sum of the row weights times

(d/t)k−1 · (eπ/(kv))kf · (2k√rd(E))f hE 2f · H11+3b.

The proof cancels the finite positive genus mass in the row identity. An empty row family satisfies the inequality directly. To return to flags, interchange the row sum and the finite determinant sum from saturation and apply this bound for each 1 ≤ d ≤ ⌊G⌋. A separate divisor-sum estimate absorbs the remaining powers and the fixed-witness allowance. For ordered pairs the possible corank is larger and the proof needs the mean for primitive sublattices of higher corank.

How many perpendicular line lattices can a fixed level distinguish?

The hyperplane estimate needs a smaller gluing allowance than one obtains by counting arbitrary submodules. Keep the orthogonal decomposition V = U ⊕ W, with U a hyperplane and W a line. Fix integral full intersections P ⊂ U and Q ⊂ W. Count full integral lattices L with precisely these intersections. Assume a nonzero algebraic integer T ∈ R = 𝒪E, kills L∨/L. The form is totally definite and the CM extension is unramified at finite places, as in the row count. Write q for the projection onto W.

The projection Q′ = qL can be larger than Q. To bound its possibilities, record its dual C in W. A vector of W pairs integrally with qL exactly when it pairs integrally with L, since it is orthogonal to U. Thus C = L∨ ∩ W. We have Q ⊂ C by integrality, and TC ⊂ L ∩ W = Q by the level. The label therefore satisfies

Q ⊆ C = (qL)∨ ⊆ T−1Q,   Q′ = C∨.

Every finite quotient between two lattices on a line is cyclic over R, by the rank-one case of the generator bound. Fix y generating T−1Q/Q. For each intermediate C, its quotient by Q has one generator, a multiple ry modulo Q. Replacing r by r + Ts adds an element of Q. All candidates are therefore covered by the |R/(T)| residues of r. This is N((T)), the absolute norm of the level ideal. The cyclic modules here are finite quotients. The line lattice Q itself can be a nonprincipal ideal in line coordinates.

Why does just one hyperplane residue finish the gluing?

Fix the label C of a candidate lattice. Its dual recovers the projected line lattice Q′. Choose once a vector yC generating Q′/Q. Because Q′ is the image of L, some a ∈ U makes a + yC ∈ L. Pairing this vector with P shows a ∈ P∨. Two choices for that lift differ in L ∩ U = P. The residue of a modulo P is therefore uniquely determined once L and the line generator have been chosen.

L = (P ⊕ Q) + R(a + yC).

Indeed the right side is contained in L. For the reverse inclusion, take x ∈ L. Subtract a suitable multiple of the chosen lift so that its line projection belongs to Q. Subtract that element of Q as well. What remains lies in P. This proves the identity even when Q′ = Q, in which case one may choose the zero generator. Counting the two labels now gives

# gluings ≤ N((T)) · |P∨/P| = t²d²  in the row.

Here the row field has degree 2f, T is its specified rational level prime, t = Tf and the hyperplane discriminant order is d². The argument uses the annihilator T and the one-dimensional perpendicular. Counting both discriminant modules by all possible generating tuples would lose this sharper exponent.

In the plane with Gram matrix diag(1,2), keep u = (1,1), w = (−2,1), P = Ru and Q = Rw. Take T = 2, which kills the ambient dual quotient. The projected lattice is Q′ = (1/3)Q. Because h(w,w) = 6, its dual is C = (1/2)Q. A generator for Q′/Q is w/3, with lift (w−u)/3 = (−1,0). Together with (1,1) this lift generates R². The two data used by the proof are the line label (1/2)Q and the hyperplane residue −u/3 modulo P. In this example Q′ itself is outside the level interval, since w/3 does not lie in (1/2)Q. Dualizing the projected lattice before counting is essential.

Which sublattices of a line survive a discriminant cutoff?

Fix the rational line W perpendicular to one hyperplane. The bound on the perpendicular discriminant allows several orders for the lattice Q = L ∩ W. To sum over those possibilities, first keep a containing integral lattice A in W fixed. Let n(Q) = |Q∨/Q| and let X be a positive integer. Which full sublattices satisfy n(Q) ≤ X²?

Choose a nonzero vector in W as coordinate and write R for the integers of E. The coefficient modules of A and Q are fractional ideals J and I with I ⊆ J. Their quotient ideal 𝔞 = IJ−1 is integral and Q = 𝔞A. This works even when A has no single generator over R. Multiplying I and J by the same denominator makes them integral. The index is the ratio of their absolute norms and the common denominator cancels. Applying the index-square identity then determines the discriminant order from 𝔞. Milne, theorem 3.32 on invariant factors[35] and proposition 4.2 on relative index[36].

[A ∶ Q] = N(𝔞),   n(Q) = N(𝔞)² n(A).

Since n(A) ≥ 1, it suffices to count ideals with N(𝔞) ≤ X. If D = [E∶ℚ], the count by prime factors gives at most klog₂ D ideals of norm k. There are at most X possible integers k, hence at most X1+log₂ D candidates inside A. This one sum includes all permitted discriminant orders.

Where does the first new lattice enter? Take the finite-unramified example E = ℚ(ζ₁₂) and the standard line A = R with Gram matrix (1). Here n(A) = 1. The integer ring is generated by ζ₁₂, whose polynomial is x⁴−x²+1. It reduces to (x²+x+1)² modulo 2 and (x²+1)² modulo 3. Both quadratics are irreducible in their respective residue fields. Thus there is no ideal of norm 2 or 3, and precisely one of norm 4, the kernel of reduction to the quadratic residue field at 2. Indeed an ideal of norm 4 must be prime, since a proper factor would have norm 2. Inside this fixed A, the bound X = 3 retains only A. Increasing X to 4 adds exactly one sublattice, at discriminant order 16. Milne, theorem 6.4 on cyclotomic integers[37].

What is the total mass of the eligible perpendicular lattices?

Now let the integral lattice vary over the entire fixed Hermitian line W, totally definite over a CM field of degree 2f and unramified over its real subfield at all finite places. For each order n, write mW(n) for the sum of 1/|Aut(Q)| over the isometry classes with n(Q) = n. Each Q has a maximal integral enlargement A. Its automorphism group permutes these enlargements. By counting the marked pairs (Q, A), we count the mass of each Q at least once. Grouping the pairs by A instead gives

∑1 ≤ n ≤ X² mW(n) ≤ ∑[A] maximal #{Q ⊆ A ∶ n(Q) ≤ X²} / |Aut(A)|.

The numerator counts actual full sublattices in each representative A. Partitioning them into Aut(A)-orbits gives the reciprocal stabilizer weights of the marked pairs. All maximal A in W belong to one genus by the local classification. In the maximal-lattice mass formula, a bad inert place of residue size q contributes (q+1)/(q+1) = 1 in rank one. The genus therefore has the same mass M₁ as the genus of the standard orthonormal line, even when W has a different determinant class. Multiplying this mass by the bound for one A gives the theorem, since 1 + log₂(2f) = 2 + log₂ f.

∑1 ≤ n ≤ X² mW(n) ≤ M₁ X2 + log₂ f.
Can one lattice really have two maximal enlargements?

Keep E = ℚ(ζ₁₂) and write ζ = ζ₁₂. Put α = 2−ζ, β = 2−ζ⁻¹ and γ = α/β. Conjugation exchanges α and β, so γ has Hermitian norm one. Thus R and γR are isometric self-dual lattices and both are maximal. They both contain Q = αR, since α = γβ. To see that the two enlargements are distinct, the norm of α is Φ₁₂(2) = 13. In R/(α) = 𝔽₁₃, the images of ζ and ζ⁻¹ are 2 and 7. Thus β has nonzero residue, so the ideals (α) and (β) differ. This rules out γR = R. Every scalar stabilizing Q fixes R as well, by cancelling α. Consequently the two choices of maximal enlargement give distinct marked pairs above the same unmarked lattice. Its discriminant order is 13².

In the row, the hyperplane lattice has discriminant order d² and the ambient lattice has order t². The perpendicular order is at most d²t². Taking X = dt gives the line factor M₁(dt)2+log₂ f in the marked hyperplane mass. The separate gluing factor counts the ways to put two chosen intersection lattices back together.

Which rational hyperplanes share the determinant budget?

Fix a positive integer d. We want the sum of the lattice masses on rational hyperplanes that admit an integral full lattice of discriminant order d². The ambient Hermitian space is totally positive definite over a CM field E, unramified at finite places over its real field F. Write R = 𝒪E, D = [E ∶ ℚ] = 2f, λ = log₂ D, and j ≥ 1 for the hyperplane dimension. A rational hyperplane is counted up to the E-linear isometries of the ambient space. Its lattices are counted up to isometry within the hyperplane, with weight 1/|Aut(P)|. In the row count the chosen lattice will be the intersection with an ambient lattice. Here we sum over all qualifying lattice classes inside each hyperplane.

Take an integral lattice P of the required order in a hyperplane U and enlarge it to a maximal integral lattice A in U. Let S be its set of bad prime ideals of R. At a bad prime 𝔓 the dual quotient has one residue line. If q𝔓 is the residue size of the underlying place of F, the order of that line is q𝔓². Let m be the product of these q𝔓 and i the additive index of P in A. The local classification and the index-square identity give the first two equalities below. Taking positive square roots gives the third. Bad primes and the dual quotient · Index-square identity.

|A∨/A| = m²,   d² = m²i²,   d = mi.

The set S determines the rational isometry class of U at this rank by the classification and extension theorem. Choose one representative for each realized set. Several sets may have the same product m. To count them, fix a rational prime p dividing m > 1. Some q𝔓 in the product is divisible by p, so 𝔓 lies above p. There are at most D choices for 𝔓 by the prime decomposition formula. Removing it leaves product m/q𝔓 ≤ m/2. At m = 1 only the empty set occurs. Induction bounds the number at m by D(m/2)λ = mλ. Counting a set by more than one removal only increases this upper bound. Extension to the ambient space · J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 3.34[38].

How much mass can one set of bad primes carry?

For one representative U let μU(d²) be the sum of 1/|Aut(P)| over integral lattice classes of discriminant order d² in U. Write Mj for the genus mass of the standard orthonormal lattice of rank j. All maximal lattices in U lie in one genus. The maximal-lattice mass bound gives that genus mass at most Mj(m²)j/2 = Mjmj. For each maximal lattice the number of sublattices of index i is at most ij+λ. Marking a maximal enlargement counts each smaller lattice with its automorphism weight at least once. The maximal genus and its local density factors · The fixed-index count and the weights of marked pairs.

Keeping i = d/m in this calculation gives a different allowance for each value of m. Put B = Mjdj+λ. Then

μU(d²) ≤ Mjmj(d/m)j+λ = B/mλ.

Two hyperplanes at the same order. Write E = ℚ(ζ₁₂), where ζ₁₂ is a primitive twelfth root of unity. Its real subfield is ℚ(√3), and the absolute discriminants 144 and 12 give relative discriminant of norm one. Give E³ its standard Hermitian form. Frobenius at 11 takes ζ₁₂ to ζ₁₂11 = ζ₁₂−1, so it is complex conjugation. Hence 11 splits into two places of the real subfield, each inert in E. Each of the two primes of R over 11 has absolute norm 121. Milne, §§2–3 on discriminants, Theorem 6.4 and Example 8.18 on cyclotomic fields[38].

In the plane spanned by e₁,e₂, take P = 𝔓e₁ ⊕ Re₂ for either prime 𝔓 above 11. Its index in the unimodular coordinate lattice is 121, so (m,i) = (1,121). For the second plane take e₁ and v = 3e₂ + (1+i)e₃, where i² = −1 in E. The full lattice they generate has Gram matrix diag(1,11), since 9 + |1+i|² = 11. At each place above 11 the dual permits a denominator 11 only in the second coordinate. A vector using that denominator in lowest terms has squared length of valuation −1, since the first coordinate is integral. Such a vector cannot enter an integral enlargement. The dual quotient has one residue line there. At every other finite place it is unimodular. Thus (m,i) = (121,1). Both lattices have discriminant order 121². They witness the two orbit classes before any ambient intersection or level is prescribed. With j = 2 and λ = 2, the respective bounds for the full masses of their rational isometry classes are B and B/121², where B = M₂ · 121⁴. The two local maximal lattices.

Fix a divisor m of d. At most mλ sets of bad primes contribute, and each contributes at most B/mλ. Their total at this one divisor is at most B. There are at most d positive divisors. The empty set at m = 1 already accounts for every admissible rational class with a unimodular maximal lattice at this rank. Taking one representative of each realized orbit gives

Σ[U] μU(d²) ≤ ∑m∣d B ≤ dB = Mjdj+2+log₂f.

The last exponent uses λ = log₂(2f) = 1 + log₂ f. The saving comes from the index d/m in the fixed-index count. Replacing that index by d before summing would discard the denominator that pays for the possible sets of bad primes.

Return to the row at its completely split level prime T, with t = Tf. Marking a hyperplane in an ambient lattice counts each pair with weight the reciprocal of its stabilizer order. Once its rational hyperplane is fixed, the perpendicular is a line. Its integral intersection has discriminant order at most (dt)². The summed line mass is therefore at most M₁(dt)2+log₂f, uniformly in the chosen hyperplane. For any fixed pair of intersection lattices at most t²d² gluings give an ambient lattice. Both bounds can be taken outside the sum over [U]. Multiplication by the displayed hyperplane mass gives the marked numerator. Division by the ambient genus mass then gives the row mean. How many common witnesses can two flags have?

Two flags on the same row may share a witness of smaller dimension than a hyperplane. First fix its codimension s in the definite complement of dimension k. For each row we want to count the possible witnesses, with the row weights from the genus averaging identity. The saturation argument reduces this question to primitive lattices at each exact determinant. A primitive lattice here has the form P = L ∩ U for an E-subspace U. Write Ns,d(L) for the number of these subspaces with dimension j = k − s and |P∨/P| = d².

Theorem (primitive sublattices in a row genus). Fix the integral complement lattice of a row. Its Hermitian form is totally definite of rank k over a CM field E of degree 2f, unramified over its real subfield at the finite places. Its dual quotient is isomorphic over 𝒪E to 𝒪E/(T), with T ≥ 3 a rational prime splitting completely in E. Put t = Tf, and let Mr be the standard Hermitian lattice mass in rank r. The frame has a scale b ≥ 1, a rank parameter m ≥ 2, and a positive constant cl for which log rd(E) ≤ (log b)/cl. Fix any 0 < c₀ ≤ cl. The bound holds for every real C ≥ max(16, 1/c₀), every H ≥ bCm²f, every integer d ≥ 1, and every 2 ≤ s ≤ k. If mgen = ∑[L] 1/|Aut(L)| is the mass of the row genus, then

(1/mgen) ∑[L] Ns,d(L)/|Aut(L)| ≤ (d/t)k (dt)Cs + C log f Ξs.

When j ≥ 2, the remaining factor is Ξs = MsMj/Mk. When j is 0 or 1, it is (Ck)kf(Ht)Ck. The distinction comes from how we count the subspaces.

Proof for two factors of rank at least two. Mark a subspace in each lattice. A mark with orbit of size q contributes q/|Aut(L)|, the reciprocal of the order of its stabilizer. We may therefore fix the subspace first and count the compatible lattices with these weights. Put n = d², X = nt² and λ = log₂(2f). Three estimates give the count.

  1. Rational subspaces. The rational subspace orbit bound covers every rank-j subspace admitting an integral lattice of discriminant order n by at most n1+λ rational isometry classes.
  2. Intersections. For a fixed subspace, the fixed-discriminant mass bound in rank r is Mra(r+λ)/2 at discriminant order a ≥ 1. The intersection in U has order n. In its perpendicular space the order lies between 1 and X, by the projection bound for complementary discriminants, with ambient order t². Thus the two masses are bounded respectively by Mjn(j+λ)/2 and MsX·X(s+λ)/2. The extra X allows every possible order of the second intersection.
  3. Gluing. A lattice can strictly contain the direct sum of its two intersections. For fixed intersections of orders n and a, the gluing bound permits at most (na)2s+1 ambient lattices here. The two generator bounds use cyclicity of the ambient discriminant module. The discriminant modules on the two sides can be generated by at most s+1 and s elements, respectively. An ambient lattice gives an intermediate submodule between the sum of the intersections and the sum of their duals. Here is the finite-module count. If a finite module Q over the ring of integers has g generators, each of its submodules also has at most g. At each prime supporting Q, lift the submodule to the free module of rank g over the discrete valuation ring. Its preimage is free of rank at most g, so its images generate the submodule locally. Pad each list with zeros and combine corresponding entries across the primary components by the Chinese remainder theorem. Hence every submodule is generated by some ordered g-tuple in Q, and there are at most |Q|g of them. The Stacks Project, Lemma 15.22.11 on modules over a discrete valuation ring[39] · Lemma 10.15.4 on simultaneous residues[40]. Finally a ≤ X bounds its base by nX.

Multiply the three estimates. Keep nj/2, replace the remaining factors of n by X, and use (nX)2s+1 ≤ X4s+2. The exponent of X is (1+λ) + λ/2 + 1 + (s+λ)/2 + 4s+2. Consequently the unnormalized marked mass is at most

MjMs dj(dt)9s+8+4λ.

The split-prime genus mass is at least Mktk−1. Dividing leaves a numerator djt over tk. Increase dj to dk and absorb t in one further power of dt. Since λ ≤ 1 + 2 log f, we have 9s+9+4λ ≤ Cs+C log f for s ≥ 2 and C ≥ 16. This gives the stated mean.

On a line of discriminant order n, the rank-one short-vector bound supplies a nonzero lattice vector whose squared length at every embedding is at most B = rd(E)n1/(2f), where rd is the root discriminant. The vector determines the line. The ambient packing estimate gives at most (1+2√B)2kf choices, hence at most (9 rd(E))kfdk because B ≥ 1. This bound holds for each lattice. Indeed f log rd(E) ≤ (f/c₀) log b ≤ Cm²f log b ≤ log H, so rd(E)f ≤ H. Factoring out (d/t)k leaves at most the announced Ξs.

Count the first two determinants in a four-dimensional Gaussian lattice

Use the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]⁴. A saturated plane has a Gaussian basis u, v. Put pab = uavb − ubva. Its Gram determinant d is the sum of the six squared absolute values of these minors, by Cauchy–Binet. The dual quotient has order d². A single nonzero minor forces the field plane to be the corresponding coordinate plane, whose saturated lattice has determinant 1. There are six such planes. Andrew Putman, The Cauchy–Binet formula, Theorem 0.1[41]

At determinant 2, precisely two minors must therefore be units. Their index pairs share an index, since expanding the definitions gives p₁₂p₃₄ − p₁₃p₂₄ + p₁₄p₂₃ = 0. Disjoint pairs would leave a single nonzero product. With common index a, the plane is spanned by ea and eb + εec with b < c and ε one of the four Gaussian units. The two coefficients of value one along a and b show that these vectors already generate the whole intersection. There are 4 choices of a, 3 unordered pairs {b,c}, and 4 phases, or 48 planes. They form a single orbit under the 4!·4⁴ = 6,144 coordinate isometries, so their contribution for this lattice is 48/6,144 = 1/128. This calculation illustrates the marked mass for one lattice. The genus theorem uses the split-prime hypotheses stated above.

Why mark a maximal lattice before counting smaller ones?

Fix a totally positive definite Hermitian space of rank r ≥ 1 over the CM field E of degree D over ℚ. Assume E is unramified at finite places over its real subfield. For an integral full lattice L let L∨ be the lattice of vectors pairing integrally with all of L. Write n = |L∨/L|. The quantity to bound is the sum of 1/|Aut(L)| over isometry classes with this fixed order. Positive definiteness at infinity makes each stabilizer finite. A change of coordinates may identify many of the smaller lattices, so we keep these weights throughout.

Every integral lattice L is contained in a maximal integral lattice A. Indeed any integral enlargement lies between L and L∨, whose quotient is finite. If i = [A:L] is the cardinality of the quotient, duality gives [L∨:A∨] = i. To check the index identity locally, diagonalize the inclusion of the two lattices over the discrete valuation ring. In the dual bases the corresponding inclusion has the conjugate elementary divisors. Conjugate prime ideals have equal norms, so multiplication over the finite places gives the same global index. The chain L ⊆ A ⊆ A∨ ⊆ L∨ gives

|L∨/L| = [A:L]² |A∨/A| = i² n₀.

The local classification of maximal integral Hermitian lattices applies here. In this fixed space they are all in one genus, meaning that at every finite place there is a local isometry between any two. The places with a nontrivial dual quotient are determined by the determinant of the ambient form. At other places the maximal lattices are unimodular. At a bad place the classification compares two maximal lattices by extending each to a unimodular lattice in one extra dimension and then aligning and removing the added line by an integral isometry. In particular n₀ is common to the maximal lattices. If any L with order n exists, its index in every maximal lattice containing it is therefore the same positive integer i.

Mark the pair (L,A). For a fixed L, its finite automorphism group permutes its maximal enlargements. An orbit of b marks contributes b/|Aut(L)| to the pair mass, by orbit–stabilizer. Since there is at least one mark, forgetting A gives the original mass as a lower bound on the pair mass. Counting pairs in the other order gives an upper bound. Over each maximal representative A, there are at most as many marks as sublattices of additive index i, each counted with weight 1/|Aut(A)| before passing to orbits.

How many sublattices have that index? We claim that a projective rank-r module over the integers of E has at most irDΩ(i) submodules of index i, where Ω counts rational prime factors with multiplicity. Index one has just the module itself. For i > 1 fix a rational prime p dividing it. The p-primary part of each quotient of cardinality i has a simple quotient over some prime ideal 𝔭 above p. This puts the submodule inside an intermediate kernel with quotient the residue field of size q = pf. Modulo 𝔭 the original module has dimension r because it is locally free. There are (qr−1)/(q−1) possible kernels, one for each nonzero functional up to scalar. This is at most qr.

Each intermediate kernel is again a torsion-free rank-r lattice over a Dedekind domain and hence projective. Apply induction inside it at index i/q. For any given 𝔭 the product of the two bounds is at most irDΩ(i)−1, since f ≥ 1. There are at most D primes above p. Adding the bounds proves the claim even when different intermediate kernels count the same submodule. Since 2Ω(i) ≤ i, the number is at most ir+log₂D.

Count and mass in a split example. In ℤ[i]² with the standard form, consider sublattices of index 5. There are two primes above 5. At each one the possible kernels are the six lines of 𝔽₅², giving twelve sublattices. Each has discriminant order 25 by the index square. The automorphisms of the standard lattice permute the two coordinate lines and may multiply each by one of the four Gaussian units, giving 2·4² = 32 automorphisms. The pairs lying over this one maximal class thus have mass 12/32 = 3/8. The extension ℚ(i)/ℚ ramifies at 2. Here the example tests the marking and index identities at the split prime 5.

The genus mass at a fixed discriminant order

Let cE,r be the genus mass of the standard orthonormal lattice of rank r over E. The standard lattice may lie in another Hermitian space. The maximal-lattice mass formula has the same constant cE,r for all totally positive definite spaces of this rank. The distinction between spaces enters through the factors at bad places. More precisely, a bad prime ideal of E is inert over a place of the real field of residue size q. The maximal lattice has a one-dimensional residue defect there, so the place contributes q² to n₀ and

λq = (qr − (−1)r)/(q + 1)

to its genus mass relative to cE,r. At unimodular places the factor is 1. In the local density formula the exceptional Jordan component has length one. Its isometries are the norm-one elements in the quadratic residue field, a group of size q+1. This gives the denominator. The last factor in the standard rank-r unitary density is 1−(−1)r/qr, which gives the numerator after scaling by qr. The global mass formula and this local classification are the inputs in this comparison. W. T. Gan, J. P. Hanke and J.-K. Yu, On an exact mass formula of Shimura, Propositions 4.4 and 4.5, p. 110[42].

For q ≥ 2 the local factor is positive and at most qr, since even qr+1 is at most (q+1)qr. Multiplying gives a maximal genus mass at most cE,r n₀r/2. Put λ = log₂D. The marked-pair count now bounds the desired mass by cE,r ir+λ n₀r/2. Because n₀ ≥ 1 and λ ≥ 0, we may add λ/2 to its exponent and use n = i²n₀. We obtain

Σ[L], |L∨/L|=n 1/|Aut(L)| ≤ cE,r n(r+log₂D)/2.

An empty set of lattices contributes zero. In the primitive-sublattice count the formula is used twice. For a fixed j-dimensional subspace U the discriminant order of its intersection lattice is exactly n. For the perpendicular space of dimension s the order lies among the integers from 1 to X = nN₀, where N₀ is the order of the ambient discriminant module. For the row at a completely split rational prime T, we have N₀ = t² with t = Tf and [E:ℚ] = 2f. The second application therefore costs at most X times the rank-s bound evaluated at X. The other factors in the row estimate count subspaces and gluings.

Where can a maximal integral lattice fail to be self-dual?

Fix a nondegenerate Hermitian form h on an E-vector space V, with conjugation in the first variable. The quadratic CM extension E/F is unramified at every finite place. A lattice M is integral if all its pairings belong to 𝒪E. Its dual M∨ consists of the vectors pairing integrally with M. In the marked enlargement count, we need to compare two maximal integral lattices in this same space at one finite place v at a time. Write q for the size of the residue field of F there.

Maximality can be tested locally. An integral enlargement gives a submodule of the finite module M∨/M on which the pairing modulo 𝒪E vanishes. Conversely the inverse image of such a submodule is integral. The primary components over different places of F pair to zero, since their annihilators are coprime and conjugation preserves each fibre over F. Thus an enlargement found at one place gives a global enlargement by taking zero in the other components.

At a split place the two factors of the completed coefficient ring are exchanged by conjugation. Write the completed lattice as A ⊕ B. The form pairs the two summands perfectly over the fraction fields and vanishes on each summand separately. Integrality gives B ⊆ A∨, where the dual here lives in the other summand. Replacing B by A∨ preserves integrality. Maximality forces equality, so the whole lattice is self-dual.

At an inert place write R = 𝒪E,𝔭, take a uniformizer π from the real field, and write v(π) = 1. In an orthogonal R-basis the norms are πbⱼuⱼ with bⱼ ≥ 0 and uⱼ fixed units. Here is why diagonalization also works above 2. Divide the Gram matrix by the smallest power of π occurring in its entries. The reduction is a nonzero Hermitian form over 𝔽q². If all diagonal values vanished, evaluating on x + t y for all residue scalars t would give Tr(t h(x,y)) = 0 for every t. The trace pairing of the separable quadratic residue extension is nondegenerate. Thus some vector has unit norm in the scaled form. Lift it, subtract its orthogonal projection from the remaining vectors and continue on its complement. The Stacks Project, lemma 9.20.7 on the trace pairing[43].

If bⱼ ≥ 2, adjoining the basis vector divided by π preserves integrality. If two exponents equal 1, write their basis vectors as x, y with norms πu, πu′ respectively. Choose a unit c with residue norm −u/u′. Indeed the residue norm sends a to aq+1. Its kernel has at most q + 1 elements by the polynomial root bound. Its image in 𝔽q× therefore has at least (q² − 1)/(q + 1) = q − 1 elements, hence fills that group. Then (x + c y)/π pairs integrally with the lattice and with itself, giving a strict enlargement. Thus a maximal lattice has either all unit norms in this basis or exactly one norm of valuation 1. In the latter case that basis vector x, with a = h(x,x), supplies the entire defect.

M∨/M = R·(x/a + M) ≃ R/πR,   |M∨/M| = q²  locally.

The bad inert places are the ones where the valuation of a Gram determinant is odd. Indeed a change of basis multiplies the determinant by the norm of the determinant of the change, whose valuation is even. In the orthogonal basis the valuation is the sum of the exponents just computed. This identifies the bad places for both maximal lattices before choosing a comparison map. The local classification also appears in W. T. Gan, J. P. Hanke and J.-K. Yu, On an exact mass formula of Shimura, §3, pp. 105–107[44].

How can one extra line absorb the defect?

At a bad inert place let M now denote its localization. Choose the same fixed-field uniformizer π for both lattices. Give a new vector e norm π, orthogonal to V. The direct sum M ⊕ R e has two defects of length one. We glue them by adjoining a single vector. With x and a as above, choose c ∈ R× such that c̄c ≡ −π/a modulo π and put

w = (c x + e)/π,   L = M + R w.

We have e = πw − c x and h(w,e) = 1. The pairings of w with M are integral because h(M,x) ⊆ πR. Its norm is (c̄c a + π)/π². The norm congruence makes the numerator divisible by π². The change from a basis of M together with e to the same basis together with w has determinant 1/π. The old Gram determinant had valuation two, so the new one has valuation zero. An integral Gram matrix with unit determinant has an integral inverse, proving that L is self-dual. Its intersection with V is exactly M, since the coefficient of e in m + r w is r/π. We can therefore recover M once the distinguished vector e is identified.

A dyadic calculation. Take the unramified quadratic extension ℚ₂(ζ₃)/ℚ₂ and its ring of integers R, with residue field 𝔽₄. On the line R x put h(x,x) = 2. Its dual is ½R x. A vector in the dual outside R x has norm of valuation −1, so the lattice is maximal. Take π = 2 and c = 1, whose residue norm equals −1 in 𝔽₂. With w = (x + e)/2 the Gram matrix on (x,w) has rows (2,1) and (1,1). Its determinant is 1 and e = 2w − x pairs to 1 with w. This calculation uses division by the uniformizer only for the new vector in the extended space.

How does the isometry return to the original space?

At every place where both lattices are self-dual, apply the unimodular isometry theorem directly. In the rational formulation it gives an E-linear isometry identifying the two localizations at that place. At a split place the localization allows denominators from the real integers away from v, so both conjugate primes are kept. At a bad inert place apply this theorem to the two self-dual extensions L, L′ just constructed in V ⊕ E e. The constructions can be made in the localized rational space. The coefficients lift from the residue field, and clearing denominators away from the place gives a full global lattice with the prescribed localization. The isometry g taking L to L′ may move e. The vectors p = ge and y = e both have norm π in L′ and each pairs to 1 with a vector of L′.

Correcting the distinguished vector. For u ∈ L′ and a unit b with b + b̄ = h(u,u), the map

S(z) = z − b−1h(u,z)u

is an integral isometry. Expanding the two pairings gives cancellation by the trace identity for b, and replacing b by b̄ gives the inverse. Put d = π − h(y,p). When d is a unit, take u = p − y and b = d. Then h(u,p) = d and S p = y.

Otherwise choose u with both h(u,p) and h(u,y) units. Use the two witnesses pairing to 1. If neither works on the other vector, their sum works on both. Choose θ ∈ R whose residue differs from its conjugate and put δ = θ − θ̄, a unit. The scalar b = (θ/δ)h(u,u) has the required trace. If it reduces to zero, add δ, whose trace is zero. Now the new difference π − h(y,S p) equals d + b−1h(u,p)h(y,u). Its second summand is a unit, so the previous step sends S p to y. This proves the required correction even in residue characteristic two.

Checking the second case above 2. In the example take p = −e, y = e and u = w. Then d = 4, h(u,p) = −1 and h(y,u) = 1. With θ = ζ₃ and θ² + θ + 1 = 0 we have δ = 1 + 2θ and b = θ/δ = (2 + θ)/3. Thus b−1 = 1 − θ. The new difference is 4 − (1 − θ) = 3 + θ, which reduces to the nonzero element 1 + θ in 𝔽₄. The second isometry now has a unit denominator.

Composing the correction with g fixes e. It preserves e⊥ = V because h(e,v + t e) = πt. Restriction therefore takes L ∩ V to L′ ∩ V, the two original localized lattices. Repeating this argument at each finite place proves that the two maximal lattices belong to one genus. The isometry may depend on the place. This is the genus used in the weighted count of marked pairs.
