Which ideal records the isometry class of a rational subspace?

The row count first chooses a subspace, then counts its possible intersection lattices. At this first stage two subspaces count as one choice if an E-linear isometry of the ambient Hermitian space carries one onto the other. Fix their dimension j and a positive integer n. We want to cover all subspaces U that admit an integral lattice L of discriminant order |L∨/L| = n. The ambient form is positive definite at every infinite place. The CM field E is quadratic over its real subfield F and unramified at all finite places of F.

Enlarge L to a maximal integral lattice M inside U. A prime ideal 𝔓 of 𝒪E is bad for M if its dual quotient is nonzero there. By the local structure of maximal lattices, this happens only above inert places. The quotient at such a prime is a line over the residue field. Multiplying these orders and applying the index-square identity gives

𝔞 = ∏𝔓 bad 𝔓,   N(𝔞) = |M∨/M|,   n = N(𝔞)[M ∶ L]².

Here N is the absolute ideal norm and the index counts elements of the additive quotient. The empty product gives the unit ideal. The ideal retains the identity of every bad prime by unique factorization of ideals. Its integer norm bounds the size of the label. Two different prime ideals can have the same norm.

Why does this information determine the rational space? Choose an E-basis of U, let β be its Gram determinant, and consider a second space of the same dimension with Gram determinant β′. Both determinants belong to F and are positive at every real embedding. At an inert prime a basis change multiplies the determinant by a norm, whose valuation is even. In a basis of a maximal lattice at that place the valuation is zero for a unimodular lattice and one for a lattice with a defect line. Thus equal bad ideals say exactly that β and β′ have the same valuation parity at each inert place.

The following consequence of Landherr’s theorem is used here. A totally positive definite Hermitian space over this E that admits a unimodular lattice contains an orthonormal E-basis. Indeed, at every inert place the Gram determinant in a local integral basis of a unimodular lattice is a unit, and units are local norms in an unramified quadratic extension. Passing to any rational basis multiplies this determinant by another norm. At a split place the local space is determined by its rank. At every real place the signature agrees with that of the identity matrix. Landherr’s local-to-global classification therefore identifies the space with the standard space. The integral span of the resulting orthonormal basis can be a different lattice from the one we started with. B. H. Gross, Incoherent definite spaces and Shimura varieties, §3, Theorem 3.1[45].

Add the same Hermitian line of squared length β to each space. Their determinants become β² and ββ′. Both have even valuation at every inert place. Take a maximal integral lattice in each enlarged space. Such a lattice exists by clearing denominators in a basis and enlarging an integral lattice. The determinant test just proved rules out defects at every inert place. The split places are already unimodular. A finite dual quotient vanishing at every prime is zero, so both enlarged lattices are unimodular. The preceding consequence of Landherr gives an orthonormal basis for each enlarged space. Matching those bases gives an isometry between them. It remains to remove the common line.

How does an isometry of two subspaces move them inside the ambient space?

Witt extension in the definite case. In a finite-dimensional positive definite Hermitian space over E, any E-linear isometry between two subspaces extends to an isometry of the entire space. We give the construction because the argument uses it twice. Write h conjugate-linear in its first entry. If x and y have the same squared length and x ≠ y, put w = x − y and α = h(w,x). Equal lengths give h(w,w) = α + ᾱ. Positivity implies α ≠ 0. Define

R(z) = z − w · h(w,z)/α.

Substituting x gives y, and substituting a vector orthogonal to w fixes it. Expand h(Rz,Rt) − h(z,t). The coefficient of h(z,w)h(w,t) is (−ᾱ − α + h(w,w))/(ᾱα) = 0. Thus R preserves the form, so it is injective, hence bijective in finite dimension. To extend a specified subspace isometry, match the images of its basis vectors one at a time. The difference between the current and prescribed image of the next vector is orthogonal to all already matched images, since all their pairings agree. The displayed map makes the correction and fixes the earlier images. Equal vectors require no correction.

Apply this first in the enlarged target space. The isometry constructed from the two orthonormal bases can send the distinguished line generator somewhere else. Its image and the prescribed generator both have squared length β, so the correction sends one to the other. The resulting isometry carries the orthogonal complement of the source line onto the orthogonal complement of the target line. These complements are the two original spaces. Apply Witt extension a second time, now in the original ambient space V. It extends the resulting isometry between the two subspaces of V. This proves that all subspaces with the same bad ideal and rank lie in a single ambient rational orbit.

One orbit can meet the ambient lattice in different ways. In the standard plane over any such field, the unit vectors x = (1,0) and y = (3/5,4/5) each span a unimodular lattice on their own line. They give n = 1 and the unit ideal. The map above has matrix (1/5) times the matrix with rows (3,4) and (4,−3). It moves the first line onto the second. In the ambient lattice 𝒪E², however, the second line meets that lattice in 𝒪E(3,4). Indeed, if 3c and 4c are integral then c = 4c − 3c is integral. In the coordinate with unit vector y, the intersection is 5𝒪Ey. On the slice with rational coordinates its integer points are the multiples of (3,4), since the rational algebraic integers are precisely ℤ. Over 𝒪E it is the intersection module that the row argument counts after choosing a rational orbit.

How many rational subspace orbits can one discriminant order require?

Orbit bound. Write D = [E ∶ ℚ]. For fixed dimension j and n ≥ 1, at most n1+log₂D rational isometry orbits suffice to cover all subspaces admitting an integral lattice of discriminant order n. If j = 0 the only candidate is the zero space, whose lattice has order one. For positive rank, select one representative for each bad ideal that occurs at that rank with norm at most n. Every admissible subspace has such a label by the index-square identity. The two isometry extensions show that the representative for its label covers it. This covering argument only uses ideals that occur on some subspace of the chosen dimension.

It suffices to count all nonzero integral ideals of norm at most n. To count ideals of a single norm k > 1, fix a rational prime p dividing k. Factorization of ideals shows that each ideal of norm k has a prime divisor 𝔓 above p. If its residue degree is f𝔓, removing this factor leaves norm k/pf𝔓. There are at most D choices for 𝔓, because ∑𝔓∣p e𝔓f𝔓 = D, with all summands positive. J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, §3, ideal factorization and Theorem 3.34[38].

Let Ω(k) count the rational prime factors of k with multiplicity. Each removal decreases Ω by at least one. The unit ideal is the only possibility at norm one. Induction gives at most DΩ(k) ideals of norm k, allowing repeated counts if several prime divisors work. Since 2Ω(k) ≤ k, we obtain

# orbits ≤ ∑k=1n DΩ(k) ≤ ∑k=1n klog₂D ≤ n1+log₂D.

For n = 4, the index-square identity alone permits ideal norms 1 and 4, with indices 2 and 1. There is a further check. Each bad prime lies above an inert place and has norm q² ≥ 4. A bad ideal of norm 4 would therefore contain exactly one such prime. At that place the determinant has odd valuation. Everywhere else it is a local norm, including all real places by positivity. Landherr’s product condition requires the product of these local signs to be +1, excluding this single negative sign. Only the unit ideal can occur in this example. The general bound deliberately counts all ideals of norm at most n and needs no test of which ones are realized. Gross, §3, Theorem 3.1, product condition[45].

In the row count the order is n = d² and D = 2f. The factor n1+log₂(2f) counts the rational choices once. For each choice the two intersection masses and the gluing count supply the remaining factors of the mean.

What do the two projections of an integral lattice remember?

Fix a full integral lattice L in a totally definite Hermitian space V over E. Write R = 𝒪E. A rational subspace U and its perpendicular W give a direct sum V = U ⊕ W. Write p and q for the two orthogonal projections. Set P = L ∩ U and Q = L ∩ W. Clearing denominators on a rational basis shows that each intersection spans its subspace. They are primitive: if a nonzero element of R times an element of L lies in P, the element itself lies in U, hence in P. The same holds for Q.

Although the ambient space splits, the lattice need only contain P ⊕ Q. A vector in L can have fractional components on both sides. The finite quotient C = L/(P ⊕ Q) records these pairs of components. Each component determines the other modulo its intersection lattice:

pL/P ≃ C ≃ qL/Q.

For the first isomorphism, send the class of x to the class of px. It is surjective by definition. If px belongs to P, then qx = x − px belongs to L ∩ W = Q. This proves injectivity. Exchanging the projections proves the second isomorphism. In particular the number of paired residue classes is counted only once.

For any lattice A denote its Hermitian dual in its own space by A∨. We have P∨ = p(L∨) and Q∨ = q(L∨). To see the first identity, test a vector u ∈ U against p(L∨). Orthogonality gives h(u,pz) = h(u,z) for every z ∈ L∨. This is integral for all z exactly when u belongs to the double dual of L, which is L itself. Thus the dual of p(L∨) is P. Taking duals once more proves the claim. The double-dual identity applies to these full lattices because they are finite projective over a Dedekind domain. For a free module it is evaluation on a basis and its dual. A finite projective module is a direct summand of a finite free one, so the evaluation identity restricts to it. The form identifies the conjugate-linear dual with the indicated Hermitian dual. The Stacks Project, Lemma 15.22.11[39] · Lemma 10.78.2, finite projective modules[46].

Why is the perpendicular discriminant at most the product of the other two?

Write n = |P∨/P|, a = |Q∨/Q| and N₀ = |L∨/L|. Let c = |C|. Integrality of L places pL between P and P∨ and places qL between Q and Q∨. The first chain shows c divides n. In the second chain Q∨/qL is an image of L∨/L, since Q∨ = q(L∨). Its order divides N₀. Multiplying the two successive indices on the perpendicular side gives

a = c · |Q∨/qL| ≤ nN₀.

Equality in a plane. Take L = R² with Gram matrix diag(1,2). For u = (1,1) and w = (−2,1), the two lines are orthogonal, and their intersections are P = Ru and Q = Rw. The squared lengths are 3 and 6. In x = (s,t), the coefficient of u is (s + 2t)/3 and the coefficient of w is (t − s)/3. In particular the vector (1,0) supplies the residue pair (1/3,−1/3), generating the common quotient R/(3). Meanwhile L∨ allows a half in the second coordinate, so q(L∨) = (1/6)Q. Consequently Q∨/qL has order |R/(2)|. Writing D = [E ∶ ℚ], the orders are n = 3D, N₀ = 2D and a = 6D. This attains the general product bound. As a second check, the index-square formula for P ⊕ Q ⊂ L reads na = N₀c². Here both sides equal 18D. This example tests the lattice lemma before the row specifies its level prime.

Why does the gluing count cost only twice the perpendicular rank plus one?

Let s be the dimension of W, and assume L∨/L can be generated by e elements over R. A finite quotient of one full lattice in an s-dimensional space by another contained in it needs at most s generators. At each prime in its support the upper lattice is free of rank s, so the images of a local basis suffice. The finite module is a direct sum of its primary parts. Pad their generating lists with zeros to length s and assemble the first entries into one element, then the second entries into another, and so on. The Chinese remainder theorem supplies scalars which select a single primary part, proving that the assembled elements generate the whole module. Local freeness over a Dedekind domain[39] · Chinese remainder theorem[40].

Apply this to qL/Q. Through the common residue module, the same s generators suffice for pL/P. The quotient P∨/pL is the image of L∨/L under p, so e more generators suffice. Lifting these latter generators and adjoining the former ones generates P∨/P. On the perpendicular side the preceding rank bound applies directly to Q∨/Q. Thus the two budgets are s + e and s, even when U has much larger dimension.

Fix both intersections. Every candidate ambient lattice lies between P ⊕ Q and P∨ ⊕ Q∨, because its vectors pair integrally with P and Q. Taking the quotient by the lower lattice embeds the choices into the set of submodules of the finite module A = (P∨/P) ⊕ (Q∨/Q), of size na. In the row, the ambient discriminant module is cyclic, giving e = 1 as a sufficient bound. Each submodule of a finite module generated by g elements over R needs at most g generators, by the local lifting argument. Counting ordered tuples yields

# compatible lattices ≤ |A|2s+1 = (na)2s+1,   1 ≤ a ≤ nN₀.

Only some submodules produce an integral lattice with exactly these intersections. Counting all tuples gives an upper bound valid for every fixed pair. The genus mean multiplies it by the weighted counts of the two intersections and the number of rational subspace orbits.

How short a vector does every integral line contain?

Let E be the CM field in the rank-one row count, unramified at finite places over its real subfield. Write 2f = [E ∶ ℚ], Δ = |disc(E)| and ρ = Δ1/(2f), the root discriminant. Fix a one-dimensional E-space with a Hermitian form h positive at every archimedean place. For an integral full lattice M in it put n = |M∨/M|. There exists a nonzero x ∈ M satisfying the following bound at every embedding σ. The expression on the left is the squared length at that embedding.

σ(h(x,x)) ≤ B,   B = ρ n1/(2f).

To keep track of a possibly nonprincipal lattice, choose any nonzero m ∈ M, put b = h(m,m) and write x₀ = m/b. The algebraic integer b is totally positive and fixed by conjugation. Since h(m,x₀) = 1, each element r x₀ of M has integral coefficient r. These coefficients form a nonzero integral ideal I. Thus M = I x₀, and h(x₀,x₀) = 1/b. Pairing with every element of I x₀ gives M∨ = b Ī−1x₀. Here Ī is the conjugate ideal. The ratio of the covolumes of these two ideals yields n = N(I)²/N((b)), where N denotes absolute ideal norm.

Choose one embedding in each of the f conjugate pairs and consider a product of open complex disks of radii Rσ = √(Bσ(b)). The product of their squared radii is Bf√N((b)) = √Δ N(I). Under the ordinary real and imaginary coordinates of these embeddings, the ideal lattice has covolume 2−f√Δ N(I). The volume of the disks is πf√Δ N(I), strictly greater than 22f times that covolume. Minkowski’s convex body theorem therefore gives a nonzero a ∈ I in the disks, by shrinking them slightly to closed disks first. Take x = a x₀. Its squared length at σ is |σ(a)|²/σ(b) < B. Conjugate embeddings give the same value. The ideal covolume calculation uses the same real measure. J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, theorem 4.19[47].

How does one short representative bound the number of lines?

Let L be an integral full lattice in a totally positive definite Hermitian E-space of rank k ≥ 1. We count the rational lines U for which L ∩ U has discriminant order n ≥ 1. This intersection is a full lattice on U. It is finitely generated as a submodule of L, and clearing the denominators of any vector of U brings a nonzero scalar multiple into L. The short-vector theorem applied to the intersection gives a nonzero x ∈ L spanning U over E. Thus the number of these lines is at most the number of vectors of L satisfying the bound at all embeddings. Several short vectors can span the same line.

Use the real Euclidean norm ‖x‖2 = TrE/ℚ(h(x,x)) on the real vector space of dimension 2kf obtained from the rational lattice. For every nonzero difference of lattice vectors, its squared Hermitian length is a totally positive algebraic integer. The product of its 2f conjugates is a positive integer, hence at least one. Their arithmetic mean is at least their geometric mean. Consequently distinct lattice points are at distance at least √(2f) in this norm. Every vector with squared length at most B at all places lies in the ball of radius √(2fB).

Put disjoint open balls of radius √(2f)/2 around these lattice points. They all lie in the ball with that radius added to √(2fB). Comparing volumes bounds their number by (1 + 2√B)2kf, including the origin. Since B ≥ 1, each factor 1 + 2√B is at most 3√B. Substitution now gives

# {U of order n} ≤ (9ρ)kf nk/2.

The rank-one row bound takes n = d². The last factor becomes dk. The estimate holds for each individual lattice in the genus, so summing with weights 1/|Aut(L)| multiplies the uniform bound by the genus mass. Rank zero has at most the single zero subspace.

A line whose chosen basis vector is too long. In E = ℚ(ζ₁₂) with real field ℚ(√3), the two absolute discriminants are 144 and 12. The discriminant tower formula gives relative discriminant norm 144/12² = 1, so this example satisfies the finite unramified hypothesis. Write ε = 2 + √3, a unit with inverse 2 − √3. In the standard coordinate lattice 𝒪E² put the Hermitian Gram matrix diag(2ε²,1). On the first coordinate line the intersection is 𝒪Ee₁. Its dual is (2ε²)−1𝒪Ee₁, so n = 16. Here ρ = √12 and B = 2√12. At one place the vector e₁ has squared length 14 + 8√3, greater than B. The single vector ε−1e₁ lies in the same lattice and has squared length 2 at both places. Its trace squared norm is 8, the sum over four embeddings. Milne, §§2, 3 and 6 on discriminants and cyclotomic integers[47].

What replaces vanishing when the two words coincide?

The subseries Buu still excludes the identity and has geometric Gram label zero. Now the two infinite-place representations agree. An intertwiner from a representation to itself can be a nonzero scalar. The goal is to control the size of the surviving sum. Write Q for the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm, du for the full word dimension, k for the weight parameter and f for the number of infinite places in the product. We will obtain Q(Buu) ≤ du exp(−kf log k). The other diagonal contribution, Kuu − Buu − I, has its own estimate.

Each orbital term involves two flags. Call their distinguished subspaces X and X′, each of dimension r. Group terms by the dimension lost in their intersection, j = r − dim(X ∩ X′), and by a list δ of leading minors of their pairing matrix through size j. This j belongs to one term. The corank used for two terms on a common row in the preceding argument compares different data. Terms whose characters disagree on the common stabilizer vanish. For the remaining terms in this subseries, the geometric input gives 1 ≤ j ≤ r. This lower bound matters. At j = 0 the power that pays for summing the terms would disappear.

The square of the norm pairs two terms on the same row. First fix the list of minors of each term and bound the contribution of all such pairs together. Then count the distinct lists by size on each side of the pair. For the consequence in linear algebra, each vector of an orthonormal basis of the kernel contributes one unit to the squared distance between the Gram matrix and the identity. The dimension bound starts from this observation.

Where does the half-power of the last minor come from?

Keep one nonidentity term t that survives the character test in the diagonal subseries. Its two flags determine a positive rank j and an arithmetic list of minors δ. Consider the last minor of that list at each of the f infinite places. In the coordinates adapted to the flags, let Dτ be its positive normalized absolute size. The comparison of Gram minors identifies the local factor in the normalized ideal norm Δ of the last minor with Dτ². Consequently the product P of the Dτ is positive and Δ = P² under the discriminant identity of the family. The local amplitude bound contains one inverse power of the absolute size for each of the k − 1 − j occurrences. Multiplication over the places gives

∏τ Dτ−(k−1−j) = P−(k−1−j) = Δ−(k−1−j)/2.

For an arithmetic check of the exponent, assign the two local sizes 2 and 3 and take k − 1 − j = 3. Their inverse cubes multiply to 1/216. The norm is 36, and 36−3/2 gives the same 1/216. These numbers check the product identity. A realized flag pair also has to satisfy the level, normal-form and size hypotheses. For all nonzero minors up to and including the last, divide the absolute sizes at each place by the common scale (2H₁)2r. Take their maximum and 1, whichever is larger. The product of these maxima gives the label size S. Taking an inverse power reverses the local comparison and gives the upper-bound factor S−Cₛk.

How large can one orbital term be before summing the row?

The representative of a term can be changed by its stabilizer. Bounding the orbital integral therefore has two costs. One measures the volume of a fundamental set for that stabilizer. The other measures the size of the integrand at the infinite places. Write a for the norm of the term vector, w for its weight, V for the volume of the word’s unipotent fundamental set (the same for every term in this word), U for the volume of the term’s stabilizer fundamental set with its adapted measures, and J for the product of the local amplitude norms. Unfolding gives aV ≤ wUJ. The volume estimate uses L = (8v)2(r+1)²f. Since 1 ≤ VL, multiplication by L gives a ≤ wUJL. In each adapted normal form N the volume estimate gives U ≤ ωN vk(r−j)fL, where ωN is its index weight. This accounts for both copies of L in the scalar estimate. Here r is the flag dimension and v is the arithmetic volume parameter.

Each local norm also contributes the square root of a representation dimension. Their product is √dπ, where dπ is the product of those dimensions. To see one cancellation before the constants are enlarged, the common factor at each place is 2r²/vrk. Taking its f-th power and multiplying by the positive power of v from the volume leaves 2r²f/vkjf ≤ 2r²f. The scalar majorant absorbs this and the two volume losses into a family-wide cost. The resulting inequality holds for every adapted normal form. Their weights have infimum ωt. To pass to it, write c for the common nonnegative prefactor. If c > 0, the inequality makes a/c a lower bound for the weights, hence a/c ≤ ωt. If c = 0, evaluating at any adapted form gives a = 0.

‖vec(t)‖ ≤ w √dπ ωt · A(j, δ).

The deterministic factor A contains the rank gain (C/k)j(k−1−j)f, the discriminant and size factors just derived, and a cost depending on the family parameters. A label can have many representatives. In a squared row norm two terms occur together, so one still needs a bound on the sum of wωt · w′ωt′ for pairs with prescribed labels. That estimate supplies the positive powers of Δ and S in the label sum.

How can the estimate cover infinitely many lists of minors?

For a realized list δ at fixed j, write Δ > 0 for its normalized ideal norm at the last minor and S ≥ 1 for its size across the infinite places. At each place take the maximum of 1 and the normalized sizes of its nonzero leading minors, then multiply the maxima. One input bounds the amplitude for a fixed label, and another accounts for how much weight its representatives can carry. The label-dependent factors in their product are

Δ−(k−1−j)/2 Δk/2 · S−CₛkSCₚk = Δ(j+1)/2 S(Cₚ−Cₛ)k.

The minor bound Δ ≤ H S², with H independent of δ, costs Sj+1. Choose the decay parameter Cₛ ≥ Cₚ + 4. Since j ≤ r and k ≥ 2r + 2, the remaining exponent j + 1 − 4k is at most −3r. A separate arithmetic estimate bounds the sum of S−3r over every finite set of realized labels, uniformly in the set. The next calculation counts the possible entries in each size interval, then sums their weights. Multiple terms with the same list have already been paid for by the fixed-label bound.

How many lists of minors have a given size?

Fix a diagonal word u and an intersection defect j with 1 ≤ j ≤ r. Each surviving term supplies an ordered list δ = (δ₁, …, δj) of leading determinants. The map from terms to realized lists is surjective. The fixed-list estimate already bounds the contribution from all terms in each fibre, so we count each distinct list once. Vanishing intermediate determinants retain their positions.

Both frames belong to the same self-dual Hermitian lattice. Pairing a vector in its dual with a lattice vector gives an element of the ring of integers 𝒪E. Every matrix entry therefore lies in this ring, and its determinant does too by the permutation formula. This puts each δℓ in a set whose spacing we can control.

Separation of algebraic integers. Let τ range over one embedding from each of the f conjugate pairs of the CM field E. For distinct x, y in 𝒪E, the product ∏τ|τ(x) − τ(y)|² equals |NmE/ℚ(x − y)| ≥ 1. Indeed the norm multiplies all conjugates, and each conjugate pair contributes a squared modulus. Multiplication by the nonzero algebraic integer x − y on the integral lattice 𝒪E has nonzero integral determinant. This also covers units, whose absolute norm equals one.

Divide each complex plane into half-open squares of side ½. Two points in the same square differ by less than 1 in modulus. If two algebraic integers occupied the same square at every place, their product of squared differences would be less than 1. Thus a choice of one square at each place contains at most one algebraic integer.

Counting at a fixed size

Let d be the root discriminant of E and H₁ the positive height scale of the fixed-list estimate. For a minor of order ℓ set eℓ = ∑a=1ℓ(r + 1 − a), ρℓ = d2eℓ(2H₁)2r and Rℓ = max(1, ρℓ). At place τ the size of a list is στ = max(1, max1≤ℓ≤j |τ(δℓ)|/ρℓ). Its global size is S = ∏τστ. Different places can attain their maxima at different minors.

Record the integer aτ for which 2aτ ≤ στ < 2aτ+1. Write A = ∑τaτ. Fixing these integers places τ(δℓ) in a disk of radius 2aτ+1Rℓ. Each real or imaginary coordinate in that disk meets at most 8·2aτRℓ + 2 ≤ 10·2aτRℓ half-unit intervals. Multiply the choices for two coordinates, for all places, and then for the j positions. Separation makes the map from realized lists to tuples of cells injective. Counting all tuples, including those that contain no realized list, bounds the number of distinct lists with this profile by Bj22jA, where Bj = ∏ℓ=1j(10Rℓ)2f.

Shell bound. Let Nj(h) count the realized lists with 2h ≤ S < 2h+1. Multiplying the local inequalities gives 2A ≤ S < 2A+f, so A ≤ h ≤ A + f − 1. For an upper bound it suffices to include every profile with A ≤ h. There are exactly binom(h + f, f) nonnegative profiles with this property. To see this, put the unused h − A in a final slot and choose the positions of f separators among h + f symbols. This gives

Nj(h) ≤ binom(h + f, f) · Bj · 22jh   (h ≥ 0).

A list may have zero entries. In this one-place experiment, fix a single nonzero entry x in the Gaussian integers and take unit radius, so S = max(1, |x|). The shell 2 ≤ S < 4 contains 36 possible entries. For |x| < 4, the vertical lines with real part 0, ±1, ±2 and ±3 contain respectively 7, 14, 14 and 10 points in total. The smaller disk |x| < 2 contains 9, including the origin. The origin cancels in the difference 45 − 9 = 36. Any realization condition on the minor can only reduce this count.

What changes if the list has two entries? With the same unit radii, count ordered Gaussian pairs (δ₁, δ₂) with δ₂ ≠ 0. Inside the outer disk there are 45 choices for δ₁, including zero, and 44 for δ₂. Inside the smaller disk there are 9 and 8. Subtraction gives 45·44 − 9·8 = 1,908 candidates in the shell. One large coordinate already places a pair in the shell. In the general dimension argument, the bound for each shell is multiplied by the bound for one list before summing the diagonal error.

Why the remaining power pays for every list

Each list in a profile of total A has weight S−3r ≤ 2−3rA. Put κ = 3r − 2j ≥ r ≥ 1. The whole profile contributes at most Bj2−κA. For the shell bound we allowed every profile of total at most h. ∑δ∈T S(δ)−3r ≤ Bj(1 − 2−κ)−f ≤ 2j ∏ℓ=1j(64Rℓ)2f.

The last inequality follows from (1 − 2−κ)−1 ≤ 2 and j ≥ 1. The bound is independent of T, so taking the supremum over finite subsets also bounds the full nonnegative sum. Why does the ideal norm cost only the square of the size?

The count bounds a sum of weights in S. The amplitude also contains the normalized ideal norm Δ of the last minor. To put these two quantities on the same scale, fix the real subfield F of E and write DF, DE for their absolute discriminants. Then [E : F] = 2, [F : ℚ] = f and d2f = DE. At order ℓ, put e = eℓ and x = δℓ. The word gives x through its two flags. The ideal used to normalize it is fixed by the fields. It is 𝔞 = 𝔇F/ℚ𝒪E, the extension to E of the different of F. For x ≠ 0, let Δℓ be the absolute norm of the fractional ideal (x)𝔞−2e. Set Δℓ = 0 when x = 0.

The norm of the different of F is DF. Extending an ideal to E squares its absolute norm, since 𝒪E is locally free of rank two over 𝒪F. Thus Nm(𝔞) = DF². For x ≠ 0, the principal ideal has norm ∏τ|τ(x)|². Multiplicativity gives Δℓ = DF−4e ∏τ|τ(x)|². Put Mτ = |τ(x)|/d2e. Removing this power of d at every place brings out the ratio of discriminants. A. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Lecture 6, Remark 6.13[48] · Lecture 12, Theorem 12.17 and Proposition 12.27.[49]

Δℓ = (DE/DF²)2e · (∏τ Mτ)².

The arithmetic family satisfies DE = DF². At each place the maximum defining στ includes Mτ/(2H₁)2r whenever x ≠ 0. Multiplying gives √Δℓ ≤ (2H₁)2rfS. A zero intermediate minor has norm zero and satisfies the squared inequality as well. The amplitude also uses an inverse power of Δ = Δj. For that step we need to know why the last minor is nonzero.

Why the last minor is nonzero. Let X and X′ be the two totally isotropic spaces in the flags. Thus the Hermitian pairing vanishes on each space separately. Write I = X ∩ X′, and let U and U′ be the spans of the first j frame vectors on each side. The normal-form theorem for a surviving term gives U ∩ I = 0 and X′ = U′ + I. It also relates the last frame vectors z and z′. Each is orthogonal to its own isotropic space, and z′ − cz lies in X + X′ for some nonzero scalar c in E. We use one more flag hypothesis. Every isotropic vector orthogonal to both X′ and z′ belongs to X′. In the arithmetic flags, a vector outside X′ meeting these orthogonality conditions has strictly positive squared length at the chosen infinite place.

If δj vanished, a nontrivial linear combination of the first j rows of the pairing matrix would be zero. The corresponding combination of frame vectors gives a nonzero x in U, because those vectors are independent. The zero row says that x is orthogonal to U′. It is already orthogonal to all of X, including I. The decomposition of X′ now gives x orthogonal to X′ as well. Since x is orthogonal to z and to z′ − cz, it is orthogonal to z′. Finally x is isotropic since it lies in X. The flag hypothesis places it in X′, so x belongs to U ∩ I = 0. This contradiction proves δj ≠ 0. Its normalized ideal norm is therefore positive.

0 < Δ ≤ (2H₁)4rf S² ≤ bCm²f S².

For the last step use H₁ = bCHm, b ≥ 2, CH ≥ 0 and m = 2r + 2. Then 2H₁ ≤ bCHm+1, while 4r ≤ 2m and CHm + 1 ≤ (CH + 1)m. Any C ≥ 2(CH + 1) works for every word and every defect. In the fixed-list estimate the ideal factor is Δ(j+1)/2. Raising the bound to this power costs precisely Sj+1.

A zero before the last position. Consider two isotropic planes with bases (e₁, e₂) and (f₁, f₂). Pair e₁ with f₁ and e₂ with f₂ with value 1, and give the other two pairs value 0. Read the second basis in the order (f₂, f₁). The resulting matrix has rows (0, 1) and (1, 0). Its list of leading determinants is (0, −1). The zero occupies the first slot in the shell count, while the inverse power in the amplitude applies to the second slot.

Checking the field hypothesis. Set r = j = f = 2 and H₁ = 1. Take the candidate list (ρ₁, ρ₂), so both normalized entries equal one at each place, S = 1 and e₂ = 3. In ℚ(ζ₁₂) with real subfield ℚ(√3), the discriminants are 144 and 12. Here d = √12 and ρ₂ = 16 · 12³. Directly from the ideal norm, Δ = (16 · 12³)⁴/144⁶ = 2¹⁶. This attains (2H₁)4rf exactly. Discriminant of ℚ(ζ₁₂)[50] · Discriminant of ℚ(√3).[51]

In the shell example over ℚ(ζ₈) the real subfield ℚ(√2) has discriminant 8, so DE/DF² = 256/64 = 4. With the same choice (ρ₁, ρ₂) for this field, Δ = 65536⁴/64⁶ = 2²⁸. The extra factor is 4⁶ = 2¹², exactly as in the product formula. The shell count uses the spacing of integers in either field. The sharper ideal-norm bound uses the family’s discriminant identity. Discriminant of ℚ(√2).[52]

Fix the defects j, j′ and the two ordered lists of minors δ, δ′. Take any finite set P of ordered pairs of surviving terms on a common row, subject to the following requirement on every pair (t, t′) in P. The first term has defect j and list δ, and the second has defect j′ and list δ′. Write vt for the vector contributed by t, dπ for the local representation dimension, and M for the total row mass of the word. Let Hj(δ) denote the nonnegative product of the amplitude and representative bounds for one label, whose δ-dependent factors occur in the fixed-list estimate. The arithmetic estimate for two prescribed lists gives

∑(t,t′)∈P ‖vt‖ ‖vt′‖ ≤ dπ M Hj(δ) Hj′(δ′).

The single factor M accounts for the shared row. Two separate averages over rows would lose the information that both terms occur on that row. For example, on two rows of equal mass, two conditions that both select the first row have joint mass 1/2, while the product of their masses is 1/4.

Now allow both lists to vary in a finite collection of pairs. Partition the collection by (δ, δ′) and apply the estimate to each part. All terms of the bound are nonnegative, so we may sum over the Cartesian product of the two sets of lists that occur. The resulting two sums separate. At fixed j, the weighted count and the one-label bound give ∑δ Hj(δ) ≤ Aⱼ, with Aⱼ as below after enlarging the common constant. Thus the contribution for defects j, j′ is at most dπ M Aⱼ Aj′. Summing over ordered defects gives dπ M(∑j Aⱼ)². The bound is uniform over finite collections and hence bounds the full nonnegative sum.

In the expansion of the squared Gram error, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each inner product by the product of these vector norms. If Γ₁ is the Gram normalization, the dimension estimate gives Γ₁dπM ≤ du. The remaining Gram factor is at most 2. For a common constant C ≥ 1 we obtain an error proportional to the number of source columns, namely

Q(Buu) ≤ 2du (∑j=1r Aⱼ)²,   Aⱼ = exp(Cm⁶fL) (C/k)j(k−1−j)f.

Here m = 2r + 2 and L = log b, with b ≥ 2. The estimate comes with thresholds for the arithmetic family and the tied local data. Once those hypotheses hold, the final comparison is a scalar inequality.

Why does the rank sum leave exp(−kf log k)?

A sufficient numerical threshold is (16C + C³²)m⁶L ≤ k log k, with C ≥ 1 and f ≥ 1. It ensures k ≥ 8, k ≥ m and k ≥ C¹⁶. Since (j − 1)(k − 2 − j) ≥ 0, every exponent j(k − 1 − j) is at least k − 2. The base C/k is at most 1. Thus we can bound the sum by r times its first-rank bound. For r = 0 the sum is empty. For positive r put T = kf log k. In the logarithm of twice the squared sum there are three costs. The rank count contributes log(2r²) ≤ m⁶ ≤ T/8, the height contributes 2Cm⁶fL ≤ T/8, and the constant in the base contributes 2(k − 2)f log C ≤ T/8. The denominator in that base contributes −2(k − 2)f log k ≤ −3T/2. Together they give at most −T. Multiplying by du proves the promised bound.

For a check using integers alone, take C = r = f = 1, b = 2 and k = 8192 = 2¹³. Then m = 4. After division by log 2 the threshold reads 17 × 4096 ≤ 13 × 8192. There is one term A₁ = 24096−13×8190 = 2−102374. Twice its square is 2−204747, below the allowance 2−106496. This checks the scalar estimate before inserting any row dimensions or orbital data.

5.15How many rows can the period maps share?

All the word maps take values in the same target. Its dimension D counts the independent ways the chosen archimedean representation occurs in automorphic L² after applying the finite-place projector e. The main term M for this integer is a real number. If dv is the formal degree at the real place v and V is the Haar volume of a fundamental domain F, then M = c0V, where c0 = (∏v dv) Re e(1). Why should this expression approximate a dimension? Both arise from one kernel.

Let φ be the product of the normalized archimedean matrix coefficients, their formal degrees and the finite-place function e, with the archimedean coefficients conjugated. Summing φ(x⁻¹γz) over rational group elements γ gives a kernel K(x,z). It represents an orthogonal projection of rank D. Choose continuous representatives F1, …, FD of an orthonormal basis of the range. The geometric kernel and the basis expansion give the same action on compactly supported test functions. Continuity and uniqueness of the automorphic representatives identify the two kernels pointwise. In particular,

Re K(x,x) = ∑j |Fj(x)|² ≥ 0,   ∫F Re K(x,x) dμ = D.

Each basis vector contributes one to the integral. On the geometric side the identity γ = 1 gives the constant c0 on the diagonal. Its integral is M. The real parts of the remaining summands can have either sign.

Which parameters enter the dimension comparison?

Fix a positive level-growth exponent Cg. The theorem chooses a lower bound for the ambient dimension n before varying the field and level. At each of the f infinite places the discrete series has the prescribed signature (p, q), with p + q = n and q² ≤ n. The CM field has root discriminant d with log d ≤ exp(n), and log f ≤ √n. The scale b ≥ 2 satisfies log b ≤ exp(nf log n/16). The congruence level g lies between 1 and bCg. The auxiliary rational prime exceeds 4n and splits completely in the CM field.

The absolute values of the archimedean weight entries are ≤ b². Whenever two entries at the same place have opposite signature signs, their distance is at least 8·10¹⁴(Cg + 4)n¹⁹f⁵ log(bd). This gap supplies rapid decay for the far terms. The threshold for a point to lie in the deep cusp uses the same field and level data and equals τ∗ = (nf d g b)−11q.

What does a short sublattice measure?

Let Λ be the lattice at the point and let B be a nonzero sublattice of rank s over the CM field E. Embed B at the f conjugate pairs using the positive metrics at that point. Its real covolume is taken in its own span, of real dimension 2fs. Multiply the covolume by 2fs|disc E|−s/2 and take the (2fs)th root. This is its normalized size. The least size is the infimum over all such B. The root makes it meaningful to compare different ranks. The canonical lattice filtration has a nonzero step strictly below t precisely when the least size is < t. Its step at or below t is already nonzero at equality.

For example, give the two coordinate directions of ℤ[i]² lengths ½ and 2, respectively. Here f = 1 and |disc E| = 4, so the prefactor is one in every rank. The fundamental square of the first Gaussian line has area ¼ and its normalized size is ½. The full lattice has four-dimensional covolume one. To find the least size, project a line sublattice onto a nonzero coordinate. This identifies it with a Gaussian ideal. An element of least nonzero norm generates that ideal. Round the real and imaginary parts of each quotient to integers. The remainder has smaller norm than the divisor and belongs to the ideal, so it must be zero. Thus the line has a generator (a,b) with squared length |a|²/4 + 4|b|² ≥ ¼. Every full-rank sublattice has positive integer index, hence covolume at least one. The least size is exactly ½. The strict test used in the short-flag bound therefore excludes this example at the boundary.

Write n for the unitary rank, f for the number of real places, and put U = nf log n, α = exp(−U/4), δ = exp(−n²f). A point is moderate when its least sublattice size reaches the threshold τ∗, and deep when it falls below it. Write K(x) for the real diagonal of the projector. The four estimates compare different quantities.

The four contributions to |D − M|
Part of the quotientQuantity integratedUpper bound
Moderate, nearSum of absolute values of near nonidentity termsαM
Moderate, farSum of absolute values of far termsδM
Deep, identityThe constant identity density c₀αM
Deep, projectorThe full nonnegative diagonal K(x)δD

On the moderate region, remove the identity and take absolute values term by term. On the deep region, both K(x) and c₀ are nonnegative, so |K(x) − c₀| ≤ K(x) + c₀. Adding the four rows gives

|D − M| ≤ (2α + δ)M + δD.

For a two-point illustration, take counting measure and project onto the unit vector (2,1)/√5. The diagonal is (4/5, 1/5) and its sum is 1. Compare with the constant 3/5 on each point. The two local differences are +1/5 and −2/5, even though both diagonal entries are positive. Their sum −1/5 is precisely the rank minus the reference mass. This illustrates the sign in the trace subtraction. The exponential estimates come from the arithmetic of the unitary quotient.

What can contribute close to the identity?

In the four contributions to the trace error, the first is an integral of a count with weights. At a point x of the fundamental domain, let A(x) be the sum of |φ(x⁻¹γx)| over nonidentity rational elements γ whose summand is nonzero and passes the near test. At each infinite place the Euclidean length of the vector of logarithms of the singular values of x⁻¹γx must be at most ε = 10−6n−8f−2. This test measures stretching. A unitary matrix has singular values one even when it moves vectors. The integral trace argument turns small stretching into closeness to the identity for these rational elements. The test coefficient imposes the finite lattice condition. The resulting bound is ‖x⁻¹γx − I‖HS ≤ t = 3√(nε) at every infinite place.

Near-term estimate. In signature (p, q) put n = p + q, with q ≥ 1 and q² ≤ n. Fix the level-growth exponent. Under the field, level and spectral-gap hypotheses of the dimension comparison, for all sufficiently large n one has

∫moderate A(x) dμ(x) ≤ M exp(−U/4),   U = nf log n.

Here M = c₀V is the identity contribution, with V the volume of the fundamental domain. To describe the integration region put X = nf d g b, where d is the root discriminant, g the finite-level parameter and b the height parameter. A point is moderate when its least normalized sublattice size is at least τ∗ = X−11q. This lower cutoff matters because more rational transformations can preserve a lattice with a very small subspace.

First consider a point whose least size is at least ½. Let L≤s denote the step in its size filtration generated by sublattices of largest normalized size at most s. Self-duality puts the entire lattice in L≤2. The filtration estimate for an integral near transformation gives (γ − I)L≤2 ⊆ L≤2t. Since 2t < ½, the latter step is zero. Thus γ fixes a spanning lattice and is the identity. Here A(x) = 0. At every remaining moderate point there is a nonempty canonical flag of short isotropic subspaces. Write j₁,…,ja for the successive increases in rank, and τ₁ < … < τa for the normalized sizes of the successive quotients. Then τ∗ ≤ τ₁ and τa < ½. The total rank J = ∑i ji is at most q, since projection onto the negative subspace is injective on an isotropic subspace.

Why a near term has exactly the traces of the identity

The near part of the trace count tests stretching at each archimedean place. A rotation can have zero stretching and still move every nonzero vector. To detect that motion we use the finite level of the same rational isometry. Let G be its matrix over the CM field E, of size n ≥ 1, and put f = [F ∶ ℚ] for the totally real field F below E. Take a positive integer level g0 > 4n for which (g0) in 𝒪E is radical, meaning that no prime ideal occurs twice in its factorization.

At a point x of the adelic quotient, take a rational term with nonzero test coefficient. The finite support condition says that the conjugated finite matrix preserves the reference lattice and its difference from the identity is nilpotent modulo g0 with exponent at most n. Let Λx consist of the rational vectors that enter that finite lattice after applying xf−1. The finite-lattice construction makes it a finitely generated 𝒪E-module spanning En. Moving the conjugation from the matrix to the vector gives

GΛx ⊂ Λx,   (G − I)nΛx ⊂ g0Λx.

For example, to check the second inclusion on a rational vector v ∈ Λx, apply xf−1 to (G − I)nv/g0. The finite support condition puts the result in the reference lattice, which is exactly the membership test for Λx.

Localize this lattice at a prime ideal 𝔭. It is free of rank n there, since it is finite and torsion free over the ring of integers. The matrix of G in a local basis is integral. Its power traces are therefore integral at every prime. For 𝔭 dividing (g0), the reduction of G is I + N with Nn = 0. In a basis adapted to the kernels of the powers of N, it is triangular with diagonal entries 1. Every power still has trace n in the residue field. Since (g0) is the product of its distinct prime divisors, these congruences give, for every j ≥ 1,

tr(Gj) − n = g0 aj,   aj ∈ 𝒪E.

The Stacks Project, lemma 15.22.11, local freeness over a Dedekind domain[39].

Now impose the archimedean test. Choose 0 < c ≤ 10−5 and set ε = c/(n8f2). At each real place the Euclidean length of the vector of logarithms of the singular values of the conjugated matrix A is at most ε. Every singular value is then at most exp(ε), so ‖Aj‖op ≤ exp(jε). Each diagonal entry has absolute value at most this operator norm. For 1 ≤ j ≤ n, we have jε ≤ 1/4 and hence |tr(Aj) − n| ≤ n(exp(1/4) + 1) < 3n. Trace is invariant under conjugation. The CM embeddings above each real place form a conjugate pair, so this bound holds for every conjugate of tr(Gj) − n.

It follows that every conjugate of aj has absolute value at most 3n/g0 < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has a nonzero integer field norm, the product of all its conjugates. Such a product cannot have absolute value less than 1. Thus tr(Gj) = n for 1 ≤ j ≤ n.

From the power traces to a distance from the identity

Write det(I − zG) = ∑k=0n bkzk, with b0 = 1. Over a splitting field, differentiate the product of the factors 1 − λz, one for each eigenvalue λ with multiplicity. Its logarithmic derivative is −∑j≥1 tr(Gj)zj−1. Multiplication by the original polynomial and comparison of coefficients give Newton’s recursion

k bk = −∑j=1k bk−j tr(Gj),   1 ≤ k ≤ n.

The first n power traces coincide with those of I. Since the field has characteristic zero, division by k gives the same coefficients successively. The characteristic polynomial of G is therefore (T − 1)n. Cayley–Hamilton states that a matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial, giving (G − I)n = 0. This identity passes to the finite and infinite components and survives conjugation. The Stacks Project, lemma 10.16.1, Cayley–Hamilton[53].

Unipotent matrices can still have large entries. To get the distance actually needed in the count, use both the first trace and the stretching bound. In the polar decomposition write A = U exp(X) with U unitary and X Hermitian. The eigenvalues of X are the logarithms of the singular values, so its Frobenius norm is at most ε. Write B = exp(X) − I. The exponential series gives ‖B‖F ≤ exp(ε) − 1 ≤ 2ε. Since tr(A) = n, the identity A = U + UB gives n − Re tr(U) ≤ |tr(UB)| ≤ √n ‖B‖F by Cauchy–Schwarz on the diagonal. For unitary U, expanding ‖U − I‖F2 gives exactly 2(n − Re tr(U)). As √n ≤ n, this yields ‖U − I‖F ≤ 2√(nε). Adding ‖UB‖F ≤ 2ε ≤ √(nε) proves

‖A − I‖F ≤ δ = 3√(nε).

This radius satisfies δ < 1/4. For a signature index q with q2 ≤ n, substitution gives δqnf = 3√c · q/n5/2 ≤ 3√c/n2 < 1/100. The one-type count uses c = 10−6. Every contributing rational matrix now belongs to the set defined by the finite lattice condition and the archimedean δ-bound.

A Gaussian transvection. In dimension two over ℚ(i), give the basis e, f zero norms and pairing ⟨e,f⟩ = 1. The matrix G fixing e and sending f to f + ie preserves this form and the Gaussian lattice. Here (G − I)2 = 0, and the level 13 > 8 splits into the distinct Gaussian primes 3 + 2i and 3 − 2i. Its first two traces are both 2. Newton’s recursion gives b1 = −2, then 2b2 = −((−2)·2 + 2) = 2.

Take the finite coordinate of x to be the identity and its real coordinate to scale e,f by R,R−1 with R = 20,000. The upper entry of x−1Gx is now ia, with a = R−2 = 2.5 × 10−9, so its Frobenius distance to I is a. Its squared singular values have product 1 and sum 2 + a2, the determinant and trace of A*A. Thus its logarithmic singular values are ±arsinh(a/2). Their Euclidean length is less than a/√2 < 1.77 × 10−9. For c = 10−6 the permitted ε is 3.90625 × 10−9 and δ ≈ 2.65 × 10−4. This verifies the lattice and metric bounds on a nonidentity matrix. On the same space −I also has zero stretching, but its first trace differs from 2 by −4, failing the congruence modulo 13.

How much does one flag type contribute?

Fix the ordered ranks j = (j₁,…,ja). Two estimates use the same factors in the size variables. The lattice count bounds the number of possible group elements for those sizes. The flag-measure theorem bounds the volume of points with those sizes. Their product is small enough to integrate even when the count alone becomes large.

To see the cancellation, form a list of positive numbers λ with the following multiplicities. Every λ is less than one because the τi are strictly increasing and lie below ½.

Size factors for the ordered ranks of a short flag
Size factor λMultiplicity
τi/τk and τiτk (i < k)2fjijk each
τi2fji(n − 2J)
τi²f ji²

Lattice count and flag-measure estimates. For a point of this type the number of admissible near elements is at most ∏λ(1 + 12t/λ), including the multiplicities in the table. Each weight is at most c₀. For the same type there is a constant κj such that the proportion of the fundamental domain with ordered sizes in any measurable region is bounded by the integral there of κj(∏λ λ) ∏i(2f ji dτi/τi). The measure bound for sets extends to nonnegative weights by simple-function approximation. Now each matched pair gives (1 + 12t/λ)λ = λ + 12t ≤ exp(12t). The sum of the multiplicities is f(2Jn − 2J² − ∑iji²), as one sees by expanding J². It is at most 3qnf. The choice of ε gives tqnf ≤ 1/100, so the product of all matched factors is at most exp(36/100) < 2.

The remaining integral is over ordered sizes between τ∗ and ½. Enlarge this simplex to the whole box [τ∗,½]a. Each coordinate now integrates separately, with ∫τ∗½ ds/s = log(1/(2τ∗)). If Ij is the near integral for this flag type, it follows that

Ij ≤ 2M κj ∏i [2fji log(1/(2τ∗))] ≤ 2M κj Ya,   Y = 22f q² log X.

For the second inequality use ji ≤ q and τ∗ = X−11q. To check the box enlargement alone, take f = 1, ordered ranks (1,2) and lower endpoint ⅛. The integral of (2/s)(4/v) on the square [⅛,½]² is 8(log 4)². Exchanging s and v preserves this integrand. The triangle s < v therefore gives 4(log 4)². The example isolates the integration step from the choice of arithmetic parameters.

Why do all flag types together cost at most exp(−U/4)?

The arithmetic estimate for the flag constant gives κj ≤ exp(−JU/2). The scale bounds give Y ≤ exp(U/8) and 2q+1 ≤ exp(U/8) beyond a single rank threshold for the fixed level-growth exponent. The first inequality pays for integrating the sizes. Since every rank increment is positive, a ≤ J. Thus −JU/2 + aU/8 ≤ −3JU/8 ≤ −3U/8.

The second scale inequality pays for summing the flags. Ordered positive ranks of total J are compositions of J. Choose which of the J − 1 gaps between consecutive units carry a divider. This gives 2J−1 choices and hence 2q − 1 possible types in total. For q = 3 there is one type of rank one, two of rank two, and four of rank three, including both (1,2) and (2,1). Every nonzero near contribution has one of the counted types. Summing the nonnegative upper bounds gives (2q − 1)·2M exp(−3U/8) ≤ M exp(−U/4). This is the near part on the moderate region in the trace inequality. The deep region has its own volume and kernel-mass estimates.

How many distant terms can survive at a point?

In the trace estimate, the variable x describes a lattice and γ runs over rational group elements. Fix x for now. At a real place v, take the polar decomposition of the matrix of x⁻¹γx as k exp(X), with k unitary and X Hermitian. Write zv(γ) = ‖X‖HS. This is the square root of the sum of the squared logarithms of its singular values. A nonzero summand is far when some zv exceeds the chosen radius ε. Equality with ε belongs to the inner interval. Zero summands may be dropped throughout.

Rational point count. Write tx = min(½, least(x)), where least(x) is the smallest normalized sublattice size, interpreted as an infimum. Among rational elements whose finite component after conjugation lies in the supporting compact subgroup, the number with zv(γ) ≤ Rv at every place, for prescribed nonnegative radii, satisfies

# {γ in the box} ≤ P(x) exp(κ ∑v Rv),   P(x) = (3√n/tx²)2n²f,   κ = 2n².

Here n is the matrix size and f is the number of real places. To see the lattice in this count, subtract two distinct rational elements from the box. Their finite support condition makes the difference a nonzero map from the lattice at x into itself. The lattice size inequality, using self-duality, gives a lower bound for the geometric mean of the operator norms of this difference across all places, namely tx². Thus the matrices form a separated set, even though two of them may approach one another at an individual place.

Why does the exponent contain 2n²f?

At place v the matrices lie in a ball of operator radius exp(Rv), since the largest log singular value is at most zv. Put R̄ = (∑ Rv)/f. Rescale that space of matrices by exp(R̄ − Rv). The product of the rescalings is one, so geometric-mean separation persists, while every coordinate ball now has radius exp(R̄). In the maximum norm on the product, distinct centers are therefore at least tx² apart. Open balls of radius tx²/2 around them are disjoint and fit in the concentric ball of radius exp(R̄) + tx²/2. The product space has real dimension 2n²f. Scaling its Lebesgue volume bounds the count by (1 + 2 exp(R̄)/tx²)2n²f. Since n ≥ 1, tx ≤ ½ and R̄ ≥ 0, the base is at most 3√n exp(R̄)/tx². Raising this to the indicated power yields the box bound.

Why does the decay beat the number of distant terms?

Let h be a common lower bound for |λa − λb| whenever the two parameter entries have opposite signature signs, with h ≥ 120nq3/2. The polar matrix coefficient estimate at each place gives the following bound for the absolute kernel summand. The formal degrees and the maximum of the finite projector give the identity density c₀.

|φ(x⁻¹γx)| ≤ c₀ ∏v exp[−(h/8) min(zv², zv/√(2q))].

Sum outside the inner box. Assume 0 < ε ≤ 1/√(2q), κε ≤ log 2, 32κ ≤ hε and T = hε²/16 ≥ 1. Use index zero for [0, ε] and index j ≥ 1 for (2j−1ε, 2jε]. For a fixed tuple of indices, use the outer radius of each interval to count the terms and the inner radius to bound each coefficient. In a positive interval, both z² and z/√(2q) are at least εz. Their common lower bound exceeds 2j−1ε². After including the counting factor exp(κ2jε), a positive interval costs at most exp(−T2j−1), because κε ≤ T/2. The zero interval costs at most exp(κε) ≤ 2.

Write a for the zero-interval bound and b₊ for the sum of the positive-interval bounds. Since T ≥ 1, successive positive terms decrease by a factor at most exp(−T) ≤ ½. Hence b₊ ≤ 2 exp(−T) ≤ 1. A far element has a positive index at some place. The sum of the product bounds over the allowed profiles is (a + b₊)f − af. Factoring the difference of powers makes this at most fb₊(a + b₊)f−1. Every finite set of summands obeys this same estimate, so its nonnegative infinite sum converges and satisfies the slightly enlarged bound

∑γ far |φ(x⁻¹γx)| ≤ c₀P(x) · 2f·3f exp(−T).

With two places, temporarily allow only indices zero and one. Radii (ε, 2ε) have indices (0, 1), so a term at those radii is far. The surviving profiles are (0, 1), (1, 0) and (1, 1). With bounds a = 2 and b₊ = ¼ their weights sum to ½ + ½ + 1/16 = 17/16, also (2 + ¼)² − 2². This checks the counting identity on two intervals, independently of the arithmetic parameters.

Where does the factor exp(−n²f) enter the trace?

Let d be the CM root discriminant, g the level parameter, b the height parameter and Cg ≥ 0 its level-growth exponent. In the indefinite counting family, n ≥ 8, q² ≤ n, log f ≤ √n, d ≥ 1, b ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ g ≤ bCg. The moderate set consists of points of the fundamental domain with least(x) ≥ τ, where τ = (nfdgb)−11q ≤ ½. Thus tx ≥ τ and the packing factor is bounded on the entire moderate set. Put ε = 10−6n−8f−2. The family takes its spectral gap at least 8·1014(Cg + 4)n19f⁵ log(bd). These choices satisfy the shell hypotheses and give

∫moderate ∑γ far |φ(x⁻¹γx)| dμ(x) ≤ M exp(−n²f).
How does the gap pay for a possibly small τ?

Write s = √n and L = log(bd) ≥ log 2. The gap gives T ≥ 50(Cg + 4)n³fL. We compare this with the logarithms of the other factors. Since log n ≤ s, log f ≤ s and log g ≤ CgL, one has log(1/τ) ≤ 11s[2s + (Cg + 1)L]. Consequently the logarithm of (3s/τ²)2n²f · 2f·3f, plus the desired margin n²f, is at most

2n²f [2 + s + 22s(2s + (Cg + 1)L)] + 4f + n²f.

Divide by n³f, use s² = n and n ≥ 8. The result is at most 93 + 44(Cg + 1)L ≤ 50(Cg + 4)L, since 156 log 2 > 93. The shell sum at each moderate x is therefore bounded by c₀ exp(−n²f). Integrating uses only that the moderate volume is at most the full volume V and M = c₀V.

This supplies the term δM in the four-term trace inequality. The rare-flag volume and the concentration of the projection on the deep region enter through separate integrals.

How much of the fundamental domain can lie in the deep region?

Choose a point x using Haar measure on the fundamental domain divided by its volume V. The question is now about the point itself. If its least normalized sublattice size is below the deep cutoff τ∗, how often can this occur? Since τ∗ < ½, it suffices to bound the probability that some step of the lattice filtration occurs below ½.

Short-flag probability. For the finite-unramified CM data of the dimension count, let the unitary group have signature (p,q) at each of the f real places, and put n = p + q. Suppose log n ≥ 15, q² ≤ n, the root discriminant d satisfies log d ≤ exp(n) and log f ≤ √n. With U = nf log n,

Pr(least size < ½) ≤ exp(−U/3),   μ(deep) ≤ V exp(−U/3).

By the filtration criterion, a least size strictly below ½ is equivalent to a nonzero step strictly below ½. Its canonical flag ends in a totally isotropic subspace. The positive jumps j₁,…,ja in its ranks add to the rank J of that subspace, so 1 ≤ J ≤ q. The successive sizes satisfy 0 < τ₁ < … < τa < ½. Thus the event is covered by measurable sets indexed by ordered compositions of these ranks. This cover lets us bound its volume with the same flag density that appeared in the near orbital integral.

What is the probability of one ordered rank type?

The flag-measure theorem bounds that probability by κj times the integral of the size density over the ordered simplex. Its arithmetic input is a comparison of quotient volumes: unfold a marked flag of rank J, use the residual Hermitian space of signature (p−J, q−J), then divide the resulting bound by the full volume. The arithmetic estimate for the resulting coefficient is κj ≤ exp(−JU/2).

How does marking a flag change the volume being counted?

Fix the positive rank jumps j₁,…,jₐ and let B be a measurable region of admissible ordered sizes. A point whose canonical flag has those ranks and sizes supplies one saturated isotropic flag. If we count all such flags over the point, the indicator of the event is bounded above by the number of markings. For instance, if three points have probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 and carry respectively zero, one and two eligible markings, the points with a marking have probability 3/4. Counting all markings gives 1/2 + 2(1/4) = 1. This inequality permits the geometric proof to use arithmetic stabilizers.

Choose a basis adapted to a marked flag. Its data include one full lattice class for each successive quotient, of rank jᵢ, and a finite-adelic double class in the fixed residual Hermitian model supplied by the volume-ratio theorem, of signature (p−J, q−J), where J = ∑ jᵢ. On that space two finite representatives are equivalent when a rational isometry on the left and an element of the compact lattice stabilizer on the right identify them. The construction of an integral frame and the comparison of two markings put any marking with the same data into the chosen representative by these changes of basis. The archimedean flag sizes are preserved under the corresponding simultaneous change of frame. For each realized tuple of data it therefore suffices to integrate on the quotient by the subgroup preserving its marked flag. These slices cover the original event. Counting an overlap twice gives an upper bound.

The sum is countable. Each block lattice has finitely many generators in a countable number field, and the open compact subgroup at the finite places has at most countably many cosets in a second-countable group. The residual double quotient is a further quotient of that countable set.

Why does the probability lose the residual volume?

For one stabilizer the real group is integrated in unipotent, block diagonal and compact coordinates. For the fixed marked flag the sizes at umk equal those at m, with the unipotent element u on the left and the compact element k on the right. The block diagonal coordinate gives the size variable τ and its density, whose integral on B we denote by I(B). The mass of a single marked slice is at most the product of this integral, a common factor from the unipotent covolume and the real Haar measures, one lattice weight for each block, and a stabilizer covolume on the residual Hermitian space. All these quantities are nonnegative.

We can now sum over every tuple of block classes and residual class, including tuples for which no marked flag was found. The sum of products separates. The sum over coefficient-lattice classes evaluates the weight of each block. At rank jᵢ this gives 2f jᵢ² times the normalized general linear volume of that rank. The sum of residual stabilizer covolumes with their real gauge factors is bounded by the normalized residual volume V₀. Write Aj for the common factor multiplied by all the block bounds. If M(B) is the unnormalized mass in the original fundamental domain, and H is the product of the archimedean Haar gauge factors divided by the measure of the finite compact stabilizer, then

H M(B) ≤ Aj V₀ I(B),   H V = V₀ RJ.

The second equality is the Hermitian volume-ratio theorem, with V the full fundamental-domain volume and RJ the product of its rank factors from n−2J+1 through n. Both volumes and the gauge are positive and finite. Dividing gives Pr(event) = M(B)/V ≤ (Aj/RJ) I(B). The quotient of these constants is precisely κj. This is the use of the smaller Hermitian space in the probability estimate. To resume the dimension argument from here, sum over the possible rank lists to bound the volume lost in the trace. To check the arithmetic constant, follow the general linear class masses in its numerator and the Hermitian rank factors in its denominator.

What must an adapted frame remember?

A rational basis that follows a flag identifies its vector spaces. The volume calculation also needs to know which coefficients give integral vectors. Let E/F be the CM extension, unramified at every finite place. Write O for the integers of E, h for the nonsingular Hermitian form (linear in the second entry), and L for the self-dual lattice at the finite point. Self-duality means that x lies in L exactly when h(y,x) lies in O for all y in L. Fix a saturated flag 0 = S₀ ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Sₐ whose last space is totally isotropic. Total isotropy means that every two vectors in it pair to zero. Put jᵢ = rank(Sᵢ/Sᵢ₋₁), d = ∑jᵢ, and suppose each real signature is (p,q) with d ≤ min(p,q).

Saturation says Sᵢ = L ∩ spanE(Sᵢ). If x ∈ Sᵢ and ax ∈ Sᵢ₋₁ for some nonzero a ∈ O, then x already lies in Sᵢ₋₁. Thus the quotient is torsion-free. It is finitely generated as an O-module. Over the Dedekind domain O it is projective, so the quotient map admits a section. Its image Aᵢ gives Sᵢ = Sᵢ₋₁ ⊕ Aᵢ. Choose a basis over E for the span of each Aᵢ, and let Λᵢ ⊂ Ejᵢ be the coefficient vectors of its integral elements. This construction also works when Aᵢ is a nonprincipal ideal and has no one-element integral basis.

Set W = spanE(Sₐ). We need a second isotropic space pairing perfectly with W and a decomposition that preserves L. Apply the same projectivity argument to L/Sₐ. If π is the quotient map and s a section, then 1 − sπ projects L onto Sₐ. Extend it by scalars to a projector P on the full rational space, with image W and P(L) ⊆ L.

How can the opposite isotropic space stay integral?

Take the Hermitian adjoint Q = P†, defined by h(x,Qy) = h(Px,y). For x,y ∈ L the right-hand side is integral, so self-duality gives Qy ∈ L. Since the image of P is totally isotropic, QP = 0. Both P and Q are idempotent. The unramified hypothesis supplies an integral w of relative trace one, as in the real-layer calculation. The corrected projector satisfies

T = Q − wPQ,   QT = Q,   T² = T,   T†T = (1 − w − conj(w))PQ = 0.

Indeed (PQ)† = PQ and PQP = 0. The last identity makes W′ = im T isotropic. On im Q the map u ↦ u − wPu has left inverse Q, so dim W′ = rank Q = rank P = d. For x ∈ W, h(x,Tz) = h(x,z). Thus if Tz pairs to zero with all of W, then Qz pairs to zero with the full space, so Qz = 0 and Tz = 0. Equal dimensions give a perfect pairing between the opposite spaces.

For an integral vector z take y = Tz and x = P(z − y). The remainder r = z − x − y lies in both ker P and ker Q. It is orthogonal to W = im P and to W′ = im T, because T†r = 0. All three summands remain in L. The perfect pairing makes their sum direct.

For a two-coordinate check, take the Gram matrix [[0,1],[1,1]]. The form takes value one on its second coordinate vector. Subtracting half of the first coordinate vector would make that value zero. In the Eisenstein integers O = ℤ[ω] with ω = (1 + √−3)/2, the integral vector (−conj(ω),1) also has form value zero, since 1 − ω − conj(ω) = 0. It still pairs to one with (1,0), and these two vectors have determinant one. This plane illustrates the trace-one correction over a ring where 1/2 is unavailable. The global theorem imposes additional unramified conditions on the field.

Which lattice and frame data determine the marking?

Choose in W′ the basis dual to the concatenated rational bases of the Aᵢ. The Hermitian pairings between corresponding vectors are one, and all cross pairings are zero. Write V₀ = (W ⊕ W′)⊥ and L₀ = L ∩ V₀. For a coordinate lattice Λᵢ, its Hermitian dual consists of the vectors v for which conj(u) · v ∈ O for every u ∈ Λᵢ. A vector in W′ with these dual coefficients pairs integrally with L because only the W component contributes. Conversely, every integral vector pairs integrally with the marked lattices. Self-duality of L identifies the opposite coefficients exactly. The same pairing test on V₀ proves that L₀ is self-dual there. Thus in the chosen coordinates

L ≃ (⊕i Λᵢ) ⊕ (⊕i Λᵢ∨) ⊕ L₀,   Sₖ ≃ ⊕i≤k Λᵢ.
Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place?

At an inert finite place, work first over the completed unramified quadratic extension. A self-dual lattice has an integral Gram matrix with unit determinant in an integral basis. Its reduction is a nonsingular Hermitian space over a quadratic extension of finite fields. In positive dimension it has a vector whose Hermitian value is nonzero. Otherwise, expanding the value on x + ay would give Tr(a h(x,y)) = 0 for every residue scalar a. The trace pairing of finite fields is nondegenerate, so every pairing would vanish. This argument includes residue characteristic two.

Lift such a vector. Its value is a unit of the base ring. Every unit is a norm in an unramified quadratic local extension, so scaling the vector gives Hermitian value one. Integral orthogonal projection now splits off its line and leaves a unimodular complement. Induction gives an orthonormal basis, with the empty basis as the rank-zero case. At a split place the two integral components pair perfectly and one can take an arbitrary basis on the first and its dual on the second. Thus in both cases a completed integral isometry matches any two self-dual lattices of the same rank in a common Hermitian space.

For a finite place v of the real base field, a rational vector belongs to the localized lattice when some base integer outside v takes it into the original lattice. At a split place this condition retains both primes above v. The genus comparison uses a rational isometry that matches these localized lattices. The condition on the completed lattices is open because their stabilizers are open. To see why rational isometries meet this open set, take a local isometry U. Multiply by a rational scalar λ of norm one so that 1 + λU is invertible. Only finitely many λ are excluded by the determinant polynomial, and the ratios (1 + kθ)/(1 − kθ) for integers k give infinitely many choices when θ is a nonzero purely imaginary element. Set

X = (1 − λU)(1 + λU)−1,   X† = −X,   λU = (1 − X)(1 + X)−1.

Approximate X by rational matrices Y and replace each by (Y − Y†)/2. They are exactly skew-adjoint and still approximate X. At a place above two the denominator costs a fixed precision, which can be supplied by a closer initial approximation. At a split place use simultaneous approximation in the two completions. The inverse displayed transformation is continuous on its domain and sends these rational skew-adjoint matrices to rational isometries. Undo the scalar λ. A sufficiently close choice lies in the same open lattice coset as U, so it takes the first localized lattice into the second. Duality reverses this inclusion, and both lattices are self-dual, giving equality. The rational choice here may depend on the finite place.

From the local lattices to a marked class

Each pair of opposite basis vectors contributes one positive and one negative direction at a real place, by taking their sum and difference. The residual signature is therefore (p−d,q−d). To compare it with the prescribed residual model, identify the CM fields by the given isomorphism respecting conjugation. Both forms now have self-dual lattices. At a finite place the extension is split or unramified, and local classification identifies their unimodular forms. At infinity their signatures agree. The local-to-global theorem for Hermitian forms gives a rational isometry of the residual spaces. In the resulting common space the transferred lattice is locally isometric to the reference lattice everywhere. A finite family of nontrivial local changes carries one to the other, since two full lattices agree at almost all places. Their product is the finite adelic representative of this residual lattice class.

Finally compare two markings expressed with the same coefficient lattices and residual representative. Their full frame matrices B and B′ have the same nonsingular Gram matrix, so B′B−1 is a rational unitary isometry. The coefficient description takes each integral partial sum to its namesake and gives the equality of the full lattices. Their finite representatives then differ, after this rational change of frame, by an element of the compact lattice stabilizer. The sizes of the graded pieces agree in the transported archimedean frame. This is the identification used in counting the marked slices.

Which powers of the flag sizes enter the volume?

Fix one saturated isotropic flag with its integral lattices. Assume the Hermitian space has the same signature (p,q) at every real place. Write E for the CM field and f for its number of pairs of complex embeddings. A flag with successive rank jumps j₁,…,jₐ determines a decomposition into an isotropic part, a residual space and the dual isotropic part. In that order the block ranks are r = (j₁,…,jₐ, n−2∑jᵢ, jₐ,…,j₁). Let τ⁰ denote the positive sizes in this fixed frame. The height of the ith isotropic block is hᵢ = (τᵢ⁰)2f jᵢ. Its dual has reciprocal height, and the residual block has height one.

An upper triangular unipotent matrix can move one block into each earlier block. Group those rectangular entries by their distance k above the diagonal. For a pair of blocks b < c, the rectangle has rbrc entries and represents a map from block c to block b. The determinant contribution of its integral lattice is hbrc/hcrb. To see the two powers, a change of basis in the range acts on each of the rc columns. The inverse change of basis in the domain acts on each of the rb rows. The arithmetic normalization for the coefficient lattice is νEf per entry, where 2νE is the root discriminant of E.

dₖ = ∑c−b=k rbrc,   Cₖ = νEf dₖ ∏c−b=k hbrc/hcrb.

Here Cₖ is the covolume of the full complex block lattice across all places. Write P(τ⁰) for the positive square root of the product of the height ratios over all pairs. For two isotropic pieces i < j, pairing them and their duals gives (τᵢ⁰/τⱼ⁰)2f jᵢjⱼ(τᵢ⁰τⱼ⁰)2f jᵢjⱼ in P. Pairing piece i with the residual block of rank r0 gives (τᵢ⁰)2f jᵢr₀. Pairing it with its own dual gives ((τᵢ⁰)²)f jᵢ². The next step explains why that square root also occurs in the real covolume.

From integral matrices to unitary matrices on one layer

Use orthonormal skew-adjoint coordinates on the layer. Its full lattice L lies in ℂs, with s = f dₖ, and is stable under complex conjugation. A skew-adjoint leading term has real coordinates in this basis. Put A = L ∩ ℝs and iB = L ∩ iℝs. For x + iy ∈ L, adding its conjugate gives 2x ∈ A. In the quotient by A ⊕ iB, the class of x modulo A determines the entire class. Indeed, if x ∈ A, subtraction leaves iy ∈ iB. The quotient therefore injects into (½A)/A, of order 2s. The index formula gives cov(A) cov(B) ≤ 2sCₖ.

Why can we take a square root? The two covolumes are equal. In a CM extension unramified at finite places, for each rational prime p there is a purely imaginary algebraic integer whose absolute norm is prime to p. For this existence assertion write the scalar as z − conj(z). At a split pair of primes above p, choose the residues of z to be 0 and 1. At an inert prime choose a residue moved by conjugation in its quadratic residue field. The Chinese remainder theorem realizes these choices simultaneously. The difference is a unit above p. Multiplying by it exchanges the two real coordinate spaces and maps their lattices into one another. If D is the absolute determinant of this real scaling and I, J are the two indices, then I = D cov(A)/cov(B) and J = D cov(B)/cov(A). Their product D² is the dₖth power of that norm, prime to p. Consequently the positive rational number I/J = (cov(A)/cov(B))² has zero valuation at every prime. It is one. For a planar example of the index bound, the lattice of x + iy with integral coordinates of the same parity has area 2. Both axis lattices have spacing 2, attaining √(2 · 2) on the real axis.

To use the real lattice in the group, each of its leading terms must lift to an integral unitary matrix. The same unramified hypothesis gives an integral w with w + conj(w) = 1, where conj denotes conjugation. Indeed the residue trace is onto at every finite prime, both for the split pair and for the unramified quadratic residue field, including residue characteristic two. The ideal of integral traces is therefore contained in no maximal ideal and equals the base integer ring. If an integral block matrix Y has the required real leading coordinates, then X = wY − (wY)† is skew-adjoint and has the same leading coordinates. Start with g = 1 + X. Its defect D = g†g − 1 equals X†X, already in a deeper layer. Replace g by g(1 − wD). Its new defect is (1 − conj(w)D)(1 + D)(1 − wD) − 1. The linear term vanishes because w has trace one. All remaining terms lie deeper. The filtration ends after finitely many diagonals, so this produces an integral unitary lift.

Reduce the first nonzero layer modulo its real lattice, then reduce the next. A correction in a deeper layer preserves the earlier coordinates since the cross term in (1 + X)(1 + Y) lies strictly deeper. The product of the layer domains thus covers the quotient. In these triangular coordinates Haar volume is the product of the real coordinate volumes with the chosen orthonormal normalization. Multiplying the bounds √(2f dₖCₖ) gives, with dN = ∑dₖ,

covolume of the integral unipotent radical ≤ (2νE)f dN/2 P(τ⁰).

From block determinants to the volume of a marked slice

Next let the block-diagonal element m vary. In block i, set Dᵢ = ∏v |det mᵢᵥ|² over the complex embedding pairs, and Nᵢ = 2f jᵢ. Write bᵢ for the volume of the quotient of this general linear block by its lattice automorphisms in the slab 1 ≤ Dᵢ < exp(1). The determinant of a lattice automorphism has absolute norm one. Scaling a block by a positive real scalar translates log Dᵢ by any prescribed amount and preserves its Haar measure. The scalar-stable choice of representatives and the unit-slab calculation give the determinant measure bᵢ dDᵢ/Dᵢ. The fixed frame gives τᵢ = τᵢ⁰ Dᵢ−1/Nᵢ. Reversing the integration limits changes dDᵢ/Dᵢ to Nᵢ dτᵢ/τᵢ.

The unitary metric counts a general linear tangent block twice, once in the block and once in its dual. The squared norm doubles in 2jᵢ² real dimensions at each place. Its volume factor across all places is 2f jᵢ². The residual group contributes the gauge-normalized covolume g₀ of its one chosen lattice class. The block domains and that residual domain cover the required quotient, giving the product of these factors as an upper bound for nonnegative tests.

Finally write the real group element in unipotent, block-diagonal and compact coordinates. The change of Haar measure in these coordinates contributes a positive factor δᵥ at each real place. Block sizes multiply under the block-diagonal change of frame, so their height ratios give P(τ⁰)∏vδᵥ(mᵥ) = P(τ(m)). The initial height factor from the radical has now become the variable weight in the integral. For a measurable subset B of 0 < τ₁ < ⋯ < τₐ < 1/2, let cIw be the one-place Iwasawa normalization for this signature and flag type, with compact mass one. Then the gauge-normalized mass of this single marked slice with sizes in B satisfies

mass ≤ cIwf (2νE)f dN/2 g₀ (∏i 2f jᵢ²bᵢ) ∫B P(τ) ∏i (2f jᵢ/τᵢ) dτ.

To check the size density by itself, take one isotropic line in dimension four and formally set f = 1. Then the ranks are (1,2,1) and the heights are (τ²,1,τ−2). Each of the three pairs contributes τ⁴ before the square root. Thus P(τ) = τ⁶, and the size density is 2τ⁵ dτ. Integrating from zero to 1/2 gives 1/192 before multiplication by the arithmetic and measure constants. The remaining sum over the marked classes is where the residual covolume is absorbed into the total volume.
