Can one choose the block representatives at every scale at once?

For one block of rank j ≥ 1, let Γ be the group of automorphisms of its coefficient lattice Λ. Its elements act by left multiplication on tuples g of invertible complex j × j matrices, one matrix per embedding pair. We want one representative of each Γ-orbit. We also want the representative of the orbit of rg to be r times the representative of g, for every real r > 0. This lets a single unit interval of logarithmic determinants measure every other interval.

First minimize the largest absolute value of an entry, taken over all matrices in the tuple, as the tuple varies over its orbit. A minimum exists because only finitely many translates can have size bounded by any fixed number. Indeed, choose nonzero integers a, b in O with aOj ⊂ Λ ⊂ b−1Oj. For γ ∈ Γ the entries of abγ are integral. A bound on γg bounds γ after multiplication by the fixed inverse g−1. At every embedding these integral entries now lie in a bounded set. The simultaneous embedding of O is a lattice, so only finitely many entries, and hence matrices, occur.

Break a tie by dividing each matrix tuple by its size and assigning the normalized tuple a real number in a fixed, injective, measurable way. For instance, enumerate the open balls with rational centers and radii in its coordinate space and use ternary digit 2 for membership in a ball, 0 otherwise. These balls distinguish points. On the finite set of minimizers, choose the least such number. Conditions of the form “its size and tie breaker precede those of γg” are Borel, and Γ is countable, so the selected points form a measurable set D. Positive scaling multiplies all sizes by the same number and preserves all normalized coordinates. Hence D is stable under positive scalars. Left multiplication on invertible matrices is free, so the translates of D partition the matrix group.

Why does a unit slab determine the whole determinant measure?

Set s(g) = log ∏v|det gᵥ|². For γ ∈ Γ the product is one because it is the absolute real determinant of a lattice automorphism. The function s thus descends to the quotient. Multiplying g by r > 0 adds 2fj log r to s. This map preserves D and Haar measure. Let b be the mass of 0 ≤ s < 1 in D.

Here is the averaging argument for any nonnegative measurable test F. For every real s, the set of shifts t with t ≤ s < t + 1 has length one. Insert its indicator and integrate first over g in the translated slab. The substitution g = exp(t/(2fj))h moves this slab back to the original one. The inner integral over t then has the same value at every h, because it integrates all real translates of F.

∫D F(s(g)) dg = ∫{h∈D, 0≤s(h)<1} (∫ℝ F(s(h) + t) dt) dh = b ∫ℝ F(u) du.

Tonelli’s theorem justifies both orders of integration. The block argument only requires a totally complex field. For a Gaussian line, Γ consists of the four units acting on ℂ× by quarter-turns. Choose the sector 0 ≤ arg z < π/2. With Haar measure dx dy/|z|², a unit slab in log |z|² has log-radius width 1/2. Its mass is (π/2)(1/2) = π/4. The general block uses b with its specified matrix Haar normalization. Changing from s to the flag size now gives the factor 2fj dτ/τ in the marked-slice integral.

Which way does the Jacobian go in the real-place integral?

At one real place let G = U(p,q), with n = p + q. Fix a totally isotropic flag with positive rank jumps jᵢ. Its stabilizer has unipotent radical N and block-diagonal subgroup M. The maximal compact group K = U(p) × U(q) preserves the ordinary positive Hermitian norm as well as the signed form. Every element of G has the form umk. The compact group L = M ∩ K accounts for the ambiguity, since replacing (m,k) by (mℓ,ℓ−1k) gives the same element. These are all the repetitions because (NM) ∩ K = L. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Proposition 8.44[54].

For each matrix group H among G,N,M, choose the left Haar measure for which the ball ‖h−1‖HS ≤ r has volume asymptotic to the Euclidean unit-ball volume times rdim ℝ H. The Hilbert–Schmidt norm is the square root of the sum of squared absolute entries. Write these three measures as dg, du, dm, and give K its Haar probability dk. If μG is the initial Haar measure and c its gauge correction, then dg = c dμG. For every nonnegative measurable test φ the one-place formula is

∫G φ(g) dg = cIw ∫N ∫M ∫K φ(umk) δ(m) dk dm du.

To find δ, conjugate the radical by m. Put D(m) = |detℝ(Ad(m) on Lie(N))|. Conjugation multiplies the volume of an image set by D(m), so its pushforward measure assigns that set the factor D(m)−1. Under left multiplication by m₀ the coordinates change to (m₀um₀−1, m₀m, k). The change in du cancels precisely against the change in the weight when δ = D−1. The parabolic integration theorem supplies the equality of the measures up to a constant. Casselman, Representations of SL₂(ℝ), Proposition 18.5[55].

Let sᵢ = |det mᵢ|−1/jᵢ on the ith graded block. Conjugation on a rectangular block sends X to mbXmc−1. Taking its determinant and pairing the reflected rectangles gives the flag product δ(m) = P1(s), where the subscript indicates one place. For the real unitary radical the modulus of the complex determinant of its complexification equals the absolute real determinant. Each local size enters the global size by τᵢf = (τᵢ⁰)f ∏vsᵢᵥ. Since the flag product is a monomial in the sizes, Pf(τ⁰)∏v δ(mᵥ) = Pf(τ), as used in the marked slice.

What fixes the constant when the compact group has mass one?

Write d = dimℝ N, and use Hilbert–Schmidt volumes on K and L. Integrating m first absorbs right multiplication by ℓ ∈ L, which preserves dm and has δ(ℓ) = 1. The compact variable then ranges over the left cosets L∖K. Its probability density is vol(L)/vol(K) times Riemannian volume there. One more factor comes from the angle at which the radical directions meet the compact directions.

Use an ordinary orthonormal basis adapted to the isotropic blocks and their duals. Choose a Hilbert–Schmidt orthonormal real basis X₁,…,Xd of Lie(N). These matrices are strictly upper block triangular, so their adjoints are perpendicular to them. The skew-Hermitian matrices Yᵢ = (Xᵢ−Xᵢ∗)/√2 are unit compact directions perpendicular to Lie(L). They span that complement because dim K − dim L = d. The derivative of multiplication adds the tangent vectors. For each pair its columns Xᵢ, Yᵢ have inner product 1/√2 and hence span a parallelogram of area √(1−1/2) = 1/√2. Different pairs are perpendicular, and the block-diagonal directions of Lie(M) are perpendicular to all of them. The transverse Jacobian at the identity is therefore 2−d/2. The Hilbert–Schmidt small-ball normalization makes this tangent Jacobian the ratio of the corresponding local volume densities. Combining it with the quotient probability gives

cIw = 2−d/2 vol(K)/vol(L).

Put J = ∑i jᵢ and V(r) = vol U(r) for the Hilbert–Schmidt metric, with V(0) = 1. The numerator is V(p)V(q). In L, each U(jᵢ) acts on both an isotropic block and its dual. Its squared tangent norm doubles in jᵢ² real directions. The remaining U(p−J) and U(q−J) occur once. Consequently vol(L) = V(p−J)V(q−J) ∏i 2jᵢ²/2V(jᵢ). In this normalization V(r) = (2π)r(r+1)/2/∏h=0r−1 h!. Życzkowski and Sommers, Appendix A, equation (A14), metric A[56].

A hyperbolic plane. In an orthonormal Witt basis of U(1,1) the signed form exchanges the two basis vectors. Write u(t) = I + itE₁₂ and m(a) = diag(a,a−1) for real t and a > 0. Conjugating u(t) gives u(a²t), so at a = 2 the inverse density is 1/4. Here d = 1, K has volume (2π)², and L is the scalar circle of length 2π√2. Thus cIw = π. For a common signature and flag type at f places, multiplying the normalized formulas gives the power cIwf.

How much do all coefficient lines contribute?

One block in the marked-slice bound has rank j. For a full lattice Λ in Ej, let b(Λ) be the mass of its unit logarithmic determinant slab. Let Vⱼ be the sum of these masses, choosing one lattice per class under GLj(E). For example, an ideal I and the lattice 2I give the same class. Summing over all their integral multiples would count one positive contribution infinitely often. The first calculation determines V₁. The next two determine how it changes when the rank grows.

Put f = [E:ℚ]/2 and Δ = 2−f√|disc(E)|, the Euclidean covolume of the integer ring in ℂf. Thus Δ = νEf in the flag notation. A full lattice on a line is a fractional ideal. Two such ideals give the same class precisely when one is a nonzero field multiple of the other. All have the same automorphism group. Indeed, for an invertible ideal I, multiplying uI = I by I−1 gives u𝒪E = 𝒪E. Each of the h ideal classes therefore has the same slab mass.

Write zᵥ in polar coordinates and put tᵥ = log |zᵥ|². The Haar measure dxᵥ dyᵥ/|zᵥ|² becomes ½ dtᵥ dθᵥ. The slab imposes 0 ≤ ∑ tᵥ < 1. By Dirichlet’s unit theorem the logarithms of the units form a lattice in the hyperplane ∑ tᵥ = 0. In the first f−1 coordinates its fundamental parallelepiped has volume R, the regulator. Replacing the last coordinate by ∑ tᵥ has Jacobian one. Reducing the first f−1 coordinates modulo the free units leaves w roots of unity acting freely on the angles. Their quotient has 1/w of the full angular volume. Including the factors of ½ and the h classes gives

V₁ = h πf R/w = Δ Ress=1 ζE(s).

The second equality is the analytic class number formula for a totally complex field. For ℚ(i) the Gaussian integers admit Euclidean division by rounding the two real coordinates, so there is one ideal class. Here R = 1, w = 4 and Δ = 1. The answer π/4 recovers the Haar mass of the Gaussian unit slab.

Which ideal does a marked vector remember?

To compare ranks, mark one nonzero vector x of a rank-j coefficient lattice Λ. The saturated line through x consists of the multiples c x that still lie in Λ. Its coefficients form a fractional ideal I containing 1. Thus I = 𝔞−1 for a unique nonzero integral ideal 𝔞. For a primitive vector I = 𝒪E. For x = 2e₁ in the standard lattice, the coefficient 1/2 is allowed, so I = ½𝒪E and 𝔞 = 2𝒪E.

Use x as the first rational basis vector, and project to the other k = j−1 coordinates. The image Λ′ is a full torsion-free module over the integer ring. Every finitely generated torsion-free module over this Dedekind domain is projective, so the projection admits an integral linear section on Λ′. Its first coordinate extends to an E-linear functional ℓ on Ek. The shear (c,y) ↦ (c−ℓ(y),y) sends this section to the last k coordinates and fixes the marked vector. The pair now has the form

(Λ,x) ≃ (𝔞−1 ⊕ Λ′, e₁).

Every displayed pair exists, since 1 belongs to 𝔞−1. A change of basis fixing e₁ fixes its scalar multiples pointwise and induces a rational change of basis on the quotient. It therefore preserves the actual ideal 𝔞 and the class of Λ′. Conversely, a change between two quotient lattices extends by the identity on the marked line. This proves that the labels are exact. In rank one without a marking we summed over ideal classes. Marking a vector fixes the scale on its line, so here even two distinct principal ideals can supply different terms.

Why does an ideal of norm N receive weight N−j?

Start with one pair (𝔞−1 ⊕ Λ′, e₁). Move its lattice by g−1 at the complex places. Take j ≥ 2 and two nonnegative measurable functions. Test the position of the marked vector with Φ and the covolume of the moved lattice with w. Write N = |𝒪E/𝔞|, α = Δ/N for the covolume of the inverse ideal, and κ′ for the covolume of Λ′. The covolume before moving is κ = ακ′.

The vector coordinate. At one place put x = g−1e₁. On each patch where a selected coordinate of x is nonzero, complete x to a matrix s(x) of determinant one. This can be done by appending coordinate vectors and rescaling the last column. Partition by the first nonzero coordinate to use just one completion per vector. Write g−1 as s(x) times a block matrix with first column e₁, upper row (1,v) and lower-right block H. At fixed x the change on the last k columns preserves ordinary volume since det s(x) = 1. The matrix Haar density is |det H|−2j. Factoring out the rank-k Haar density leaves |det H|−2. Inversion H ↦ H−1 preserves the Haar measure of GLk(ℂ). Thus for h = H−1 and T = −v, the measure across all places is dx dT D(h) dμk(h), with D(h) = ∏ |det hᵥ|². This explains both the ordinary vector integral ∫Φ and the extra determinant.

The two covolumes. The stabilizer of the marked vector has a quotient-block automorphism and a row mapping Λ′ into 𝔞−1. Reduce the block modulo its automorphisms, then reduce the row modulo this lattice of maps. Translating the row leaves the chosen quotient block fixed. Distinct translates of the resulting coordinate domain overlap only on sets of measure zero. The rectangular Hom-lattice formula gives the row volume αkΔk/κ′. The extra determinant multiplies the block measure b(Λ′) dD/D, leaving b(Λ′) dD. The covolume input for w is t = κ/D, so this integral becomes b(Λ′) κ ∫₀∞ w(t) dt/t². The two appearances of κ′ cancel in their product.

(αk Δk/κ′)(ακ′) = Δ2j−1/Nj,   j = k+1.

For ℤ[i], take j = 2, 𝔞 = (1+i) and Λ′ = 2ℤ[i]. Then α = 1/2 and κ′ = 4. The row area is 1/8 and the full covolume is 2, giving 1/4. Varying Λ′ in the experiment changes both factors. Their product depends only on the ideal norm and rank.

How can a count with a marked vector determine an unmarked volume?

In each coefficient class integrate over the real matrix quotient, now allowing every determinant, and sum these integrals. Write ⟨·⟩ for this sum of integrals. A function of the moved lattice’s covolume t alone has integral Vⱼ ∫₀∞ w(t) dt/t by the slab formula and the substitution t = κ/D. With a sum over nonzero vectors it has the marked coefficient Cⱼ and covolume measure dt/t². For every nonnegative measurable vector test Φ the marked formula reads

⟨w(t) ∑0≠x∈L Φ(x)⟩ = Cⱼ (∫ Φ(x) dx) (∫₀∞ w(t) dt/t²).

A Gaussian lets us evaluate both kinds of integral in a single identity.

For a moved lattice L, let A(L) be ∑0≠x∈L exp(−π‖x‖²). The Gaussian has integral one. Write L∨ for the dual under the pairing ∑v,a Re(xᵥₐyᵥₐ). Conjugating the second argument converts this pairing to the ordinary Euclidean one and preserves the Gaussian. Poisson summation gives 1 + A(L) = (1 + A(L∨))/t. The two ones are the zero vectors on the two sides. The dual has covolume 1/t. Dualizing the arithmetic lattice sends full classes bijectively to full classes. The pairing of embedded field vectors is half the rational trace of their dot product, and taking the integral dual twice returns the original lattice. On moving matrices the change is inverse transpose, which preserves matrix Haar measure. Thus integrating a function of L∨ over all classes gives the same value as integrating it on L.

For t > 1 multiply the Gaussian identity by 1/t and gather the zero-vector terms on the left. This gives (t−1−t−2) + t−1A(L) = t−2A(L∨). Integrate only over t > 1. The first term is unmarked, giving Vⱼ∫₁∞(t−2−t−3) dt = Vⱼ/2. The second is marked, giving Cⱼ∫₁∞ t−3 dt = Cⱼ/2. On the right use the dual lattice as variable. Its covolume u = 1/t satisfies 0 < u < 1, so its marked integral is Cⱼ∫₀¹ u² du/u² = Cⱼ. Consequently

Vⱼ/2 + Cⱼ/2 = Cⱼ,   Vⱼ = Cⱼ.

The previous rank has finite mass by induction from V₁, and ζE(j) is finite for j ≥ 2. The right side is therefore already finite when the identity is used to determine Vⱼ.

Where do the class sums enter the flag probability?

Each increase from rank r−1 to rank r contributes Δ2r−1ζE(r). The line contributes Δ times the residue at one. Adding the odd exponents 1+3+⋯+(2j−1) = j² gives the total:

Vⱼ = Δj² Ress=1 ζE(s) ∏2≤r≤j ζE(r).

For one marked flag the block of rank jᵢ contributed 2f jᵢ²b(Λᵢ). Its metric factor is independent of Λᵢ. Enlarge the set of realized markings to all tuples of coefficient classes and residual classes. Every summand is nonnegative. Summing first over each coefficient class therefore bounds the combined block contribution by ∏i 2f jᵢ²Vjᵢ. With two ordered blocks of the same rank, the two slots range independently in this upper bound and supply the square of the one-block factor. For the residual Hermitian class the sum of stabilizer covolumes is bounded by its own group volume. That is the volume that cancels in the normalized flag probability.

How do different residual stabilizers fit inside one volume?

The residual group has a real factor G∞, a finite-adelic factor Gf, and a diagonal subgroup Γ of rational isometries. Let K be the compact open lattice stabilizer in Gf. For a finite representative d, the real group acting on that slice consists of the real components γ∞ of rational elements with γf in dKd−1. Call it Γd. It acts discretely. In any compact real set, the corresponding diagonal points belong to the product of that set with the compact dKd−1, which meets the discrete rational lattice in finitely many points. A rational matrix with identity real component is itself the identity, since a field embedding is injective.

Choose one d per finite double class and a measurable fundamental domain Fd for Γd in the real group. Such a domain exists by the measurable section theorem for a closed discrete subgroup. Consider the rectangles Fd × dK. To put a point in one of them, first move its finite coordinate into dK by a rational element. Next move its real coordinate into Fd using Γd, which preserves dK. Conversely, if a rational element takes a point in one rectangle to another, the finite coordinates force the same double class. Within that rectangle the real coordinates force γ∞ = 1, so γ = 1. The rectangles give one domain for the diagonal rational action.

μf(K) ∑d covol(Γd) ≤ vol(Γ ∖ (G∞ × Gf)).

Indeed each stabilizer covolume is at most the measure of its chosen real domain. Each finite-side translate dK has the same positive finite measure, and there are at most countably many, since K is open and the group of finite-adelic points is second countable in its topology. Multiplying by the common product of real gauge factors and dividing by μf(K) yields the normalized residual volume V₀ used in the flag comparison.

How much volume is lost when one Hermitian direction is removed?

The residual rectangle argument uses the volume of the smaller unitary group. To compare it with the original group, remove one direction at a time. Let E/F be the chosen CM extension, f = [F:ℚ] and νE = |disc(E)|1/(2f)/2. Assume the full signature (p,q) is the same at every real place. Write X for the original gauge-normalized volume in rank M ≥ 3, and Y for the corresponding volume in rank M−1. Fix a sign σ equal to +1 or −1 that occurs in this signature. The classification of the self-dual models lets us work in a signed diagonal model of this signature and carry its integral lattice to a representative in the genus. Choose a coordinate vector of the required sign. Its norm is a unit, so projection along it splits the lattice integrally and leaves a self-dual orthogonal complement. Thus Y is the volume for an actual complementary model. This comparison requires the unramified finite-place hypotheses of the flag theorem.

Consider the Gaussian sum over lattice vectors of norm σ, integrated over the original quotient. In both evaluations multiply that same integral by the product of its real gauge factors and divide by the finite measure of its compact level K. At each real place write Q(z) = ∑ εa|zₐ|² and let dᵥ be the density at σ obtained by pushing exp(−∑|zₐ|²) dz forward by Q. The density is positive. A small patch around the chosen unit vector has positive Gaussian mass and a nonzero derivative in its radial direction. Put d = ∏ dᵥ. In applying the one-vector mean, first take the indicator of the self-dual lattice at finite places and smooth compactly supported functions at the real places. Then increase the real cutoffs to the Gaussian. The terms in the lattice sum are nonnegative, so monotone convergence passes through the sum and the quotient integral. At the nonzero target σ, the densities of the cutoffs converge to dᵥ on each regular quadric. The resulting integral equals X m d, where the product of the local unit densities gives the arithmetic scalar m = (2νE)f/2νE−Mf/LM. The Euler product LM converges to a positive finite value and has one factor at each base prime.

Now mark the unit vector before integrating. Its rational stabilizer acts on the orthogonal complement. The finite representatives containing the chosen vector form one stabilizer–level double coset. The induced level is the stabilizer of the complementary lattice. In unfolding the markings the finite measure ratio is μf(K)/μ′f(K′), where K′ is that complementary level. The numerator cancels the original gauge denominator. What remains is the normalized complementary volume Y. At a real place, the remaining integration is over the quadric Q = σ. Its Haar quotient measure is 2M times the density measure of Q. To see the constant, calculate at the chosen coordinate vector. A tangent vector in the complement of its stabilizer has one imaginary axial coordinate and M−1 free complex coordinates. In the infinitesimal isometry matrix each free coordinate occurs twice, paired with a signed conjugate. The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm thus has coefficient two on its 2(M−1) real coordinates, giving a volume factor 2M−1 relative to Euclidean tangent area on the quadric. For the density of Q, use Q as the normal coordinate. At the unit vector its derivative in the outward radial coordinate has absolute value two. Changing variables thus gives half the tangent area per unit of Q. Both measures are invariant under unitary changes of frame. The group preserves Q and has absolute real determinant one. Their ratio at one point holds on the whole orbit. For a definite ternary form this calibration can be checked on the ordinary sphere. The ball of squared radius t in ℂ³ has volume π³t³/6, by elementary polar integration in the three complex coordinates. At t = 1 its Gaussian density is therefore π³/(2e), and its quotient integral is 8 times that value. In the indefinite case the Gaussian test itself stays inside both integrals. Multiplying the real constants and comparing evaluations gives

X m d = Y 2Mfd,   X = Y rM,   rM = (2νE)f(M−1/2)LM.

Indeed m rM = 2Mf, and m and d are positive and finite. Choosing an absent sign would make the quadric empty and defeat this cancellation.

Which local factors survive along the rank interval?

Let 𝔭 be a prime of the totally real base field with residue field of size Q. The extension is unramified at finite places. If 𝔭 is inert there is one prime above it of norm Q², fixed by conjugation. If 𝔭 splits there are two prime ideals of norm Q and conjugation exchanges them. In the product over prime ideals of the CM field each member of the split pair has weight (1−Q−M)−1/2. Multiplying the two members yields the factors indexed by base primes:

LM = ∏𝔭 split (1−Q−M)−1 ∏𝔭 inert (1−(−1)MQ−M)−1.

For a numerical check of these local formulas set Q = 2. In rank three the split and inert possibilities give 8/7 and 8/9. In rank four both give 16/15. At every step used here M ≥ 3. There are at most [F:ℚ] base primes above each rational prime p, and Q ≥ p. Thus the sum of the absolute logarithms of the factors is bounded by a constant times ∑n≥2 n−M. This proves the strict positivity and finiteness used in cancelling m.

Write (p₀,q₀) for the target signature and suppose its rank is at least two. While a positive direction is still to be removed, take σ = +1; once the positive target is reached, take σ = −1 for each remaining negative direction. Each step starts in rank at least three. The next factor depends only on the field and current rank, so their product is ∏p₀+q₀<M≤p+qrM. At the final signature the rational isometry given by classification and the finite-adelic change of lattice representatives transport the stabilizer and its level to any of the specified models; the gauge-normalized volume is the same. For an isotropic flag of total short rank J we remove J directions of each sign. For instance (3,1) to (2,0) uses r₄r₃. This gives the denominator RJ of the probability bound.

Why is there just one finite orbit for the unit vector?

Fix a rational vector x of Hermitian norm σ = +1 or −1, a reference finite representative xf whose lattice contains it, and the full finite stabilizer K of the reference lattice. Let H be the group of isometries fixing x. If a second finite representative g gives a lattice containing x, the assertion needed for unfolding is

g ∈ H(𝔸fin) xf K.

Work first over the local integer ring at one finite place. On a self-dual lattice L containing x, the coefficient of the projection of y onto its line is ⟨x,y⟩/σ. It is integral, since σ is a unit. Subtracting that multiple of x gives the integral decomposition L = 𝒪x ⊕ B, where B is the orthogonal complement in L. A vector in the rational complement that pairs integrally with B pairs integrally with the whole lattice, hence belongs to B by self-duality. Thus B is itself self-dual. The local classification of self-dual lattices identifies the complements for g and xf by an integral isometry between them. Extend it by the identity on x. Outside finitely many places the two original lattices already agree, so these maps can be chosen to be the identity there. Their product h is an adelic isometry fixing x and taking one local lattice family to the other. Then (hxf)−1g belongs to K, as claimed. Conversely, multiplying on the right by K fixes the lattice, and multiplying on the left by h preserves the condition that it contains x.

This argument also identifies the level. An isometry fixing x preserves L exactly when it preserves B. For an integral modulus c, the image of h−1 on L is just its image on B. As this lies in the perpendicular space, containment in cL is equivalent to containment in cB. This identifies the subgroup induced on the complement by a congruence condition. The double coset above uses the full lattice stabilizer. For example, −1 preserves the reference lattice. At principal level 3 it takes a primitive unit vector to a different residue class, so one may have more than one finite orbit at that finer level. The same calculation applies over the two factors at a split place and over an unramified extension in residue characteristic two.

One residue calculation illustrates the dyadic case. Over 𝔽₄ with conjugation z ↦ z², take the standard Hermitian form in three coordinates and x = (1,1,1). Its norm is 1. Its complement has basis b₁ = (1,1,0), b₂ = (1,0,1). Each basis vector has norm zero and their pairing is 1. For ω²+ω+1 = 0, the norm of b₁+ωb₂ is ω+ω² = 1. The projection along x and this choice of a nonsingular direction both make sense in characteristic two.

How many vectors represent a unit at a finite place?

Fix a finite place of F. Write O for its valuation ring, π for a uniformizer and k for its residue field of size Q. The quadratic algebra is unramified. Its residue algebra is either k × k (put η = +1) or the field of Q² elements (put η = −1). Write h for the Hermitian form, with norm h(x,x), and let Λ be a self-dual Hermitian lattice of rank M ≥ 1 and let β be any unit of O, in particular either sign in the rank comparison. Normalize additive Haar measure to give volume one to Λ and to O. The density at β is the mass of vectors with norm in β + πjO, divided by the volume Q−j of that target ball, as j increases.

Start with one coordinate. At a split place its norm is uv. There are Q−1 ways to make any prescribed nonzero value and 2Q−1 ways to make zero. At an inert place the norm is zQ+1. On the cyclic multiplicative group of order Q²−1 it has image of order Q−1 and kernel of order Q+1. Only zero has norm zero. In both cases the number for a prescribed value b is Q−η, with an extra ηQ when b = 0. Keith Conrad, Finite Fields, Theorem 5.7 (trace and norm)[57].

The reduction of Λ is nondegenerate by self-duality. In the split case it is a pair of spaces in perfect duality, so dual bases give the sum of M products. In the field case it has a vector with nonzero norm. Indeed, if all norms vanished, expanding the norm of x + az for every scalar a would give Tr(a h(x,z)) = 0 for every a. The nondegenerate field trace pairing would then force h = 0. Scale a vector of nonzero norm to norm one by surjectivity of the field norm, split off its orthogonal complement, and repeat. In either case the reduced form is a sum of M copies of the one-coordinate norm.

Let ZM count the vectors of norm zero, including the origin. With the first M coordinates fixed, the last norm has to cancel their sum. Each choice gives Q−η possibilities for the last coordinate, plus the correction ηQ on ZM choices. Hence Z₀ = 1 and ZM+1 = Q2M(Q−η) + ηQZM. Substitution gives QZM = Q2M + (Q−1)(ηQ)M. Multiplying all coordinates by a scalar of prescribed nonzero norm permutes the nonzero fibres. Dividing the remaining Q2M−ZM vectors by Q−1 therefore gives the count for one nonzero target.

BM = Q2M−1 − ηMQM−1.   Density at β = BM/Q2M−1 = 1 − ηMQ−M.

Why does the first residue digit suffice? Given a solution x modulo πj, write a lift as x + πjz. For j ≥ 1 the next digit of its norm changes by the linear functional Tr h(x,z) on the 2M residue coordinates. Here the next digit means the coefficient of πj, viewed in k. The quadratic term in z vanishes modulo πj+1. At an inert place x is nonzero modulo π, so nondegeneracy makes h(x,·) onto the residue extension, and the trace onto k is surjective even in characteristic two. At a split place the functional is u·δv + v·δu, which is nonzero at a unit value u·v. Thus exactly Q2M−1 lifts hit each prescribed next digit. The density ratio stays fixed at every level. This extends the good-place lifting calculation for one unit target to primes above 2. In rank one, successive lifting and completeness also give an integral scalar of any prescribed unit norm. Scaling by this scalar preserves Λ and its Haar measure, so the unit fibres have equal density. This also recovers the answer by dividing the total mass of vectors of unit norm by the volume 1−1/Q of the units.

Take the base field ℚ₂ and M = 3. In the split case, each of the seven nonzero triples u admits four triples v with u·v = 1 over 𝔽₂. In the inert case every nonzero element of 𝔽₄ has norm one. An odd number of the three coordinates must be nonzero, giving 3·3 + 3³ = 36 possibilities. Thus the counts modulo 2 are 28 and 36 among 64, respectively. Modulo 4, a prescribed lift of 1 has 28·32 = 896 or 36·32 = 1152 representations among 4096 vectors. Dividing those proportions by the target mass 1/4 gives 7/8 and 9/8 again. The inert density exceeds one because the mass is measured per unit of target volume.

How do the local densities give the discriminant in the mean?

Return to a totally real field F of degree f, its CM extension E unramified at every finite place, and a lattice self-dual at all those places. In rank M ≥ 3 the one-vector mean identity expresses the normalized average for the target ±1 as a product of densities. Its global proportionality constant is fixed to one by the genus-mass argument. It initially applies to smooth compactly supported archimedean tests. The rank comparison uses nonnegative tests and then exhausts the Gaussian. Each local density uses Fourier self-dual measures for the same additive character on both the vector space and the scalar target. To use the count above, we need the volume of each of the two integral lattices in these measures. At a finite place u, define the integer tᵤ by declaring the annihilator of Oᵤ under the character pairing to be π−tᵤOᵤ. Put Dᵤ = Qᵤtᵤ. The integral trace pairing of an unramified quadratic algebra is perfect, so Hermitian self-duality gives the vector annihilator π−tᵤΛ. For a compact open additive subgroup A, the Fourier transform of its indicator equals vol(A) on its annihilator and zero elsewhere, by translation invariance. Fourier inversion at zero gives vol(A) vol(A⊥) = 1. Enlarging or shrinking by π−tᵤ scales the volume by Dᵤ in one base dimension. The vector lattice has 2M base dimensions, the scalar lattice one. Their respective volumes are therefore Dᵤ−M and Dᵤ−1/2. Dividing the vector volume by the scalar volume gives the corrected density.

αu(β) = Dᵤ1/2−M(1 − ηuMQᵤ−M).

At a real place v, let λv be the nonzero frequency of the character relative to exp(2πit). In the signed diagonal frame the trace pairing on ℂM has real diagonal entries ±2λv, each complex coordinate supplying two real entries. Fourier inversion gives the square root of the absolute determinant as the self-dual volume multiplier, namely 2M|λv|M. The real scalar line contributes |λv|1/2. The local factor for the test function is thus 2M|λv|M−1/2 times its ordinary real density dᵥ at the chosen sign.

All these characters are components of one character trivial on the diagonal copy of F. The adelic character theorem expresses it as the standard trace character scaled by some b ∈ F×. The real frequencies are the real embeddings of b. At finite places the trace-dual of the integers is the inverse different. Thus tᵤ is the valuation of the fractional ideal (b)𝔇 at u, where 𝔇 is the different of F/ℚ. Taking ideal norms gives ∏uDᵤ = |disc(F)| ∏v|λv|, with only finitely many Dᵤ different from one. Bjorn Poonen, Tate’s Thesis, §5.2, Corollary 5.4[58].

The finite Euler factors left in αu multiply to 1/LM for M ≥ 2 by the split and inert Euler product. Thus every frequency cancels. Since the relative different of the unramified quadratic extension E/F is the unit ideal, the discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = |disc(F)|². Equivalently |disc(F)| = (2νE)f. Andrew Sutherland, Definition 12.2, Theorem 12.26 and Proposition 12.27 (different and discriminant in towers)[49].

m = 2Mf|disc(F)|1/2−M/LM = (2νE)f/2νE−Mf/LM.

For instance, rescaling the character by the rational number 2 multiplies ∏v|λv| and ∏uDᵤ by 2f. Their powers M−1/2 and 1/2−M cancel. With the original quotient volume X, the arithmetic evaluation of the integral in the rank comparison is now Xm ∏vdᵥ.

To return to the period maps, compare that mean with its evaluation by unfolding a marked unit vector. This gives a quotient of Hermitian volumes and thereby the denominator in the short-flag probability bound. Controlling the volume lost to those flags enters the upper bound on the available rows. The lower bound on the rank detected by the period maps also needs estimates for the diagonal and mixed entries of their Gram matrices. Those estimates are separate inputs to that dimension argument.

Why does removing a few directions cost so much volume?

Consider a short isotropic flag of total rank J in signature (p, q). Removing it and its dual changes the signature to (p − J, q − J). The flag coefficient involves a quotient of compact volumes. Its largest decrease comes from the last J sphere factors on the p side. To isolate them, write Am for the area of the unit sphere in ℂm+1 and S(r) for the product of the first r such areas, with S(0) = 1.

Am = 2πm+1/m!,   S(p)/S(p−J) = ∏m=p−Jp−1 Am.

The area formula follows by integrating exp(−‖z‖²) over ℂm+1. The integral is πm+1 by taking products of the plane integral. Polar coordinates give the same value as the area times ∫₀∞ exp(−r²)r2m+1 dr = m!/2 times the area. The quotient above cancels all the lower-dimensional spheres. NIST, the radial gamma integral[59] · Gamma at positive integers[60].

Large-rank comparison. Suppose n ≥ 18, 0 ≤ J ≤ p ≤ n, and p − J is at least both n/2 and n − 2√n. Put c = log(2π). Then

log[S(p)/S(p−J)] ≤ J[c − (n − 2√n) log(n/(2πe))].

To prove this, keep the mth term of the exponential series at m. It gives mm/m! ≤ em, hence Am ≤ 2π(πe/m)m. Every surviving index satisfies m ≥ n/2, so the base of this power is at most 2πe/n. It is smaller than one since 2πe < 18. We may therefore replace the exponent m by its lower bound n − 2√n to get an upper bound. Summing the logarithms of the J factors proves the displayed inequality. NIST, exponential series[61].

What can the smaller blocks add back?

Let n = p + q, s = √n and L = log n. The short-flag estimate assumes L ≥ 15, q² ≤ n, and positive rank jumps j₁,…,ja with sum J ≤ q. Then p − J ≥ n − 2s ≥ n/2. At each of the f real places the compact factor is

C = [S(p)/S(p−J)] [S(q)/S(q−J)] ∏i S(jᵢ)−1.

The second bracket contains just J sphere areas. Consecutive areas have ratio Am+1/Am = π/(m+1), so the largest is A₃ = π⁴/3 < 32.5 < exp(3.49). The last inequality already follows from the terms of degree zero through nine in the exponential series. Thus this bracket costs at most 3.49J in the logarithm.

For a jump of rank j each reciprocal area with 0 ≤ m < j is at most m! ≤ jm. Multiplying gives S(j)−1 ≤ jj(j−1)/2. Since j ≤ s, its logarithm is at most (js/2) log s. Summing over the jumps and using log s = L/2 bounds the total cost by JsL/4. Together the three estimates give

log(Cf) ≤ fJ[c − (n − 2s)(L − c − 1) + 3.49 + sL/4].

For a check of the factors at one place, take (p, q) = (32, 4) and two jumps of rank one. The p bracket is A₃₀A₃₁ and has logarithm about −79.25. All the other factors multiply to A₂A₃/A₀² = π⁵/12, adding about 3.24. The compact logarithm is about −76.01. This rank satisfies the large-rank comparison above. The full short-flag probability uses the stronger assumption log n ≥ 15 and also includes the discriminant and zeta factors. It bounds the mass lost in the row-count estimate, which enters the lower bound for the common span of the period columns.

How can small ideals bound a regulator?

The flag coefficient contains one copy of the residue of ζE at 1 for each block of the flag. We first estimate this residue for any totally complex number field E of degree 2f. Write D for its absolute discriminant, Y = √D, h for its class number and R for its regulator. We will prove that for every real s > 1,

hR ≤ Ys (s/(s−1))2f.

Use one embedding σv from each complex conjugate pair, and write ℓv(x) = 2 log |σv(x)|. Their sum is log |NE/ℚ(x)|. On units the sum is zero. Delete the last coordinate. The unit logarithms then form a lattice Λ in ℝf−1 with covolume R, in the same normalization as the coefficient-line mass. We will cover its quotient torus once for each ideal class. Sutherland, Proposition 15.11 and Theorem 15.12, Dirichlet’s unit theorem[62].

Fix a class C and a nonzero integral ideal 𝔟 in its inverse class. For any point t of ℝf−1, append a last coordinate so that the full vector b has sum log(N𝔟 · Y). In ℂf take the product of open discs with radii exp(bᵥ/2). Its Euclidean volume is πfN𝔟 · Y. The lattice 𝔟 has covolume 2−fN𝔟 · Y. Thus the disc product has volume strictly greater than 22f times the covolume. It is convex and symmetric, so Minkowski’s lattice point theorem supplies a nonzero x ∈ 𝔟 with ℓv(x) < bᵥ for every v. The ideal 𝔞 = (x)𝔟−1 is integral and lies in C. The sum of the coordinate gaps is log(Y/N𝔞), so N𝔞 ≤ Y. Sutherland, Theorem 14.13, Minkowski’s lattice point theorem[63].

For each such 𝔞 fix a generator y of 𝔟𝔞. Since y/x is a unit, translating t by its unit logarithm and subtracting the first f−1 coordinates of ℓ(y) leaves the first f−1 gaps bᵥ−ℓv(x). They are nonnegative and their sum is at most log(Y/N𝔞). Thus one translated simplex per small ideal covers the torus. A simplex in k = f−1 coordinates given by uᵢ ≥ 0 and ∑uᵢ ≤ L has volume Lk/k!, by successive integration. In dimension zero its volume is one. Projecting a measurable simplex to the torus can only decrease its volume, as one sees by cutting it along translates of a fundamental domain. Hence R is at most the sum of these simplex volumes over the small ideals in C.

Sum over the h classes. Each nonzero integral ideal of norm at most Y enters once. For u = Y/N𝔞 ≥ 1 the exponential series gives (log u)k/k! ≤ u ≤ us. Extending the sum to all nonzero integral ideals therefore bounds hR by YsζE(s). Above a rational prime p there are at most 2f prime ideals, each of norm at least p. Indeed, the integer ring modulo p has p2f elements and maps onto the product of their residue fields by the Chinese remainder theorem. Unique factorization of ideals now bounds the Euler product by ζ(s)2f. Finally ζ(s) ≤ 1 + ∫1∞t−s dt = s/(s−1), proving the estimate.

What does one zeta residue cost per flag block?

Put d = D1/(2f), so Y = df. Let w be the number of roots of unity in E. The analytic class number formula identifies the coefficient of the simple pole, ρE = lims↓1(s−1)ζE(s), with (2π)fhR/(wY). In particular ρE > 0. The mass summed over the ideal classes of coefficient lines is ΔρE with Δ = 2−fY. Each rank-j block contributes this single residue when its volume is expanded. Its remaining zeta factors are the ordinary convergent values ζE(2),…,ζE(j). Sutherland, Theorem 19.12, analytic class number formula[64].

We need a positive lower bound for L = log d. Minkowski’s ideal-class bound applied to the principal class gives 1 ≤ (2f)! (2f)−2f(4/π)fY. In the factorial ratio the first f factors are at most ½ and the rest at most 1. Hence Y ≥ (π/2)f, giving d ≥ 3/2. Consequently L ≥ 2/5, since log x ≥ 2(x−1)/(x+1) for x ≥ 1, as follows by differentiation. Sutherland, Theorem 14.20, Minkowski’s bound for an ideal class[65].

Take s = 1+1/L in the bound for hR. Now Ys−1 = exp(f) and s/(s−1) = 1+L. Dividing by Y in the residue formula and using w ≥ 1 gives ρE ≤ [2πe(1+L)²]f. The lower bound for L gives 1+L ≤ (7/2)L. Since 2πe < 18 and 18(7/2)² < 16², we obtain

0 < ρE ≤ (16 log d)2f,   ρEa ≤ exp(2fJ(3+n))   if   log d ≤ exp(n).

The second inequality is the one used for one ordered flag type. There are a positive rank jumps with sum J, so a ≤ J. The ambient rank is n. Using 16 ≤ exp(3) gives ρE ≤ exp(2f(3+n)) before raising to the power a. For jumps (1,2), there are two residues and just one ordinary zeta value, ζE(2). The estimate spends the larger budget for J = 3.

The ordinary values have a smaller cost. From the same Euler-product comparison, ζE(r) ≤ ζ(r)2f for every integer r ≥ 2. Using log x ≤ x−1 and summing the nonnegative geometric series gives ∑r≥2 log ζ(r) ≤ ∑m≥2 1/(m(m−1)) = 1. Thus the ordinary values in any one block have product at most exp(2f), and all blocks together cost at most exp(2fJ).

For a check of the normalization, take E = ℚ(√−3) with f = 1 and D = 3. Minkowski’s ideal-class bound is 2√3/π < 2, so every class contains the unit ideal and h = 1. The Eisenstein integers have six units, the six lattice points of norm one, and the unit rank is zero, giving R = 1. The residue is π/(3√3). The coefficient-line mass has the extra factor Δ = √3/2, giving π/6. This example uses the residue theorem for a totally complex field. The flag application additionally assumes the finite-unramified CM data of the dimension estimate.

The large positive index p in the compact volume ratio gives the dominant decrease. The following scalar comparison displays how much of it survives the other factors.

Put s = √n, L = log n and c = log(2π). Express each upper bound as exp(fJ times a cost). The discriminant and power of two cost at most n/3 and 0. How much of the trace can lie deep in the cusp?

On the deep part of the fundamental domain two quantities enter the dimension estimate. The integral of the constant identity term is its value times the volume. The integral of the projection diagonal is the sum of the integrals of |φᵢ|² on that region, one for each orthonormal basis function φᵢ. A small region can carry the whole mass of a unit vector. In the two-point example below, choose the values (0, 1) before normalizing the vector to length one. Shrinking the measure of the deep point increases the diagonal there by exactly the amount needed to keep its trace share equal to one.

Deep-region trace bound. Use the hypotheses for the indefinite count, including the spectral gap, level and signature assumptions. Here n ≥ 8 is the dimension of the Hermitian space, f ≥ 1 the number of real places, q ≥ 1 the negative index with q² ≤ n, d ≥ 1 the root discriminant of the CM field, g ≥ 1 the congruence level, and b ≥ 2 the counting parameter. Set N = n²f and X = nf d g b. Let τ(x) be the least normalized sublattice size at x. A point of the fundamental domain is deep when 0 < τ(x) < X−11q. For the rank-D cuspidal projector the assertion is

∫deep Re K(x,x) dμ(x) ≤ D exp(−N).

The proof uses both cuspidality and a bound on variation. Along the unipotent orbit attached to a short isotropic subspace, every basis function has mean zero. Deep in the cusp, that entire orbit can be represented within a small neighborhood of the point. A function with small variation there and with mean zero must itself be small. Applying this observation also to its successive derivatives gives the power of τ needed to control the diagonal.

Which short sublattice gives the small orbit?

Fix a point x with least normalized sublattice size τ < ½. Write Λ for its lattice, g ≥ 1 for the level, f for the number of real places and d for the root discriminant. Let q bound the real Witt index at every place, the largest dimension of a totally isotropic subspace there. We seek a nonzero rational isotropic space W for which the unipotent radical N of the stabilizer of W has short representatives modulo rational translations and level g. The size we shall obtain is proportional to u = (2τ)1/q.

The canonical lattice filtration groups together the directions of Λ that enter at each successive normalized size. Below ½ its nonzero jumps give a flag 0 = S₀ ⊊ ⋯ ⊊ Sₐ. Label their sizes 0 < t₀ = τ < ⋯ < ta−1 and append the endpoint tₐ = ½. The canonical flag theorem makes every Si+1 saturated in Λ and puts its largest normalized size at tᵢ. For every lattice strictly containing Si+1 inside Λ, the normalized size of its quotient by Si+1 is at least ti+1. Self-duality gives total isotropy of Sₐ. Since the ranks strictly increase and the last rank is at most the local Witt index, 1 ≤ a ≤ q.

Why is there a canonical flag below ½?

At the point x the data are a self-dual Hermitian lattice Λ in an n-dimensional space over the CM field, and a positive definite metric at each real place. A lattice size is a normalized covolume. Its rank enters the exponent so that scaling lengths by a factor c scales the size by c. For a nonzero lattice M, its largest size is the supremum of the sizes of its nonzero quotients M/K, where K is saturated and the quotient carries the quotient metric. Saturation means that the quotient has no torsion. The least size τ of Λ is the infimum of the sizes of its nonzero sublattices.

For t > 0, let F≤t be the sum of all nonzero sublattices whose largest size is at most t, and define F<t using a strict inequality. The Harder–Narasimhan filtration theorem for Hermitian lattices, derived below, supplies the following size properties. Both sums are saturated. When nonzero, the closed step has largest size at most t and the open step has largest size strictly below t. Every nonzero lattice in Λ/F≤t has size strictly greater than t, and every nonzero lattice in Λ/F<t has size at least t. In positive rank the closed step is zero precisely when t < τ and the open step precisely when t ≤ τ.

A jump is a size t for which F<t ⊊ F≤t. Its quotient has size exactly t. Indeed the open-step inequality bounds its size below by t, and the largest size of the closed step bounds it above by t. Every nonzero closed step occurs at a jump. To see this, take s equal to its largest size. The lattice is included among the generators at s and s ≤ t, so F≤s = F≤t. Its largest size equals s, while a nonzero open step at s must have largest size strictly below s. The two steps at s are therefore distinct. The same argument at the largest size of a nonzero open step locates its last jump strictly below its endpoint.

At each jump the rank increases because the quotient of the two saturated steps is nonzero and torsion-free. If s < t, then F≤s ⊆ F<t. Thus distinct jumps have distinct resulting ranks in {1,…,n}. Listing the jumps below ½ in increasing order gives the finite flag. When τ < ½ the first jump is τ, since its open step is zero and its closed step is nonzero. The last lattice is exactly S = F<½. Any jump at ½ itself falls outside this list.

Why do all pairings on the short part vanish?

For a saturated sublattice M, write M⊥Λ = Λ ∩ (span M)⊥. This operation reverses inclusions and takes a step of rank r to one of rank n−r. In the self-dual lattice, successive perpendicular quotients are Hermitian duals of the original quotients, with reciprocal normalized sizes. For example, the quotient dual to M′/M is M⊥Λ/(M′)⊥Λ. The reciprocal formula follows from the determinant pairing, using the dual metrics and the integral Hermitian dual, as shown below. Reversing a semistable filtration preserves semistability after dualizing its pieces. A lower bound on the size of every sublattice in a semistable piece of size s gives an upper bound s on the size of each nonzero quotient, by multiplicativity of determinant volumes. The dual sublattices consequently have size at least 1/s. Thus reversing the canonical list of sizes and inverting each size gives the canonical list again. The endpoint convention is important.

(F<t)⊥Λ = F≤1/t,   (F≤t)⊥Λ = F<1/t.

Indeed the jumps remaining after the strict step have sizes at least t, so the corresponding dual jumps have sizes at most 1/t. At t = ½ this gives S⊥Λ = F≤2. Monotonicity gives S ⊆ F≤2, so every pair of vectors of S has Hermitian pairing zero. The same implication works at any cutoff 0 < t ≤ 1. The choice ½ also ensures that the next endpoint l used in the gap estimate satisfies l² ≤ ¼.

The size inequality for a morphism answers a related question about a specified integral map. If the largest size of its domain is at most H, the least size of the target is at least L, and the map is nonzero, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least L/H. Thus it detects when a proposed small map must vanish. The reciprocal-step identity above identifies the whole orthogonal lattice and gives isotropy directly by inclusion.

To bound the rank, extend the rational span of S to one real place of the base field, hence to a complex Hermitian space of signature (pᵥ,qᵥ). Rationally independent vectors remain independent after this scalar extension. In coordinates in which the form is ‖z+‖²−‖z−‖², projection to either coordinate space is injective on an isotropic subspace. A vector in the kernel of either projection has zero norm also in the other coordinate, and hence is zero. Consequently

a ≤ rank S ≤ min(pᵥ,qᵥ) at every real place v.

Here a is the number of jumps below ½. This proves the inequality a ≤ q used to obtain the exponent 1/q in the orbit radius.

See the strict endpoint on a Gaussian hyperbolic plane

Let Λ = ℤ[i]e ⊕ ℤ[i]b, with ⟨e,b⟩ = 1 and both diagonal pairings zero. Use the compatible positive metric ‖z e + w b‖² = |z|²/16 + 16|w|². The line ℤ[i]e has normalized size ¼. The quotient by it has normalized size 4. Since the full lattice has a quotient of size 4, its largest size is at least 4. Thus the saturated step below ½ contains the first line, has rank at most one, and equals that line. At its first jump F<¼ = 0 and F≤¼ is the line. Correspondingly F≤4 is the full lattice while F<4 is the line. In fact any proper nonzero saturated sublattice is generated by a primitive vector (z,w), whose length is at least ¼. Its quotient has reciprocal size because Λ has normalized determinant volume one. The largest quotient size is therefore 4, attained for w = 0.

The open and closed steps give the finite list. Orthogonal reciprocity then supplies the totally isotropic subspace used by the orbit-cover theorem. The separate size inequality concerns the norm of a specified nonzero morphism.

The product of the a ratios tᵢ/ti+1 is t₀/tₐ = 2τ. At least one is at most (2τ)1/a ≤ u, since 0 < 2τ < 1. Choose such an index i. Put R = Si+1, h = tᵢ, and l = ti+1. The rational span of R is the required W. Two inequalities will pay for two different rounds of approximation.

h/l ≤ u,   h² ≤ u²l² ≤ u/4.

The last step uses l ≤ ½ and u ≤ 1. For example, τ = 1/128 and a = q = 2 give u = ⅛. If the intermediate size is 1/16, both ratios are ⅛. For the second step h = 1/16, l = ½, and h² = 1/256 ≤ u/4 = 1/32.

How do the rational vectors recover the finite lattice?

The filtration uses rational sublattices, although a point of the adelic quotient specifies a lattice at every finite place. Let E/F be the CM extension, h the nondegenerate Hermitian form on En, and L the fixed, finitely generated 𝒪E-lattice spanning that space. Write 𝔸F,f for the finite adeles of F and A = E ⊗F 𝔸F,f. Inside A, let S be the ring generated by 𝒪E and the integral finite adeles of F. Embed rational vectors diagonally and write S·L for the S-span of L. For the finite component gf of the point x, put

M = gf(S·L),   Λx = En ∩ M,   S·Λx = M.

For the last equality, choose nonzero a, b ∈ 𝒪F with aSn ⊆ M ⊆ b−1Sn. A set of generators of L gives an upper denominator, and expressing the coordinate vectors in their E-span gives a lower multiple. Clearing the entries of gf and gf−1 transports both bounds to M. Since E ∩ S = 𝒪E, these bounds show that Λx is a finitely generated lattice of full rank. Now take u ∈ M. Finite approximation gives u = q + aw with q ∈ En and w ∈ Sn. The lower bound puts the error in M, so q ∈ Λx. Each a times a coordinate vector also lies in Λx. Their S-linear combinations include aw, proving the equality.

Why is a diagonal element of the integral ring an algebraic integer?

Choose an F-basis bj of E consisting of algebraic integers and let b′j be its trace-dual basis. For e ∈ E ∩ S, each TrE/F(ebj) is integral at every finite place. Indeed ebj lies in S, whose elements are sums of products of an algebraic integer and an integral finite adele of F. The trace of an algebraic integer belongs to 𝒪F. A diagonal element of F integral everywhere finite has no prime in its denominator. Thus the trace coordinates of e belong to 𝒪F. The module E ∩ S lies in ∑j 𝒪Fb′j and is finitely generated over ℤ, since the ring of integers is a finite ℤ-module. It contains 1 and is preserved by multiplication by e. The finite-module criterion makes e integral over ℤ. The opposite inclusion follows from the definition of S. Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing · Factorization of fractional ideals · Finiteness of the ring of integers · The finite-module criterion.

Why can the error be put in the prescribed multiple of the integral ring?

For one finite coordinate u clear a nonzero denominator d ∈ 𝒪F, so du ∈ S. Modulo da, an integral finite adele of F is represented by one element of 𝒪F. Indeed only the prime powers dividing da impose conditions, and each local residue lifts to the local ring by density in its completion, and the Chinese remainder theorem supplies one global representative. As S is generated by these adeles and 𝒪E, there is an r ∈ 𝒪E with du − r ∈ daS. Dividing by d gives the required approximation by r/d. Residues at one prime power · Chinese remainder theorem.

Why is the lattice at the point self-dual?

Assume now that L is self-dual for h and that gf preserves h. Here h is conjugate-linear in its first argument. Self-duality means that testing the pairings against lattice vectors decides membership. For the rational intersection this gives

y ∈ Λx   ⇔   y ∈ En and h(z,y) ∈ 𝒪E for every z ∈ Λx.

First, S·L is self-dual over S. Its pairings are integral because those on L are integral and conjugation preserves S. Conversely, suppose v pairs integrally with S·L. Choose a nonzero m ∈ 𝒪F with mSn ⊆ S·L and write v = q + mw as above. For z ∈ L, subtracting h(z,mw) from h(z,v) puts h(z,q) in S ∩ E = 𝒪E. Self-duality of L gives q ∈ L, hence v ∈ S·L.

The isometry gf transports this equality with the dual to M. A rational y pairs integrally with Λx exactly when it pairs S-integrally with its full finite span M. Self-duality of M now gives the displayed test. A right factor stabilizing S·L preserves M, so the rational lattice depends only on the finite coset.

Where does the isometry hypothesis enter?

In the Gaussian hyperbolic plane take h((a,b),(c,d)) = ad + bc and 𝒪 = ℤ[i]. Start from 𝒪². At the place over 3, scale the first coordinate by 3 and the second by ⅓. Use the identity elsewhere. The rational intersection is 3𝒪 × ⅓𝒪. Its two basis vectors test 3y₂ ∈ 𝒪 and y₁/3 ∈ 𝒪, exactly the two membership conditions. Scaling only the first coordinate gives 3𝒪 × 𝒪. Its dual contains (1,0), which the lattice omits.

Which positive norms accompany the Hermitian lattice?

Fix a real place of F. It has a pair of conjugate embeddings of E, since E/F is totally imaginary quadratic. At the chosen embedding let H represent h and choose the frame P of the datum with P*HP = D, where D is diagonal with entries ±1. The archimedean component U of the point in this frame preserves D. Set X = PU. At the conjugate embedding use the conjugate frame. In either case X*HX = D for the corresponding embedded form.

vy = X−1w(y),   |w(h(y,z))| = |vy*Dvz| ≤ ‖vy‖ ‖vz‖.

Here w is the embedding used for the coordinates. The diagonal signs preserve Euclidean length, so projecting one vector onto the line of the other gives the inequality. In particular the norm in the frame is positive even on nonzero isotropic vectors. An archimedean compact factor on the right sends X to Xk, so vy changes by the Euclidean unitary transform k−1. Their lengths are therefore well defined on the quotient. The filtration uses these positive norms to measure covolumes, and the perpendicular step uses the integral pairing on the same rational lattice.

Why do the two steps exist with these sizes?

The size properties of the two steps follow from the classical Harder–Narasimhan argument once sizes are read as slopes. Let f be the number of real places of the base field and d = |disc E|1/(2f) the root discriminant of the CM field E. The frames at x realize a sublattice N ⊆ Λ of rank rk N over 𝒪E as a ℤ-lattice ρN of rank 2f rk N in ℂfn, with the majorant metric at every place. Put deg N = −log covol(ρN) and μ(N) = deg N/(2f rk N). Since 𝒪E has covolume (d/2)f in ℂf, the normalized size is

size(N) = ((2/d)f rk N covol(ρN))1/(2f rk N) = (2/d)1/2 e−μ(N).

Small sizes are large slopes. The largest size of N is therefore (2/d)1/2e−μmin(N), where μmin(N) is the least slope of a nonzero quotient of N by a saturated sublattice. Similarly τ = (2/d)1/2e−μmax(Λ), where μmax(Λ) is the greatest slope of a nonzero sublattice. Fix t > 0 and put θ = log((2/d)1/2/t). Then F≤t is the sum Λθ of all nonzero N ⊆ Λ with μmin(N) ≥ θ, and F<t is the sum of those with μmin(N) > θ.

The step at a threshold. Write degθ N = deg N − 2fθ rk N. The condition μmin(M) ≥ θ says that degθ S ≤ degθ M for every S ⊆ M. The degree is supermodular, deg A + deg B ≤ deg(A+B) + deg(A∩B), and ranks add in the same way, so degθ is supermodular too. Consequently, if M satisfies the condition, then degθ T ≤ degθ(T+M) for every T ⊆ Λ. Indeed degθ T + degθ M ≤ degθ(T+M) + degθ(T∩M), and degθ(T∩M) ≤ degθ M. Four facts follow.

  • The sum is finite. Λ is a noetherian 𝒪E-module, so each step is the sum of finitely many of its generators.
  • Lower bound on quotient slopes. If M1 and M2 satisfy the condition, so does M1+M2. For S ⊆ M1+M2, the inequality above, applied with M1 and then with M2, gives degθ S ≤ degθ(S+M1) ≤ degθ(S+M1+M2) = degθ(M1+M2). Hence μmin(Λθ) ≥ θ when Λθ ≠ 0.
  • Saturation. Let N′ be the saturation of Λθ. For S ⊆ N′, degθ S ≤ degθ(S+Λθ) ≤ degθ N′, the second inequality because S+Λθ has finite index in N′. So N′ satisfies the condition and lies in Λθ.
  • Strictness. Every N with Λθ ⊊ N ⊆ Λ satisfies deg N − deg Λθ < 2fθ(rk N − rk Λθ). Otherwise choose a saturated N0 ⊋ Λθ maximizing the ratio (deg N0 − deg Λθ)/(rk N0 − rk Λθ), which is then at least 2fθ. For S ⊆ N0, first degθ S ≤ degθ(S+Λθ). Maximality of the ratio and the bound rk(S+Λθ) ≤ rk N0 then give degθ(S+Λθ) ≤ degθ N0. Thus N0 satisfies the condition and lies in Λθ, a contradiction. The ratio attains a maximum by finiteness at bounded covolume.
Why is the largest slope attained?

Saturating a sublattice preserves its rank and can only lower its covolume. For each possible rank, a lower bound on the degree difference in the ratio gives an upper bound B on the covolume. Only finitely many saturated sublattices meet that bound.

Indeed consider the underlying ℤ-lattice. In a rank-k sublattice of covolume at most B, Minkowski’s convex body theorem gives a nonzero vector of length at most √k B1/k. Its line has a primitive generator u in the ambient lattice. Saturation puts u in the sublattice, and the length bound leaves finitely many choices. For each fixed u, projection off its line leaves a saturated sublattice of rank k − 1 and covolume at most B/‖u‖ in the quotient lattice. Induction gives finitely many projected sublattices, and each has a unique preimage containing ℤu. This argument applies also to the 𝒪E-sublattices, since their saturated quotients are torsion-free over ℤ.

Why the degree is supermodular

Let A′ be the saturation of A in A+B, and C′ the saturation of A∩B in B. Covolumes multiply along saturated sublattices, the quotients carrying the quotient metric: covol(A+B) = covol(A′) covol((A+B)/A′) and covol(B) = covol(C′) covol(B/C′). Since C′ ⊆ A′ and C′ ∩ A = A∩B, the group C′/(A∩B) embeds in A′/A, so covol(A∩B)/covol(C′) ≤ covol(A)/covol(A′). The orthogonal projection away from the span of A maps B/C′ onto (A+B)/A′. It is injective, because an element of B with zero projection lies in A′, so one of its multiples lies in A∩B. It does not increase lengths, so covol((A+B)/A′) ≤ covol(B/C′). Multiplying these relations gives covol(A+B) covol(A∩B) ≤ covol(A) covol(B).

Translating back into sizes gives the stated properties. The open step equals Λθ′ for every θ′ slightly above θ, because its finitely many generators all have μmin > θ. Both steps are therefore saturated. A nonzero closed step has largest size at most t. For the open step the quotient-slope bound holds at θ′ > θ, so its largest size is strictly below t. Every nonzero sublattice of Λ/F≤t has the form N/F≤t. Strictness at θ gives it size greater than t. Applying strictness for θ′ decreasing to θ gives size at least t for every nonzero sublattice of Λ/F<t. Finally Λθ = 0 exactly when μmax(Λ) < θ, that is, when t < τ, and the open step vanishes exactly when t ≤ τ. In the Gaussian hyperbolic plane above, both non-strict inequalities are equalities: F≤¼ is a line of size ¼, and Λ/F<4 has size 4. At t = 4 the closed step is already the whole plane. Its two slope pieces have slopes log 4 and −log 4.

Why are the perpendicular steps dual, with reciprocal sizes?

Write ht(N) = (2/d)f rk N covol(ρN), so that size(N) = ht(N)1/(2f rk N), and normalize quotients in the same way. Heights then multiply along saturated sublattices. The reciprocal formula rests on one identity: for a saturated M ⊆ Λ,

rk M⊥Λ + rk M = n,   ht(M⊥Λ) · ht(Λ) = ht(M).

The general dual lattice. Let A be a lattice spanning V, let A∨ ⊆ Hom(V,E) be its 𝒪E-dual, realized with the dual frames, and let N0 be the annihilator of a saturated N ⊆ A. After identifying the two ambient spaces, the real inner product of ρx with 2ρ∨φ is TrE/ℚ φ(x). Through this pairing, the ℤ-dual of the quotient lattice A/N is the realized trace dual of A intersected with N0, scaled by 2. A lattice and its ℤ-dual have reciprocal covolumes, and covolumes multiply along ρN ⊆ ρA. Finally A∨ is the different times the trace dual, and the norm of the different is |disc E| = d2f. Write k = rk A − rk N. Scaling the trace dual by 2 multiplies its covolume by 22fk, while multiplication by the different multiplies it by d2fk. Hence the unnormalized dual annihilator has covolume (d/2)2fk covol(ρN)/covol(ρA). Applying the height normalization in ranks k, rk A and rk N gives ht(A∨ ∩ N0) · ht(A) = ht(N).

The Hermitian case. Self-duality says that y ↦ h(y,·) maps Λ onto Λ∨. This map sends M⊥Λ onto Λ∨ ∩ M0, and it is an isometry for the dual frames. Indeed each frame satisfies Xw*JXw = diag(±1), and conjugation in E is complex conjugation at every place. The general formula with A = Λ and N = M therefore gives the identity. For M = 0 it reads ht(Λ)² = ht(0) = 1, so ht(Λ) = 1 and ht(M⊥Λ) = ht(M). By the rank formula, (M⊥Λ)⊥Λ is a saturated lattice of the same rank containing M, hence equal to M. Thus ⊥ is an inclusion-reversing involution of the saturated sublattices. By multiplicativity, ht(M⊥Λ/M′⊥Λ) = ht(M′/M)−1 for saturated M ⊆ M′. For rk M < n this gives size(Λ/M) = 1/size(M⊥Λ), so the largest size of Λ is 1/τ.

Set C = F≤t and P = C⊥Λ. Every positive-rank quotient of P by a saturated sublattice is dual to a sublattice beyond C, of size greater than t. Its own size is therefore strictly below 1/t. In the other direction, sublattices of Λ/P have size at least 1/t: saturating can only decrease their size, and each saturated one is dual to a quotient of C of size at most t. These two bounds force P to be the open step at 1/t.

Why do these bounds determine the open step?

If P is nonzero, its largest quotient size is attained and is below 1/t, so P belongs to the sum defining the open step. The inclusion is automatic if P = 0. Conversely, project any generator L of that step to Λ/P. If the image is nonzero, the quotient L/(L ∩ P) has size below 1/t. Orthogonal projection onto the quotient by P is a contraction, so the image has no greater covolume than this quotient in their common rank. This contradicts the lower bound on sublattices of Λ/P. Thus every generator lies in P.

We have proved (F≤t)⊥Λ = F<1/t. Replacing t by 1/t and taking perpendiculars gives the second cutoff identity.

In the Gaussian plane above, h(e, ze + wb) = w, so (ℤ[i]e)⊥Λ = ℤ[i]e, in agreement with (F≤¼)⊥Λ = F<4. The non-isotropic line M = ℤ[i](e + b) has M⊥Λ = ℤ[i](e − b). Here f = 1 and d = 2, so heights are covolumes, and ht(M) = ht(M⊥Λ) = 1/16 + 16 = 257/16. The class of b generates Λ/M. Its squared length after projection off e + b is 16 − 16²/(257/16) = 16/257. Thus the quotient has size 4/√257, while the perpendicular line has size √257/4.

Why are two rounds of approximation enough?

In the filtration 0 ⊂ W ⊂ W⊥ ⊂ V, each matrix of the nilpotent Lie algebra sends a term into the preceding term. Thus all products of three vanish. The matrices sending V into W and vanishing on W⊥ form the central layer. It contains every commutator. In particular exp Y = 1 + Y + Y²/2 and log(exp B exp A) = B + A + [B,A]/2. Both formulas follow by multiplying the quadratic polynomials.

Use the coordinates of the Hermitian space at all real places to write a real orbit element as exp Y. An integral matrix here is a rational matrix preserving Λ under its linear action. Write ‖·‖x for the square root of the sum of squared Hilbert–Schmidt norms in the frames at x. The first covering-radius theorem gives an integral nilpotent matrix Y₀ and a real central matrix C approximating Y/(2g). The second gives an integral central approximation to any real central matrix. With the gap inequalities just proved, their respective radii in this norm are

r₁ = n²f d u/(8√(2f)),   r₂ = n²f d u/(16√f).

The first estimate uses the upper size h of R and the lower size l of every extension quotient. It rounds modulo the real center with error at most r₁. The second uses h² ≤ u/4 and rounds inside the center with error at most r₂. The first comes from approximating maps W⊥/W → W and lifting to the nilpotent algebra. For the second, one approximates maps V/W⊥ → W and subtracts the adjoint of an integral approximation to half the central matrix. To follow the constants, see why the first lift costs √2 and why subtracting the adjoint costs 2. With the two radius bounds in hand, combine the roundings at level g.

Why do both radii involve a ratio of lattice sizes?

Both constructions round a matrix between two lattices. Suppose the source has rank a over the CM field E and the target has rank b. Every nonzero source sublattice has normalized size at least L > 0. Every nonzero quotient of the target by a saturated sublattice has normalized size at most H > 0. The supremum over these quotients is called its largest normalized size. Use the specified Hermitian frames, let f be the number of complex places of E (one over each real place of its fixed field), and write d = |disc E|1/(2f). For any family of complex matrices Tᵥ between these frames there is one E-linear map Φ carrying the source lattice into the target, with

‖T − Φ‖ ≤ ab √f d H/(2L).

Here the norm squares and adds all matrix entries at all f places, then takes a square root. A zero source or target rank makes the error zero. For positive ranks, the integral maps form a full lattice of real dimension D = 2fab. To find an integral map near a prescribed point, use Euclidean lattice transference. In dimension D, a full lattice of dual minimum λ has covering radius at most D/(2λ). Thus it is enough to show λ ≥ 2√f · L/(d H).

What does an integral covector measure? It assigns to each integral map Φ the integer TrE/ℚ(tr(ΨΦ)) for a reverse matrix Ψ. The field trace pairing is nondegenerate, so every integral covector has this form after rational extension. If 𝔇 is the different, then δΨ sends the target lattice into the source for every δ in 𝔇. Indeed, evaluating on rank-one maps tests each scalar pairing of Ψ with a target vector and a source covector. Their traces remain integers after multiplication by every element of 𝒪E. By definition these pairings belong to the inverse different 𝔇−1. The lattice is recovered from its integral dual, giving the assertion.

Suppose Ψ ≠ 0. Its image of the target lattice is nonzero. Multiplying any nonzero sublattice of that image by 𝔇 puts it in the source and multiplies its normalized size by d. In rank r, the index factor is Norm(𝔇)r, with Norm(𝔇) = |disc E| and the size takes the (2fr)th root. Thus the least size in the image is at least L/d. For the target lattice B, put K = B ∩ ker Ψ and I = ΨB, of rank r > 0. The kernel is saturated, and B/K maps isomorphically onto I as an arithmetic lattice. In orthonormal coordinates for the quotient metric and the image metric, the real volume factor at a complex place is the square of the absolute determinant, at most ‖Ψv‖2rop. Multiplying over the places and taking the (2fr)th root bounds size(I)/size(B/K) above by the geometric mean of the operator norms. The numerator is at least L/d and the denominator at most H. This proves the lower bound L/(d H) for that geometric mean. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and the bound of operator norm by Hilbert–Schmidt norm now give ∑v ‖Ψv‖²HS ≥ f(L/(d H))².

The field trace sums twice the real part at each complex place. In Euclidean coordinates the real dual vector therefore has norm 2(∑ ‖Ψv‖²HS)1/2. Substitution into D/(2λ) gives the displayed bound. For example, over ℚ(i), multiplication by 1/2 already has integral field trace on every Gaussian integer. Its real dual vector has length one. The factor two recovers the ordinary Euclidean dual of the square lattice.

How does the map act on a quotient of the original lattice?

Let S be saturated in A, meaning that A/S has no torsion. Write a for the rank of A/S. Let the target be a sublattice R of rank b. Give the quotient its quotient metric and R its induced metric. An integral matrix on these two lattices lifts to a rational matrix on the ambient space by composing projection to the quotient, the rounded map, and inclusion of R. It kills S and sends A into R. At a real place choose orthonormal bases adapted to the source quotient and target subspace. The lifted error can be taken zero on the orthogonal complement and hence has the same sum of squared entries as its rectangular block. The bound holds for this extension of the error from the span of A. In the central application that span is the whole space. In the first layer only the error on the middle quotient is controlled at this stage.
