Isometric frame realizations of arithmetic quotients and sublattices

How does the rectangular covering bound for full lattices in standard coordinate spaces transfer without metric distortion to homomorphisms A/S → R from the quotient of an ambient arithmetic lattice A ⊆ Kn by a saturated sublattice S into an arbitrary finitely generated sublattice R ⊆ Kn, as invoked in the subquotient transport above? Two linear-algebraic realizations supply standard full-rank models at every infinite place while preserving all covolumes and normalized sizes. On the source quotient, choosing an orthonormal basis of the orthogonal complement of the complex span of S inside the complex span of A at each complex place w yields a partial coisometry Qw (QwQw* = 1m) that intertwines a rational quotient matrix q ∈ Mm×n(K) with an invertible m × m frame X′w = qwXwQw*, matching every quotient covolume above S with an ordinary sublattice covolume in Km. On the target sublattice, polar decomposition of the frame-embedded rational basis matrix via the positive-definite Hermitian square root Sw = (Yw*Yw)1/2 extracts an isometric column matrix Pw (Pw*Pw = 1j) and an invertible j × j frame X″w = Sw−1 on a full lattice B ⊆ Kj, preserving the largest normalized quotient size.

1. Coisometric frame realization of a saturated quotient. Let K be a totally complex number field equipped with a ring involution (such as complex conjugation on the CM field E), let n ≥ 0 be an integer, and let X = (Xw)w be a family of invertible matrices Xw ∈ GLn(ℂ) indexed by the complex places w of K, with frame coordinates fX,w(y) = Xw−1yw ∈ ℂn for y ∈ Kn (where yw denotes the coordinatewise image of y at w, and similarly for matrices over K). Let A ⊆ Kn be a finitely generated 𝒪K-submodule and S ⊆ A an 𝒪K-submodule saturated in A under the Euclidean lattice realization ρX : y ↦ (fX,w(y))w, meaning ρX(A) ∩ ℝ · ρX(S) = ρX(S), and set m = rkK(A) − rkK(S) ≥ 0, where rkK(M) = dimK(K · M).

Theorem (Isometric realization of an arithmetic quotient). Under these hypotheses, there exist a rational matrix q ∈ Mm×n(K), invertible frames X′w ∈ GLm(ℂ), and complex matrices Qw ∈ Mm×n(ℂ) at every complex place w of K such that: (a) q vanishes on S, has kernel K · S on K · A, and maps A onto a full finitely generated 𝒪K-lattice q(A) spanning Km; (b) QwQw* = 1m, every vector Qw*z (z ∈ ℂm) belongs to U′w = spanℂ fX,w(A), and u − Qw*Qwu ∈ Uw = spanℂ fX,w(S) for all u ∈ U′w; (c) the frame coordinates intertwine on A via

(X′w)−1(qy)w = Qw fX,w(y)   (y ∈ A);

and (d) for every nonzero 𝒪K-sublattice N′ ⊆ q(A), the pullback N = A ∩ q−1(N′) satisfies S ⊊ N ⊆ A and q(N) = N′, and the normalized quotient size of N/S relative to (X, S) equals the normalized size of N′ in the frame X′.

Proof. Because K · S ⊆ K · A has K-codimension m, choose a K-linear isomorphism (K · A)/(K · S) ≃ Km and extend its composition with K · A → (K · A)/(K · S) across a K-linear complement of K · A in Kn to obtain q ∈ Mm×n(K). By construction q kills S, has kernel K · S on K · A, and maps the finitely generated module A onto an 𝒪K-submodule q(A) with K · q(A) = q(K · A) = Km, proving (a). At each complex place w, invertibility of Xw gives dimℂ U′w = rkK(A) and dimℂ Uw = rkK(S), so the Hermitian orthogonal complement Cw = Uw⊥ ∩ U′w inside ℂn has complex dimension m. Choose an orthonormal basis of Cw for the standard positive-definite inner product on ℂn and place its entrywise conjugates as the m rows of Qw ∈ Mm×n(ℂ). Orthonormality gives QwQw* = 1m and identifies the image of Qw* with Cw ⊆ U′w; for every u ∈ U′w = Uw ⊕ Cw, the vector Qw*Qwu is the orthogonal projection of u onto Cw (equivalently onto Uw⊥), whence u − Qw*Qwu ∈ Uw and ‖projUw⊥(u)‖2 = ‖Qw*Qwu‖2 = ‖Qwu‖2, establishing (b).

Next put Mw = qwXw ∈ Mm×n(ℂ). For every y ∈ S one has MwfX,w(y) = (qy)w = 0, so Mw vanishes on Uw. Setting X′w = MwQw* ∈ Mm(ℂ), every y ∈ A satisfies fX,w(y) − Qw*QwfX,w(y) ∈ Uw ⊆ ker Mw, and therefore (qy)w = MwfX,w(y) = X′w(QwfX,w(y)). Since q(A) spans Km over K, the vectors (qy)w (y ∈ A) span ℂm over ℂ, forcing the square matrix X′w ∈ Mm(ℂ) to be surjective and hence invertible, which gives (c). Finally, for any nonzero 𝒪K-sublattice N′ ⊆ q(A), the preimage N = A ∩ q−1(N′) ⊆ A is finitely generated (since 𝒪K is Noetherian and A is finitely generated), contains S, maps onto N′ because N′ ⊆ q(A), strictly contains S because N′ ≠ 0 whereas q(S) = 0, and satisfies rkK(N′) = rkK(N) − rkK(S) via (K · N)/(K · S) ≃ K · N′. Because ‖(X′w)−1(qy)w‖2 = ‖QwfX,w(y)‖2 = ‖projUw⊥(fX,w(y))‖2 at every place w, the Euclidean quotient lattice of N/S and the Euclidean realization ρX′(N′) are isometric additive images of N, giving equal covolumes and equal normalized sizes as required in (d).

2. Polar decomposition and isometric realization of a sublattice. Retain the totally complex number field K and invertible frames Xw ∈ GLn(ℂ), and let R ⊆ Kn be any finitely generated 𝒪K-submodule of rank j = rkK(R) ≥ 0.

Theorem (Isometric realization of an arithmetic sublattice). There exist a rational inclusion matrix i ∈ Mn×j(K), invertible frames X″w ∈ GLj(ℂ), isometric matrices Pw ∈ Mn×j(ℂ) satisfying Pw*Pw = 1j, and a full finitely generated 𝒪K-lattice B ⊆ Kj spanning Kj such that i maps B bijectively onto R, the frames intertwine at every complex place w via

Xw−1iw = Pw(X″w)−1   (Pw*Pw = 1j),

and the largest normalized quotient size of B in the frame X″ equals that of R in the frame X.

Proof. Choose a K-linear isomorphism Kj ≃ K · R ⊆ Kn with matrix i ∈ Mn×j(K) and choose a K-linear left inverse g : Kn → Kj satisfying g ∘ i = 1j. Set B = g(R) ⊆ Kj; since R ⊆ K · R = im i and g ∘ i = 1j, the map i restricts to an 𝒪K-linear bijection from the finitely generated module B onto R, and K · B = g(K · R) = Kj. At each complex place w, the matrix Yw = Xw−1iw ∈ Mn×j(ℂ) admits the left inverse Lw = gwXw (LwYw = 1j). Consequently Yw*Yw ∈ Mj(ℂ) is Hermitian positive definite with trivial kernel and admits an invertible positive-definite Hermitian square root Sw = (Yw*Yw)1/2 ∈ GLj(ℂ). Defining X″w = Sw−1 ∈ GLj(ℂ) and Pw = YwSw−1 ∈ Mn×j(ℂ) gives Pw*Pw = Sw−1(Yw*Yw)Sw−1 = 1j and Xw−1iw = Yw = PwSw = Pw(X″w)−1. At every place w and every y ∈ Kj, ‖fX,w(iy)‖2 = ‖PwfX″,w(y)‖2 = ‖fX″,w(y)‖2, so i induces a norm-preserving bijection across all sublattices and saturated quotients of B and R, matching their Harder–Narasimhan slopes and largest normalized quotient sizes. Combined with the quotient realization above, for any target family (Tw)w ∈ ∏w Mn(ℂ) vanishing on Uw and mapping U′w into spanℂ fX,w(R), applying the full-lattice covering estimate to (Pw*TwQw*)w between (q(A), X′) and (B, X″) and lifting Φ₀ : q(A) → B to Φ = i ∘ Φ₀ ∘ q completes the subquotient covering bound.

Orthogonal quotient covolume equality and polar rerealization of Harder–Narasimhan slopes

Write f for the number of complex places of the totally complex field K (so [K : ℚ] = 2f) and d = |disc K|1/(2f) for its root discriminant. Under Minkowski’s canonical embedding (w)w : 𝒪K → ⊕w ℂ, a ℤ-basis of 𝒪K forms an ℝ-basis of ⊕w ℂ, so for every complex place w and every scalar z ∈ ℂ an ℝ-linear combination of elements of 𝒪K embeds to z at w and to 0 at every place w′ ≠ w. Acting by such scalar combinations on S identifies the joint ℝ-span ℝ · ρX(S) inside ⊕w ℂn with the direct sum ⊕w Uw of the local ℂ-spans Uw = spanℂ fX,w(S), so the Euclidean orthogonal projection of ⊕w ℂn off ℝ · ρX(S) acts factor by factor as projUw⊥. For any nonzero sublattice N′ ⊆ q(A) with pullback N = A ∩ q−1(N′), the ℝ-linear map (uw)w ↦ (Qwuw)w vanishes on ⊕w Uw, restricts to a Euclidean isometry on ⊕w Cw, and sends the projected lattice of N/S bijectively onto {(QwfX,w(y))w : y ∈ N} = {((X′w)−1(qy)w)w : y ∈ N} = ρX′(N′). Since isometric ℤ-lattices in ℝ-inner-product spaces have equal covolumes and rkK(N′) = rkK(N) − rkK(S), dividing by (d/2)f rkK(N′) and taking the (2f rkK(N′))th root equates the normalized quotient size of N/S to sizeX′(N′).

On the target side, if z ∈ ℂj satisfies Yw*Ywz = 0, then ‖Ywz‖22 = ⟨z, Yw*Ywz⟩ = 0 gives Ywz = 0 and hence z = LwYwz = 0; thus every eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix Yw*Yw is strictly positive, making Sw = (Yw*Yw)1/2 invertible and Hermitian. Because (vw)w ↦ (Pwvw)w is an ℝ-linear isometric embedding of ⊕w ℂj into ⊕w ℂn intertwining ρX″ with ρX ∘ i, every 𝒪K-sublattice M ⊆ B satisfies covol(ρX″(M)) = covol(ρX(i(M))), rkK(M) = rkK(i(M)), and ρX″(B) ∩ ℝ · ρX″(M) = ρX″(M) if and only if ρX(R) ∩ ℝ · ρX(i(M)) = ρX(i(M)). Consequently M ↦ i(M) bijects the proper saturated sublattices of B onto those of R with μ(B/M) = μ(R/i(M)) and equal normalized quotient sizes, giving μmin(B) = μmin(R) and (taking the supremum over proper saturated sublattices, 0 when B = R = 0) equal largest normalized quotient sizes.

Archimedean base change of the orthogonal sublattice, nilradical and center

In the first-layer rounding below and the central rounding, arithmetic approximation operates on the rational lattice intersection P = Λx ∩ W⊥ inside En, whereas the archimedean norm lifts act on the complex Hermitian orthogonal complement (Wv)⊥ ⊆ ℂn at each real place v of F. Why does the complex span of P at v coincide with (Wv)⊥, and why does diagonal archimedean embedding carry rational skew-Hermitian nilradical and central matrices into the corresponding real parabolic layers? Two algebraic facts bridge the rational and archimedean spaces: because the automorphic point lattice Λx spans En over E, clearing denominators in 𝒪E identifies the E-span of P with the rational orthogonal complement W⊥; and for any ring homomorphism ι : E → A intertwining the involutions, linear duality via an E-linear coannihilator projection shows that extending scalars commutes with taking the orthogonal complement of any E-subspace.

Fix an automorphic Hermitian datum of rank n ≥ 0 over a CM extension E/F with CM involution σE and ring of integers 𝒪E, equipped with a Hermitian matrix J ∈ GLn(E) defining the pairing ⟨y, z⟩J = ∑a,b σE(ya)Jabzb on En and a chosen complex embedding φv : E ↪ ℂ above each real place v of F intertwining σE with complex conjugation (writing Jv = φv(J) ∈ GLn(ℂ)). Let x be an adelic point whose rational point lattice Λx ⊂ En is a full self-dual 𝒪E-lattice. For any 𝒪E-submodule R ⊆ En, write W = E · R ⊆ En for its E-span with rational orthogonal complement W⊥ = {y ∈ En : ∀ w ∈ W, ⟨w, y⟩J = 0}, and put P = {y ∈ Λx : ∀ s ∈ R, ⟨s, y⟩J = 0}. At each real place v of F, set spanv(M) = spanℂ φv(M) ⊆ ℂn for any subset M ⊆ En, and write U⊥Jv = {u ∈ ℂn : ∀ w ∈ U, w*Jvu = 0} for the complex Hermitian orthogonal complement of U ⊆ ℂn.

Theorem (Archimedean span of the orthogonal sublattice and parabolic layers). At every real place v of F: (1) spanv(R) = spanℂ φv(W) and spanv(Λx) = ℂn; (2) the complex span of P equals the local Hermitian orthogonal complement,

spanv(P) = (spanv(R))⊥Jv   in ℂn;

and (3) every matrix Y ∈ Mn(E) in the rational stabilizer nilradical of W—meaning Y is skew-Hermitian for J (σE(Y)⊤J + JY = 0) and maps En → W⊥, W⊥ → W, and W → 0—embeds diagonally as (φv(Y))v into the real stabilizer nilradical of (spanv(R))v, while every Y in the rational center (additionally vanishing on W⊥) embeds diagonally into the real center (vanishing on (spanv(R))⊥Jv at every real place v).

Proof. For (1), since φv : E ↪ ℂ is a ring homomorphism, every E-linear combination of elements of R maps under φv to a ℂ-linear combination of elements of φv(R), giving spanℂ φv(W) = spanv(R); because E · Λx = En, the standard basis of ℂn lies in φv(En) ⊆ spanv(Λx), so spanv(Λx) = ℂn. For (2), first identify E · P = W⊥ in En: σE-semilinearity of ⟨·, y⟩J in its first argument ensures P ⊆ W⊥ and hence E · P ⊆ W⊥; conversely, given any y ∈ W⊥ ⊆ En = E · Λx, writing y = ∑k (ak/bk)zk with zk ∈ Λx, ak ∈ 𝒪E, and nonzero bk ∈ 𝒪E over E = Frac(𝒪E) and setting c = ∏k bk ≠ 0 in 𝒪E places cy ∈ Λx ∩ W⊥ = P, whence y = c−1(cy) ∈ E · P. Thus spanv(P) = spanℂ φv(W⊥). Next, for any field E with ring endomorphism σE, any commutative ring A with ring endomorphism σA, any ring homomorphism ι : E → A satisfying ι ∘ σE = σA ∘ ι, any matrix J ∈ Mn(E), and any E-subspace W ⊆ En, scalar extension commutes with taking orthogonal complements: (spanA ι(W))⊥ι(J) = spanA ι(W⊥) in An. Specializing to A = ℂ with complex conjugation and ι = φv yields (spanv(R))⊥Jv = (spanℂ φv(W))⊥Jv = spanℂ φv(W⊥) = spanv(P).

Commutation of orthogonal complements with scalar extension via the dual coannihilator

In An, the inclusion spanA ι(W⊥) ⊆ (spanA ι(W))⊥ι(J) follows directly from A-sesquilinearity and ι ∘ σE = σA ∘ ι, since applying ι to ∑a,b σE(wa)Jabyb = 0 for w ∈ W and y ∈ W⊥ gives ∑a,b σA(ι(wa))ι(Jab)ι(yb) = 0.

For the reverse inclusion, let D ⊆ (En)* be the E-subspace of linear forms spanned by λw(y) = ⟨w, y⟩J = ∑a,b σE(wa)Jabyb for w ∈ W, so that K = W⊥ = {y ∈ En : ∀ f ∈ D, f(y) = 0} is the dual coannihilator of D. Because En is finite-dimensional over the field E, double-annihilator duality identifies the annihilator K0 = {f ∈ (En)* : ∀ y ∈ K, f(y) = 0} with D, and choosing a subspace complement of K in En supplies an E-linear projection π : En → En onto K satisfying π(y) = y for all y ∈ K. For each coordinate index 1 ≤ r ≤ n, the linear form gr(y) = yr − π(y)r vanishes on K and therefore belongs to K0 = D. Now let u ∈ (spanA ι(W))⊥ι(J) ⊆ An, and write e1, …, en for the standard basis of En. Orthogonality against ι(w) for w ∈ W reads ∑s=1n ι(λw(es))us = 0 in A, so E-linearity gives ∑s=1n ι(f(es))us = 0 for every f ∈ D. Evaluating at f = gr (where gr(es) = δrs − π(es)r) yields ur = ∑s=1n ι(π(es)r)us for every 1 ≤ r ≤ n, hence u = ∑s=1n us ι(π(es)) ∈ spanA ι(W⊥) since each π(es) lies in K = W⊥.

Finally, for (3), applying φv entrywise to σE(Y)⊤J + JY = 0 and using φv ∘ σE = conj ∘ φv gives φv(Y)*Jv + Jvφv(Y) = 0, so φv(Y) is skew-Hermitian for Jv. Whenever Y maps an E-subspace U₁ into U₂, ℂ-linearity sends φv(Y)(spanℂ φv(U₁)) into spanℂ φv(U₂). Applying this to En → W⊥ → W → 0 and substituting spanℂ φv(En) = ℂn, spanℂ φv(W) = spanv(R), and spanℂ φv(W⊥) = (spanv(R))⊥Jv from (1) and (2) places (φv(Y))v in the real stabilizer nilradical of (spanv(R))v; if Y additionally vanishes on W⊥, then φv(Y) vanishes on spanℂ φv(W⊥) = (spanv(R))⊥Jv at every real place v, placing (φv(Y))v in the real center.

How do we round a map on the middle quotient?

Keep the isotropic lattice R from the gap in the flag. Let W be its rational span, let Λ be the self-dual Hermitian lattice at x, and put P = Λ ∩ W⊥. Write j = dim W and n = dim V. A nilpotent infinitesimal displacement T kills W and takes W⊥ into W. Restriction to W⊥ therefore gives a map W⊥/W → W. Adding a central displacement leaves that map unchanged. The first rounding takes place in the lattice of integral maps P/R → R.

Covering estimate for maps between lattices. If R has largest normalized size at most h and every lattice M with R ⊊ M ⊆ P has quotient M/R of normalized size at least l > 0, then the restrictions of any family T as above (using the archimedean span of P) admit one rational approximation Φ. It takes P into R and kills R. At each real place choose an extension Dᵥ of the difference (Tᵥ−Φv)|Wᵥ⊥ to the whole space. The extensions can be chosen so that

‖D‖x ≤ j(n−2j) √f d h/(2l).

This is the matrix covering bound for a quotient and a sublattice. Its dimension factor is the product of the two ranks. Nondegeneracy gives dim W⊥ = n−j, so the source has rank n−2j and the target rank j. The theorem realizes both lattices isometrically in their spans, applies a covering estimate for the pair, and carries the approximating map back by the quotient and inclusion. There is one complex place of the CM field above each real place of its totally real subfield. Thus the summed norm uses f places and the discriminant factor is the CM root discriminant d. The covering estimate for the pair of Hermitian lattices is the geometry-of-numbers input here.

Lifting the integral map. We need a skew-Hermitian matrix on all of Λ that still agrees with Φ on P. Since P is the intersection of Λ with a rational subspace, Λ/P is torsion-free. It is finitely generated over the ring of integers, a Dedekind domain, and hence projective. The quotient map therefore splits. Subtracting its splitting composed with the quotient map from the identity gives a projection π from Λ onto P which fixes P. Extend π to the rational vector space and set Ψ = Φπ. Then Ψ(Λ) ⊆ R, Ψ agrees with Φ on P, and Ψ kills W. Torsion-free finite modules over a Dedekind domain[39] · Finite locally free and projective modules[46].

Write Ψ† for the adjoint relative to the original Hermitian form. Self-duality of Λ makes Ψ† integral. Indeed ⟨z,Ψ†y⟩ = ⟨Ψz,y⟩ is integral for all y,z ∈ Λ. Moreover Ψ† kills W⊥, since Ψ has image in W. Its image lies in W⊥, since Ψ kills W. It follows that Y₀ = Ψ − Ψ† is skew-Hermitian and lowers every step of 0 ⊂ W ⊂ W⊥ ⊂ V. On P it is exactly Φ. This construction preserves integrality even at primes above two.

Why does the lift cost only √2 in norm?

At one real place, use the frame at x. In its ordinary positive definite inner product the original form is represented by a Hermitian involution J, with J² = 1. Isotropy makes W and JW orthogonal for the positive definite product. Let H be their joint orthogonal complement. Then JH = H and the original form has W⊥ = W ⊕ H. Restrict D to W ⊕ H and extend by zero on JW. The resulting matrix B has just one block, H → W, because D kills W and maps W⊥ into W. Restriction by an orthogonal projection gives ‖B‖HS ≤ ‖D‖HS.

Let B* be the adjoint for the positive definite product. The matrix A = B − J B*J is skew-Hermitian for the original form and agrees with D on W⊥. Its second block goes from JW to H. These two blocks occupy disjoint entries in an adapted orthonormal basis, and conjugation by the unitary J preserves their Hilbert–Schmidt norms. Therefore ‖A‖HS² = 2‖B‖HS². Sum over the real places and take square roots to get ‖A‖x ≤ √2 ‖D‖x. Now T−Y₀−A is a skew-Hermitian nilpotent matrix that vanishes on W⊥. Its image lies in (W⊥)⊥ = W, so it is a real central matrix C. This gives exactly the approximation T = Y₀ + C + A required by the first round.

‖A‖x ≤ r₁ = n²√f d u/(8√2),   2g r₁ = n²√f g d u/(4√2).

Indeed j(n−2j) ≤ n²/8 because the difference is (n−4j)²/8. Substitute this and h/l ≤ u in the quotient bound and multiply by √2. The orbit calculation takes T = Y/(2g), so its displacement after restoring the original scale is 2gA.

Check the two blocks in dimension four

Let J exchange the first and fourth standard basis vectors and fix the middle two. Take W spanned by the first vector and choose B with its sole unit entry in row 1, column 2. The matrix J B*J then has its sole unit entry in row 2, column 4. Subtracting gives squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm 2 and leaves the prescribed map from the second vector to the first. Here j = 1 and n = 4, so the rank factor 1·(4−2) = 2 attains the bound n²/8.

The first-layer proof uses separate integral and archimedean lifts of the same quotient map. The integral lift only needs to preserve the lattice. The norm estimate is applied to the chosen archimedean residual, and their difference on the whole space is central.

Why is the central error quadratic in the size of the short lattice?

Put j = dimE W and S = Λ ∩ W⊥. A central matrix Z is skew-adjoint and kills W⊥. It has image in W since ⟨Zv,w⟩ = −⟨v,Zw⟩ vanishes for every w ∈ W⊥. The rectangular block to round is therefore a map from V/W⊥ to W. Both have rank j. We will impose the skew-adjoint condition after rounding.

The source and target scales. The largest size in R is at most h. Self-duality of Λ and saturation identify Λ/S with the Hermitian dual of R with its induced metric. To see why this reverses the size, consider a saturated sublattice of Λ/S. Its dual is a quotient of R of the same rank, obtained by restricting the pairing. Their normalized determinant sizes multiply to one. The quotient has size at most h by the definition of the largest size of R, so the source sublattice has size at least 1/h. Passing to a finite-index sublattice can only increase that size. The ratio used in the matrix covering bound is thus h/(1/h) = h².

Apply that bound to Z/2. It gives a rational Φ killing S, sending Λ into R, and satisfying ‖Z/2 − Φ‖x ≤ j²√f d h²/2. Rational spanning extends the kernel condition to W⊥. The target condition extends to the image in W.

How can the rounded map be made skew-adjoint and integral?

Write Φ† for the adjoint with respect to the original Hermitian form. Take Z₀ = Φ − Φ†. Its adjoint is −Z₀. The kernel and image conditions on Φ give the same two conditions on Φ† by taking orthogonal complements. To check integrality, let v,w ∈ Λ. The pairing of Φ†v with w is integral because it equals the pairing of v with Φw ∈ Λ. Self-duality gives Φ†v ∈ Λ. Thus Z₀ belongs to the integral central lattice.

In each adapted frame the adjoint conjugate-transposes a matrix and multiplies its rows and columns by signs. This preserves the sum of squared absolute entries. Writing D = Z/2 − Φ, the skew-adjointness of Z gives Z − Z₀ = D − D†. The triangle inequality costs a factor of two. Isotropy gives j ≤ n/2, and the selected flag gap gives h² ≤ u/4. Consequently

‖Z − Z₀‖x ≤ j² √f d h² ≤ n² √f d u/16 = r₂.

The correction created by the first rounding has central value C′. Applying this estimate to C′/g gives the error g r₂ in the factorization below.

For a Gaussian hyperbolic plane, write E₁₂ for the matrix with a single 1 in its upper-right corner. For Z = (5i/4)E₁₂ the nearest Gaussian multiple to its half is Φ = iE₁₂. Subtracting the adjoint gives 2iE₁₂, at distance 3/4 in the ordinary matrix norm. The integral central matrix iE₁₂ is only 1/4 away. The proof needs a bound on the distance to its constructed point.

Combining the two roundings at level g

Put B = 2gY₀ and A = Y − B − 2gC, so ‖A‖x ≤ 2gr₁. Multiplying exp B by exp A introduces [B,A]/2. To cancel it, the central quantity that must still be represented is C′ = 2gC + [A,B]/2. Round C′/g to an integral central matrix Z₀, and put Z = C′ − gZ₀. Then ‖Z‖x ≤ gr₂. With E = 2gY₀ + gZ₀, the two corrections give

exp Y = exp E exp A exp Z,   ‖A‖x + ‖Z‖x ≤ n²√f g d u/4.

Indeed the two costs are n²√f g d u times 1/(4√2) and 1/16. Their sum is at most ¼ because √2 ≥ 4/3. The full two-parameter family exp(sA) exp(tZ) stays in the same real unipotent radical for all real s,t. Thus the path joining the representative to x also lies on the orbit.

It remains to check what exp E does at the finite places. A central matrix has zero product with every matrix of this nilpotent algebra. Consequently exp E − 1 = g(2Y₀ + Z₀ + 2gY₀²). This sends Λ into gΛ. Replacing Y₀ and Z₀ by their negatives checks the same condition for the inverse. This explains the factor 2 in the first rounding even when g is odd. The rational element γ represented by exp E therefore has finite component satisfying xfin−1γfinxfin ∈ K(g), the level subgroup. Its inverse k also belongs to K(g). Restoring the frames, we get

(ν,1)x = γ y (1,k),   yfin = xfin.

Here ν is the given real unipotent element and y has the two real displacements just bounded. For a general adelic element m of the radical, strong approximation gives a rational δ in the radical such that xfin−1(δ−1m)finxfin lies in the open group K(g). Left rational invariance and right level invariance therefore identify each function value at mx with its value at ((δ−1m)∞,1)x. The small real representatives now control the entire orbit used for the cuspidal average.

Why can a rational correction put the finite component in the level?

The level allows an open neighborhood of the given finite component. To find a rational point in that neighborhood, use the same nilpotent coordinates as in the rounding argument. Exponential and logarithm are inverse polynomials, exp(T) = 1 + T + T²/2 and log(1 + T) = T − T²/2. They preserve rationality and are continuous over the finite adèles. A basis of the Lie algebra over the base field F thus reduces the question to approximating one finite adèle by a number in F, independently in each coordinate.

An open condition on a finite adèle prescribes precision at finitely many primes and integrality elsewhere. Multiply by a common nonzero integer d clearing all denominators. At the selected primes prescribe the required residue of the integral numerator modulo a sufficiently high prime-ideal power. At any further prime dividing d, prescribe divisibility by the local factor of (d) to preserve integrality after division. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a single numerator in the integers of F. Dividing by d gives the required rational coordinate. Applied to all coordinates and followed by exponentiation, this supplies δ in the desired open set.

How mean zero bounds the value at a single point

At a fixed deep point x write v(x) for the vector of the D values of the continuous cuspidal representatives. The orbit uses its invariant probability measure ν. The constant term vanishes in each coordinate. Strong approximation for the unipotent group brings orbit representatives to the small neighborhood modulo rational translations and the finite level, and continuity gives the zero average at the chosen point. If every orbit value differs from v(x) by at most a, then

‖v(x)‖ = ‖∫ [v(x) − v(u x)] dν(u)‖ ≤ ∫ ‖v(x) − v(u x)‖ dν(u) ≤ a.

For any point y of the neighborhood the same variation estimate gives ‖v(y) − v(x)‖ ≤ a. Adding the value at the center costs a second a. This factor of two makes the bound valid everywhere it will be used at the next step.

How many times can the variation estimate be applied?

Fix x and abbreviate τ(x) to τ. The unipotent orbit covering theorem supplies a neighborhood of radius ρ = n²√f g d (2τ)1/q/4. The filtered space of test vectors of order ≤ P is obtained by applying at most P archimedean derivatives to the lowest-type vectors. A derivative therefore takes a test vector to the next space. With a bound M per unit vector on that next space, the derivative estimate gives variation at most ρ√f βM on the orbit and in the neighborhood. The preceding argument replaces M by 2ρ√f βM one order lower. Use the common upper bound β = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3(8qN + N), valid at every order required here.

The initial bound at order 8qN is a local Sobolev evaluation estimate. Descend to order zero in 8qN applications. At a unit lowest-type vector, the squared norm of its vector of values is the projection diagonal. Squaring the repeated factor gives (2ρ√f β)16qN. In particular its power of τ is 16N. The initial squared evaluation bound contains (17√n/τ²)2N, which costs τ−4N. The product thus gains τ12N. As a scale check, halving τ while holding the counting data fixed multiplies this bound by 2−12N.

How large can an archimedean derivative be?

At order P, let VP be the span of vectors obtained from tensors of lowest compact-type vectors by applying at most P derivatives. A derivative in direction X is ∂Xw = (d/dt)σ(exp(tX))w at t = 0. A direction supported at one real place v belongs to the Lie algebra of its unitary group. Write ‖X‖HS for its Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Use the indefinite counting hypotheses. In particular n ≥ 8, the representations are unitary discrete series, and each coordinate of the Harish-Chandra parameter λ at each real place satisfies |λᵢ| ≤ b².

Derivative bound. The spaces VP are finite dimensional and preserved by the product of the maximal compact groups. Their vectors are differentiable along every real one-parameter subgroup, and one derivative takes VP into VP+1. For w ∈ VP and any one-place direction,

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ ‖X‖HS βP ‖w‖,   βP = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3P.

Here is why the dependence on P is linear. At one place write Eij for the operators representing the matrix units in the complexified Lie algebra. The compact roots eᵢ−eⱼ join two coordinates with the same signature sign. The noncompact roots join opposite signs. Let ρc and ρn be the half sums of the respective positive roots (i < j). The starting compact highest weight is Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. The counting hypotheses separate opposite-sign parameter coordinates by a common gap h ≥ 120nq3/2, where q is the real Witt index. The lowest-type multiplicity and infinitesimal-character theorems identify this compact type and give the scalar of the full quadratic Casimir operator on its generated module. Harris, Kobayashi and Speh, §2.3, formula (2.24)[66].

Moving a compact generator past a noncompact one adds their commutator, which is again a sum of noncompact generators. Thus words of length at most P lie in the compact-stable space obtained by applying at most P noncompact generators to the starting compact type. In one such step, the tensor-product rule with the off-diagonal block permits the old compact highest weight or a shift by a root joining opposite signs. The root eᵢ−eⱼ has Euclidean norm √2. By compact-type decomposition and induction, every highest weight μ seen by order P satisfies ‖μ−Λ‖ ≤ √2P. This bound on possible compact types holds for the entire span of words.

How does a bound on weights control every vector?

In matrix-unit coordinates let Ω be the sum of Eᵢⱼ Eⱼᵢ over all pairs and let ΩK be the same sum over same-sign pairs. On the common space of smooth vectors, unitarity gives Eᵢⱼ* = Eⱼᵢ for equal signs and Eᵢⱼ* = −Eⱼᵢ for opposite signs. Summing the squared norms therefore gives the energy identity

∑i,j ‖Eᵢⱼ w‖² = Re ⟨w, (2ΩK−Ω)w⟩.

On a compact type μ the scalar of ΩK is ‖μ+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖². On the generated module the scalar of Ω is ‖λ‖²−‖ρc+ρn‖². Put L = ‖λ‖ and A = ‖ρn‖ + √2P. The preceding weight bound gives ‖μ+ρc‖ ≤ L + A. Since the compact action is unitary, its finite-dimensional space splits orthogonally into compact types. The same upper bound for the compact Casimir quadratic form then applies to their sum, including linear combinations w.

The full half sum has coordinates (n+1−2i)/2 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, giving squared norm n(n²−1)/12. Each coordinate of ρn has absolute value at most n/2. Thus ‖ρn‖ ≤ n3/2/2, and L ≤ √n b². For a unit vector the energy is consequently at most

2(L+A)²−L²+n³/12 ≤ (L+2A+0.3n3/2)² ≤ βP².

For the first inequality, (L+2A)² already exceeds 2(L+A)²−L² by 2A², and 0.3² ≥ 1/12. For the second, 2√2 ≤ 3 and 1 + 0.3 ≤ 3/2. This proves a bound on the sum of the squared generator norms. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to ∂Xw = ∑ Xᵢⱼ Eᵢⱼ w gives the one-place estimate. Tensoring with the other places preserves the squared bound, as one sees by expanding in an orthonormal basis of the other factors. For simultaneous directions X = (Xᵥ), the derivative is the sum of the one-place derivatives. The product rule, the triangle inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ √f (∑v ‖Xᵥ‖²HS)1/2 βP ‖w‖.

The descent in the cusp starts at order P₀ = 8qN, where N = n²f, and uses the simultaneous-direction bound. The Sobolev estimate at the starting order needs up to N more derivatives, each in a unit direction supported at a single place. Since βP increases with P, β = βP₀+N works for both steps. For example, the dimensions n = 8, f = q = 1 give N = 64 and P₀ = 512. Taking one constant through order 576 contributes 1728 to β from differentiations. This example counts orders and leaves the parameter gap and the bound b in force.

How an integral controls the starting value

The mean-zero argument starts with a bound for evaluation at every point y in a neighborhood of a deep point x. The available norm is an integral over the whole quotient. To pass from that norm to a value at y, we first average along short curves through y, then count how often their coordinate neighborhood can cover the same point of the quotient.

Evaluation along one curve. For a continuously differentiable complex function h on [0, s], integration of its derivative and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give |h(0)| ≤ |h(t)| + √s (∫ |h′|²)1/2 for every t in that interval. Square using (a + b)² ≤ 2a² + 2b² and average over t. The resulting endpoint estimate is

|h(0)|² ≤ (2/s) ∫0s |h(t)|² dt + 2s ∫0s |h′(t)|² dt.

There are N = n²f real directions, an orthonormal Lie algebra basis of size n² at each of f places. Write Fw for the continuous representative of one automorphic image of a test vector w. Along the jth one-parameter subgroup the derivative of Fw is F∂ⱼw. Differentiating raises the allowed order of the vector by one. Suppose the integral of |Fw|² on the full parameter cube is at most C(y)‖w‖² for all vectors through order P + N, and ‖∂ⱼw‖ ≤ β‖w‖ at the orders where a derivative is taken.

Use the subgroups in a fixed product order. For fixed values of the first N − 1 parameters apply the endpoint estimate in the last one, then integrate in the first N − 1. The two full-cube integrals are bounded by C(y)‖w‖² and C(y)‖∂Nw‖². Thus removing one parameter costs at most 2/s + 2sβ². The bound on the smaller cube holds through order P + N − 1. After N removals the cube is the point y, and all vectors through order P are still covered. With s = 1/β each removal costs 4β. The stated estimate rounds (4β)N up to (6β)N.

How often does the cube cover a quotient point?

Write t(y) = min(1, τ(y)), where τ is the least normalized sublattice size. Let P∞ = ∏v cv be the product of the gauge constants that specify real-place Haar measures, and let kg be the positive Haar volume of the finite level subgroup Kg.

Change of variables in the small cube. For 12n³s ≤ 1 and 8n⁵s ≤ 1, the quantitative exponential-coordinate theorem bounds the parameter integral of any nonnegative measurable function by efP∞ times its Haar integral on a set S at the real places. Any two matrices in S differ multiplicatively by a matrix of operator norm at most 2 at each place. The factor ef allows a Jacobian loss of at most e at each place.

Extend S by Kg at the finite places. The squared representative is invariant under right translation by Kg, so this extension multiplies its integral by kg. When we fold the translate y(S × Kg) into a fundamental domain, each point z is counted once for each rational translate γz inside it. Fix one such γ₀ if any exist. The ratios γγ₀−1 are distinct rational transformations that preserve the finite lattice at y. In coordinates at y their operator norms are at most 2 at each real place.

The lattice separation inequality gives a lower bound t(y)² for the geometric mean over the real places of the operator-norm distances between two distinct such matrices. To see the two factors, take the difference of the corresponding rational transformations. It sends the lattice at y into itself and has nonzero image. For such a map between lattices, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least the least size of the target divided by the largest size of the source. Here the target has least size τ(y). The Hermitian lattice is self-dual, so duality reverses the filtration and replaces each size by its reciprocal. The largest size of the source is 1/τ(y). Their quotient is τ(y)², which is at least t(y)² after truncation. At least one local distance is therefore ≥ t(y)². In the maximum of the local norms, the open balls of radius t(y)²/2 about the matrices are disjoint. They lie in the ball of radius 2 + t(y)²/2. Volumes scale with exponent 2N, the real dimension of f spaces of complex n × n matrices. Their volume ratio bounds the multiplicity by (1 + 4/t(y)²)2N. Enlarging 4 to 4√n gives the bound used in the count. Dividing by the finite volume introduced above gives the cube constant

C(y) = ef (1 + 4√n/t(y)²)2N P∞/kg.

Under the hypotheses of the indefinite count, choose P = 8qN and β = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3(P + N). Since n ≥ 8 and n19 ≤ b², the chosen s = 1/β satisfies both small-cube conditions. Each of the D isometric automorphic maps sends a vector u to a function of quotient norm ‖u‖. The lattice-size comparison on a unipotent neighborhood of radius at most log 2 gives t(y) ≥ t(x)/2 = τ(x)/2 throughout the deep-point neighborhood. Riemannian Haar gauge and the ordered exponential-cube Jacobian bound

Two local calibrations underpin the Sobolev cube estimate and the deep-trace cancellation. On an abstract real unitary group U(ε), a Haar measure με is determined only up to a positive scalar multiple, yet its normalization must cancel between the local passage from Euclidean parameter coordinates to με and the global comparison of με with Riemannian sphere volumes. Fixing the unique scalar cε > 0 for which cεμε assigns unit asymptotic density relative to the Euclidean ball volume ωn²rn² in Hilbert–Schmidt distance provides a single intrinsic gauge connecting both ends. At the same time, the iterated endpoint inequality integrates along the ordered product of one-parameter subgroups Θ(t) = exp(t₁E₁) ⋯ exp(tn²En²) rather than the flat Lie algebra exponential. Because the factors do not commute, translating a perturbation in the ith coordinate across the remaining factors conjugates Ei and distorts Euclidean balls by at most δ = n(exp(2n²s) − 1) in operator norm; when δ ≤ 1/2, contraction inversion guarantees that the image of a closed Euclidean ball of radius r contains a left-translated Hilbert–Schmidt ball of radius λr for every 0 < λ < 1 − δ, and Vitali–Besicovitch covering converts this infinitesimal inclusion into a global Jacobian bound of at most (1 − δ)−n² ≤ exp(2n³(exp(2n²s) − 1)).

1. Existence and uniqueness of the Riemannian Haar gauge. Let n ≥ 0 be an integer and let ε = (ε₁, …, εn) ∈ {±1}n be a sign vector with diagonal signature matrix Jε = diag(ε₁, …, εn) ∈ GLn(ℂ). Define the real unitary group U(ε) = {u ∈ GLn(ℂ) : u*Jεu = Jε} and its real Lie algebra 𝔤ε = {X ∈ Mn(ℂ) : X*Jε + JεX = 0} of real dimension n², equipped with the real trace pairing ⟨X, Y⟩ = Re tr(XY*) and Hilbert–Schmidt norm ‖X‖HS = (Re tr(XX*))1/2. Let ωn² denote the Lebesgue volume of the unit Euclidean ball in ℝn², and fix any left Haar measure με on U(ε).

Theorem (Riemannian Haar gauge). There exists a unique real scalar cε > 0 such that

limr → 0+ cε με({u ∈ U(ε) : ‖u − 1‖HS ≤ r}) / rn² = ωn².

Proof. When n = 0, ℝ⁰ = {0} has ω₀ = 1, U(ε) = {1}, and {u ∈ U(ε) : ‖u − 1‖HS ≤ r} = {1} for every r > 0, so cε = 1/με({1}) > 0 is unique. For n ≥ 1, the matrix exponential exp : 𝔤ε → U(ε) is strictly differentiable at 0 with derivative equal to the Hilbert–Schmidt isometric inclusion ι : 𝔤ε ↪ Mn(ℂ). Hence exp restricts to a homeomorphism from a small closed ball B̄(0, δ₀) ⊂ 𝔤ε onto a compact neighborhood of 1 in U(ε), and because group multiplication in exponential coordinates agrees with vector addition to first order near 0, left-invariance of με makes the pulled-back measure asymptotically translation-invariant at small scales, yielding a finite positive limit A₀ > 0 for με(exp(B(0, r))) / (ωn²rn²) as r → 0+. Since ‖exp(X) − 1 − X‖HS = o(‖X‖HS) as X → 0, for every κ > 1 and all sufficiently small r > 0 the group ball {u ∈ U(ε) : ‖u − 1‖HS ≤ r} contains exp(B(0, κ−1r)) and lies inside exp(B(0, κr)). Dividing by rn², letting r → 0+, and then letting κ → 1+ identifies limr → 0+ με({u ∈ U(ε) : ‖u − 1‖HS ≤ r}) / rn² = A₀ωn² = A > 0, so cε = ωn²/A > 0 is unique.

2. Ordered exponential-cube Jacobian bound. Retain U(ε), με, and its Riemannian Haar gauge constant cε > 0. Let E₁, …, En² ∈ 𝔤ε be a real orthonormal basis for Re tr(XY*), define the ordered product exponential chart Θ : ℝn² → U(ε) by Θ(t) = exp(t₁E₁) ⋯ exp(tn²En²) for t = (t₁, …, tn²) ∈ ℝn², and let s > 0 satisfy n(exp(3n²s) − 1) ≤ 1/2.

Theorem (Ordered exponential-cube integral inequality). For every nonnegative measurable function Φ : U(ε) → [0, ∞],

∫[0,s]n² Φ(Θ(t)) dt ≤ exp(2n³(exp(2n²s) − 1)) · cε ∫Θ([0,s]n²) Φ(y) dμε(y).

Proof. On the cube [0, s]n², expanding Θ(t) − Θ(t′) telescopically around its linear part ∑i=1n² (ti − t′i)Ei yields ‖Θ(t) − Θ(t′)‖HS ≥ (1 − n(exp(3n²s) − 1))‖t − t′‖₂ ≥ (1/2)‖t − t′‖₂, so Θ is injective on [0, s]n² and hence on the interior (0, s)n², whose complement in [0, s]n² has Lebesgue measure zero. At each interior point t ∈ (0, s)n², left-multiplying the strict derivative Lt of Θ by Θ(t)−1 differs from the Euclidean-to-Hilbert–Schmidt isometric basis map v ↦ ∑i=1n² viEi by at most δ = n(exp(2n²s) − 1) ≤ 1/2 in operator norm. Quantitative contraction inversion on small closed balls around t therefore shows that for every 0 < λ < 1 − δ and all sufficiently small r > 0 with B̄(t, r) ⊆ (0, s)n², every g ∈ U(ε) with ‖g − 1‖HS ≤ λr satisfies Θ(t)g ∈ Θ(B̄(t, r)). By left-invariance of με and the Haar gauge limit at scale λr, letting r → 0+ and λ ↑ 1 − δ bounds ωn²rn² ≤ K · cεμε(Θ(B̄(t, r))) up to any slack factor above (1 − δ)−n² ≤ exp(2n²δ) = K, where K = exp(2n³(exp(2n²s) − 1)) uses 1 ≤ (1 − δ)e2δ on 0 ≤ δ ≤ 1/2. Applying the Besicovitch–Vitali covering theorem on ℝn² together with injectivity of Θ on (0, s)n² bounds Lebesgue measure on (0, s)n² by (K cε) times the pullback of με, and monotone approximation by simple functions integrates every nonnegative measurable Φ. Under the small-cube conditions 8n⁵s ≤ 1 and 12n³s ≤ 1 of the Sobolev multiplicity bound, one has n(exp(3n²s) − 1) ≤ 1/2 and 2n³(exp(2n²s) − 1) ≤ 1, so K ≤ e at each of the f real places of F; taking the product over the real places with P∞ = ∏v cv produces the prefactor efP∞.

Telescopic expansion of the ordered exponential, ball inclusion, and small-cube constants

Each orthonormal basis matrix Ei ∈ 𝔤ε satisfies ‖Ei‖op ≤ ‖Ei‖HS = 1, so for t, t′ ∈ [0, s]n² every partial product of exp(±tjEj) or exp(±t′jEj) has operator norm at most exp(n²s). Writing Pi−1(t) = ∏j<i exp(tjEj) and Si+1(t′) = ∏j>i exp(t′jEj), the telescopic sum Θ(t) − Θ(t′) = ∑i=1n² Pi−1(t)(exp(tiEi) − exp(t′iEi))Si+1(t′) differs from ∑i=1n² (ti − t′i)Ei in Hilbert–Schmidt norm by at most ∑i=1n² |ti − t′i|(exp(3n²s) − 1) ≤ n(exp(3n²s) − 1)‖t − t′‖₂ by Cauchy–Schwarz across the n² coordinates. Since ‖∑i (ti − t′i)Ei‖HS = ‖t − t′‖₂ by orthonormality, the reverse triangle inequality gives ‖Θ(t) − Θ(t′)‖HS ≥ (1 − n(exp(3n²s) − 1))‖t − t′‖₂.

Similarly, at t ∈ (0, s)n² the ith partial derivative of Θ equals Pi−1(t)Ei exp(tiEi)Si+1(t) = Θ(t)(Si+1(t)−1EiSi+1(t)), and ‖Si+1(t)−1EiSi+1(t) − Ei‖HS ≤ exp(2n²s) − 1; Cauchy–Schwarz over 1 ≤ i ≤ n² bounds ‖Θ(t)−1Lt(v) − ∑i viEi‖HS ≤ n(exp(2n²s) − 1)‖v‖₂ = δ‖v‖₂. Composing v ↦ Θ(t)−1Θ(t + v) with the local inverse of exp : 𝔤ε → U(ε) near 1 produces a strictly differentiable map Ft from a neighborhood of 0 in ℝn² to 𝔤ε whose derivative at 0 has inverse norm at most (1 − δ)−1; Banach’s contraction principle on small closed balls implies that for any 0 < λ < 1 − δ, choosing κ > 1 with κλ < 1 − δ ensures Ft(B̄(0, r)) ⊇ B̄𝔤ε(0, κλr) and hence Θ(B̄(t, r)) ⊇ {Θ(t)g : g ∈ U(ε), ‖g − 1‖HS ≤ λr} for all small r > 0. Finally, for n = 0 all exponents vanish, while for n ≥ 1 the inequalities 12n³s ≤ 1 and 8n⁵s ≤ 1 imply 3n²s ≤ 1/4 ≤ 1, 2n²s ≤ 1/6 ≤ 1, and (using eu − 1 ≤ 2u for 0 ≤ u ≤ 1) both n(exp(3n²s) − 1) ≤ 6n³s ≤ 1/2 and 2n³(exp(2n²s) − 1) ≤ 8n⁵s ≤ 1, while any two elements y₁, y₂ ∈ Θ([0, s]n²) satisfy ‖y₁y₂−1 − 1‖op ≤ exp(2n²s) − 1 ≤ 4n²s ≤ 1 and hence ‖y₁y₂−1‖op ≤ 2.

Projective endomorphism reduction and the congruence level index

Why does passing from the full finite-adelic lattice stabilizer K₀ to the principal congruence subgroup Kg of integer level g ≥ 1 multiply the quotient covolume by at most g2N = g2n²f, even when the reference 𝒪E-lattice L ⊂ En is not free over 𝒪E? Over a CM field E of nontrivial class group, L need not admit a global 𝒪E-basis, and elements of K₀ act on the finite-adelic completion Lfin rather than on L itself. Because 𝒪E is a Dedekind domain, however, every finitely generated torsion-free 𝒪E-module L is projective. Combining finite-adele strong approximation on a finite generating set with projectivity of L lifts the modulo-g action of each x ∈ K₀ to a global 𝒪E-linear endomorphism φ(x) ∈ End𝒪E(L). Left cosets of Kg in K₀ then inject into End𝒪E(L)/g End𝒪E(L), whose underlying free ℤ-module has rank at most dimℚ Mn(E) = 2n²f.

Fix an automorphic Hermitian datum of rank n ≥ 0 over a CM extension E/F of real degree f = [F : ℚ] (so [E : ℚ] = 2f), with reference finitely generated full 𝒪E-lattice L ⊂ En and finite-adelic completion Lfin = (E ⊗F 𝒪̂F) · ι(L) inside (E ⊗F 𝔸F,fin)n, where ι denotes the diagonal inclusion and 𝒪̂F = ∏v∤∞ 𝒪F,v. Let K₀ ⊂ G(𝔸F,fin) be the compact finite-adelic stabilizer of Lfin, let Kg = {x ∈ K₀ : (x − 1)Lfin ⊆ g Lfin} be the congruence level subgroup for an integer g ≥ 1, and let μfin be any Haar measure on G(𝔸F,fin), writing kg = μfin(Kg) and N = n²f.

Theorem (Congruence level index bound). For every integer g ≥ 1, the subgroup Kg contains an open neighborhood of the identity in G(𝔸F,fin), satisfies 0 < kg ≤ μfin(K₀) < ∞, and obeys

μfin(K₀) ≤ g2n²f μfin(Kg) = g2Nkg.

Proof. In the finite-adele congruence topology, K₀ is compact, whence μfin(K₀) < ∞, and the condition (x − 1)Lfin ⊆ g Lfin cuts out an open subgroup Kg ⊆ K₀, whence kg = μfin(Kg) > 0. Because L ⊂ En is a finitely generated torsion-free module over the Dedekind domain 𝒪E, L is projective over 𝒪E. For each x ∈ K₀, approximating the finite-adelic coordinates of x · ι(y) ∈ Lfin modulo g(E ⊗F 𝒪̂F) by elements of 𝒪E on a finite generating set and lifting along a projective splitting produces a global endomorphism φ(x) ∈ End𝒪E(L) such that x · ι(z) − ι(φ(x)(z)) ∈ g Lfin for all z ∈ L. Whenever x, y ∈ K₀ map to the same coset in End𝒪E(L)/g End𝒪E(L), writing φ(x) − φ(y) = gθ with θ ∈ End𝒪E(L) gives (x − y)ι(z) ∈ g Lfin for every z ∈ L, hence (x − y)Lfin ⊆ g Lfin by (E ⊗F 𝒪̂F)-linearity; since y−1 ∈ K₀ stabilizes Lfin and g Lfin, one obtains (y−1x − 1)Lfin ⊆ g Lfin, so y−1x ∈ Kg and x ∈ y Kg. Covering K₀ by at most |End𝒪E(L)/g End𝒪E(L)| left translates of Kg and bounding the ℤ-rank of End𝒪E(L) by 2n²f yields μfin(K₀) ≤ g2n²fμfin(Kg).

Projective splitting lift and ℤ-rank bound on the lattice endomorphism ring

Choose generators u₁, …, us ∈ L over 𝒪E and let π : 𝒪Es → L be the surjection sending the jth standard basis vector ej to uj. Projectivity of L over 𝒪E supplies an 𝒪E-linear section σ : L → 𝒪Es with π ∘ σ = idL. Given x ∈ K₀ and 1 ≤ j ≤ s, the vector x · ι(uj) ∈ Lfin writes as ∑k=1s αjk ι(uk) with αjk ∈ E ⊗F 𝒪̂F. By simultaneous finite-adele approximation, there exist ajk ∈ 𝒪E with αjk − ajk ∈ g(E ⊗F 𝒪̂F), so wj = ∑k=1s ajkuk ∈ L satisfies x · ι(uj) − ι(wj) ∈ g Lfin. Defining ψ : 𝒪Es → L by ψ(ej) = wj and putting φ(x) = ψ ∘ σ ∈ End𝒪E(L), every z ∈ L satisfies σ(z) = ∑j=1s bjej (bj ∈ 𝒪E) with ∑j bjuj = π(σ(z)) = z, whence x · ι(z) − ι(φ(x)(z)) = ∑j=1s bj(x · ι(uj) − ι(wj)) ∈ g Lfin.

To bound |End𝒪E(L)/g End𝒪E(L)|, select a maximal E-linearly independent tuple v₁, …, vm ∈ L (so m = dimE(E · L) ≤ n). For every z ∈ L, clearing denominators in an E-linear expression for z produces a nonzero c ∈ 𝒪E such that cz ∈ ∑j=1m 𝒪Evj; since L ⊂ En is torsion-free over 𝒪E, any θ ∈ End𝒪E(L) satisfying θ(v₁) = ⋯ = θ(vm) = 0 satisfies cθ(z) = θ(cz) = 0 and hence θ(z) = 0. Thus θ ↦ (θ(v₁), …, θ(vm)) embeds End𝒪E(L) ℤ-linearly and injectively into (En)m ≃ Em×n, a ℚ-vector space of dimension mn[E : ℚ] ≤ n²(2f) = 2n²f. Because L is finitely generated over ℤ, End𝒪E(L) is a finitely generated torsion-free abelian group—hence free over ℤ—of rank r ≤ 2n²f, so |End𝒪E(L)/g End𝒪E(L)| = gr ≤ g2n²f.

Fundamental-domain covolume and the absolute unitary volume bound

How does one bound the global fundamental-domain measure μ(𝒟) of an indefinite unitary group of signature (p, q) (p + q = n ≥ 8, q² ≤ n) without re-entering the noncompact cusp geometry? Rather than packing coordinates on the quotient Γ ∖ G(𝔸F), the proof descends by successive one-vector stabilizer steps from signature (p, q) down to a positive-definite group of signature (2, 0), picking up root-discriminant powers and convergent unramified Euler factors across ranks 3 ≤ M ≤ n. At signature (2, 0), the archimedean factor U(2)f is compact of Riemannian volume (8π³)f, and the double cosets Γ ∖ G(𝔸F) / (G∞ × K₀) are controlled by isometry classes of rank-two positive-definite unimodular Hermitian lattices over 𝒪E. Every such plane lattice contains a nonzero vector of length at most d at every complex place; splitting the plane orthogonally along that short vector reduces the class count to multiplying bounds for a real-generated scale ideal, two rank-one Hermitian line classes, and the unimodular gluings above their orthogonal sum.

1. Quotient covolume and definite double cosets. For any automorphic Hermitian datum over E/F with discrete countable rational group Γ = G(F) ⊂ G(𝔸F) and left-invariant product Haar measure μ = μ∞ × μfin (with σ-finite Haar measure μfin and μ∞ = ∏v μv, positive on nonempty open subsets), let 𝒟 ⊆ G(𝔸F) be a measurable fundamental domain for the left action of Γ. Discreteness and countability of Γ identify the quotient covolume of Γ ∖ A with μ(A ∩ 𝒟) for every Γ-left-invariant measurable subset A ⊆ G(𝔸F); in particular, covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) = μ(𝒟) > 0 since G(𝔸F) = ⋃γ∈Γ γ−1𝒟 has positive Haar measure.

Suppose now that the datum has definite signature (r, 0) at every real place v of F (with f = [F : ℚ] ≥ 1), let cv > 0 be the Riemannian Haar gauge constant of μv on U(r) so that cvμv(U(r)) = vol(U(r)) and P∞ = ∏v cv, and write hdef(E, r) for the number of 𝒪E-isometry classes of rank-r positive-definite unimodular Hermitian lattices. By the self-dual point-lattice correspondence, whenever two adelic points x, y ∈ G(𝔸F) carry E-isometric Hermitian lattices Λx and Λy, an isometry γ ∈ Γ maps Λy onto Λx, so γ−1x and y share the same rational lattice and hence the same finite-adelic completion, placing x ∈ Γ y (G∞ × K₀). Summing over at most hdef(E, r) double-coset representatives bounds μ(𝒟) ≤ (∏v μv(U(r))) · hdef(E, r) · μfin(K₀); multiplying by P∞ and dividing by μfin(K₀) > 0 yields

P∞ covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) / μfin(K₀) ≤ vol(U(r))f hdef(E, r).

2. Rank-two definite class bound and inductive assembly. Let E/F be a CM extension of degree [E : ℚ] = 2f (f ≥ 1), compatible with complex conjugation and unramified at all finite places as in the flag datum, with root discriminant d = |disc E|1/(2f) = 2νE ≥ 1.

Proposition (Rank-two definite unimodular Hermitian class bound). The number of 𝒪E-isometry classes of rank-two positive-definite unimodular Hermitian lattices satisfies

hdef(E, 2) ≤ 4f d5f (1 + f log d)5f.
Short-vector plane splitting, real-generated scale ideals, and unimodular line gluings

Let (Λ, J) be any rank-two positive-definite unimodular Hermitian lattice over 𝒪E. Minkowski’s convex-body theorem on the rank-two unimodular lattice over 𝒪E produces a nonzero vector u ∈ Λ such that Re φ(u*Ju) = φ(u*Ju) ≤ d at every complex embedding φ : E ↪ ℂ. Writing v = u*J = (v₀, v₁) in E² and setting w = (−v₁, v₀)⊤ ∈ (E · u)⊥, the orthogonal basis (u, w) diagonalizes the Hermitian form to diag(β₁, β₂) with totally positive scalars β₁, β₂ ∈ F. Intersecting Λ with the two orthogonal lines yields rank-one positive-definite Hermitian sublattices (N₁, β₁) and (N₂, β₂) in E, and unimodularity of Λ forces both lines to share the same nonzero real-generated scale ideal 𝔫 = 𝔫₀𝒪E ⊆ 𝒪E (for a nonzero ideal 𝔫₀ ⊆ 𝒪F), of absolute norm NE/ℚ(𝔫) = NF/ℚ(𝔫₀)² ≤ (df)² = d2f.

Each rank-two isometry class is therefore reconstructed from four finite choices: (i) the nonzero ideal 𝔫₀ ⊆ 𝒪F of norm NF/ℚ(𝔫₀) ≤ Y = df, for which divisor counting over F of degree f gives at most Y(1 + log Y)f = df(1 + f log d)f possibilities for 𝔫; (ii) and (iii) the rank-one Hermitian classes of (N₁, β₁) and (N₂, β₂) with fixed scale 𝔫, each parameterized by the ideal class of Ni in Cl(𝒪E) together with the parity in (𝒪E×/μ(E)) ⊗ (ℤ/2ℤ) ≃ (ℤ/2ℤ)f−1 of the unit ratio u = βi/(āβi⁰a) ∈ 𝒪E× against a class representative (Ni⁰, βi⁰) = (aNi, βi⁰)—since u = wζv² (ζ ∈ μ(E), v ∈ 𝒪E×) and total positivity force u = w v̄ v via |φ(ζ)| = 1 (at most 2f−1hE ≤ 2fhE classes per line, with Minkowski class-number bound hE ≤ df(1 + f log d)2f, hence at most (2fdf(1 + f log d)2f)² = 4fd2f(1 + f log d)4f line pairs); and (iv) the unimodular overlattice M ⊇ N₁ ⊕ N₂ inside 𝔫−1N₁ ⊕ 𝔫−1N₂, determined by the graph of an 𝒪E-module isomorphism between 𝔫−1N₁/N₁ and 𝔫−1N₂/N₂, which admits at most |𝒪E/𝔫| = NE/ℚ(𝔫) ≤ d2f gluings. Multiplying the four bounds yields 4fd5f(1 + f log d)5f.

Theorem (Absolute unitary covolume and fundamental-domain volume bound). Let the automorphic Hermitian datum of rank n = p + q ≥ 8 over E/F have common archimedean signature (p, q) satisfying q² ≤ n, and let X ≥ 2 be any real number satisfying d ≤ X and 2f d ≤ X². Then

P∞ covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) / μfin(K₀) ≤ Xn²f.

In particular, under the indefinite counting hypotheses (n ≥ 8, f ≥ 1, q ≥ 1, q² ≤ n, d ≥ 1, g ≥ 1, b ≥ 2) with N = n²f and X = nf d g b ≥ 16, combining this bound with covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) = μ(𝒟) and the congruence level index μfin(K₀) ≤ g2Nkg proves

μ(𝒟) ≤ XN g2N kg / P∞,

completing the covolume estimate (written μ(F) in the deep-cusp normalization pair).

Rank-step induction from signature (2, 0) and absorption of constants into Xn²f

Because n ≥ 8 and q² ≤ n, one has q ≤ n − 2 (indeed, at n = 8 even q ≤ 6 suffices, and (n − 1)² > n for all n ≥ 8), so p = n − q ≥ 2 and signature (p, q) dominates (2, 0) componentwise. Applying the ordered rank-step volume ratio between the datum of signature (p, q) and a same-kind definite datum of signature (2, 0) expresses the ratio of their gauge-normalized covolumes as ∏M=3n d(M−1/2)f LM, where LM is the unramified rank-M Euler product of the rank-product formula. At each base prime 𝔭 ∣ p of norm Q = pf𝔭 ≥ p, both (1 − Q−M)−1 and (1 − (−1)MQ−M)−1 are at most (1 − p−M)−f𝔭, so ∑𝔭∣p f𝔭 ≤ f gives 0 < LM ≤ ζ(M)f for every M ≥ 3; bounding ∑m>K m−M ≤ (K + 1)2−M/K by telescoping comparison at K = 30 for 3 ≤ M ≤ 8 (giving ∏M=38 ζ(M) ≤ 1.391) and at K = 2 for M = k + 9 ≥ 9 (giving ζ(k + 9) ≤ 1 + 0.00235 · 2−k) yields ∏M=3n ζ(M) ≤ 1.398 < 1.4 and hence ∏M=3n LM ≤ (1.4)f. Together with ∑M=3n (M − 1/2) = (n² − 4)/2, this bounds the inductive ratio by df(n²−4)/2(1.4)f.

At signature (2, 0), by the compact unitary sphere-volume formula the unit spheres in ℂ¹ and ℂ² have areas 2π and 2π², so with the normalization factor 22(2−1)/2 = 2 one has vol(U(2)) = 2 · (2π) · (2π²) = 8π³. Multiplying the base bound vol(U(2))fhdef(E, 2) ≤ (32π³)fd5f(1 + f log d)5f by df(n²−4)/2(1.4)f gives

P∞ covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) / μfin(K₀) ≤ (44.8 π³)f df(n²+6)/2 (1 + f log d)5f.

Since d ≥ 1 and f ≥ 1, log d ≤ d − 1 implies 1 + f log d ≤ 1 + f(d − 1) ≤ f d < 2f d ≤ X², whence (1 + f log d)⁵ ≤ X¹⁰. Moreover d ≤ X and 44.8 π³ < 1400 < 2¹¹ ≤ X¹¹ because X ≥ 2. At each of the f real places the total exponent of X is therefore at most 11 + (n² + 6)/2 + 10 = n²/2 + 24 ≤ n² because n ≥ 8 gives n²/2 ≥ 32 ≥ 24, yielding Xn²f. Finally, at X = nf d g b one has X ≥ 8 · 1 · 1 · 1 · 2 = 16 ≥ 2, d ≤ X, and 2f d ≤ nf d ≤ X ≤ X², so multiplying covol(Γ, μ, G(𝔸F)) ≤ XNμfin(K₀)/P∞ by μfin(K₀) ≤ g2Nkg gives μ(𝒟) ≤ XNg2Nkg/P∞.

Absorbing the four errors

The bound still contains the unknown D on the right. Write X = |D − M|. Since D ≤ M + X, we get (1 − δ)X ≤ (2α + 2δ)M. The threshold on n ensures n ≥ exp(15). With f ≥ 1 the proof gets α, δ ≤ exp(−U/16)/8 and δ ≤ 1/2. Hence X ≤ exp(−U/16)M. For each fixed level-growth exponent, the counting theorem chooses its rank and spectral-gap thresholds before the row data vary. The definite case has an exact identity. The family has q = m/2 ≥ 1 negative directions, so it uses the estimate just derived.

The comparison of the automorphic model with the family identifies the dimension D with Dall and the main term M with D∗. Here n = k + m − 1 is the dimension of the Hermitian space. The frames used to form the lists of minors have length m/2 − 1, denoted by r in that argument. The negative signature index is q = m/2. For example, m = 4 and k = 8 give frame length 1, negative index 2 and ambient dimension 11. These numbers illustrate the notation before imposing the large-rank threshold. The count bounds the difference in both directions. The frame proof takes its upper inequality, Dall ≤ (1 + exp(−nf log n/16))D∗, to bound the number of common target rows. The Gram estimates separately control the entries obtained by pairing the word maps.

5.16Putting the words in the same row coordinates

Choose one orthonormal basis of the target, adapted to the common arithmetic row subspace, and one orthonormal basis for each full word space. Let Mu record the coordinates of Pu in those bases. In Mu∗Mv the sum over the shared row index gives exactly the inner products between the two sets of images, by Parseval. This is why the previous bounds apply simultaneously to the matrices. The unfolding volumes and dimensions give cu ≥ 0. The lower dimension proviso gives du > 0, and the scale bound gives e0 < 1. Together they force strict positivity. Indeed, when the normalizer vanishes the normalized block is defined to be zero. Its squared distance from the identity would then equal the full positive dimension.

For each word an isometric inclusion Vu selects the ramified columns, with Vu∗Vu = I. The top rows of the resulting matrix represent the rational arithmetic map after a common invertible row change and a word-dependent invertible column change. At the chosen complex place a single simultaneous conjugation may be necessary. It preserves absolute squares. Invertibility explains how to recognize the arithmetic map. Isometry explains how the selected columns sit inside the full space. The rank computation separately measures how many columns are retained.

How many independent directions do the period maps detect?

Start with one word u. Its normalized period map Au = cu−1/2Pu takes du columns into the common row space. Its Gram matrix is Kuu = Au∗Au. Choose an orthonormal basis of the kernel and extend it to the source. For each unit vector x in the kernel basis, Aux = 0 gives (Kuu − I)x = −x. It contributes exactly 1 to the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm Q(Kuu − I). The remaining basis vectors contribute nonnegative terms. By the dimension formula for a linear map,

dim ker Au ≤ Q(Kuu − I),   rank Au ≥ (1 − e0)du   if   Q(Kuu − I) ≤ e0du.

The weighted count of minor lists bounds the contribution at each intersection defect. Squaring the norm pairs two terms, so the two sums over defects give the square of a single sum. In the resulting estimate, the factor du bounds the row mass multiplied by the local representation dimension and its Gram normalization. It counts the source columns, whose number is known before applying the period map. The scalar bound on that square gives Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu, where ξ = exp(−kf log k).

Write D∗ for the positive reference mass of the whole row space and Γ for the family scale with log Γ = CΓm⁵fL. The complementary estimate gives Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗. The chosen word sizes satisfy duΓ²/D∗ ≤ C0. Multiplying by du/Γ gives a complementary error of at most (C0/Γ)du. Applying ‖X + Y‖² ≤ 2‖X‖² + 2‖Y‖² gives e0 = 2ξ + 2C0/Γ. Since the kernel dimension is an integer, the total error bound allows at most ⌊e0du⌋ lost directions. If e0du < 1, the map is injective. At equality one direction can disappear: the projection from ℂ⁸ to ℂ⁷ that drops the last coordinate has squared error exactly 1 and rank 7. Appending zero rows leaves its Gram matrix unchanged. An upper bound for the number of available rows therefore needs additional information.

What happens when all the words share the same rows?

Write D = Dall for the dimension of the entire common row space, including the rows later discarded when the lattice map takes its top block. Let R = ∑u du count all the columns. The automorphic projection trace gives D ≤ (1 + η₁)D∗. Independently, for u ≠ v the period correlation estimate gives Q(Kuv) ≤ (1 + η₀)dudv/D∗, with Kuv = Au∗Av. To measure how many rows the columns span together, form the positive operator F = ∑u AuAu∗. Its kernel is the orthogonal complement of their span, since ⟨Fy, y⟩ = ∑u ‖Au∗y‖².

For example, take two one-column maps from ℂ to ℂ², both sending z to (z, 0). Both diagonal Gram matrices equal 1, yet the columns span just one line. Their mixed Gram entry is 1, and F has diagonal entries 2 and 0. Move the second column to (0, 1). The two diagonal Gram matrices still equal 1, but the mixed Gram entry vanishes, F becomes the identity, and the span has dimension two. In both cases tr F = 2. The second trace moment tr(F²) falls from 4 to 2 as the repeated direction is replaced by an independent one.

Cycling the factors under the trace gives tr F = ∑u tr Kuu and tr(F²) = ∑u,v Q(Kuv). Put a = √e0. On the diagonal, Cauchy–Schwarz gives |tr(Kuu − I)| ≤ √du ‖Kuu − I‖ ≤ a du, with the Hilbert–Schmidt norm throughout. The triangle inequality gives ‖Kuu‖ ≤ (1 + a)√du. For distinct words, the count of pairs of flags sharing a subspace supplies one contribution to the mixed Gram estimate. Adding the distinct-word terms gives

tr F ≥ (1 − a)R,   tr(F²) ≤ (1 + η₀)R²/D∗ + (1 + a)²R.

Dimension bound. Suppose 0 < σ ≤ 1/4, D∗ > 0, R ≥ D∗/σ, −1 ≤ η₀, and η₀, η₁, a ≤ σ/2. Then the period columns span at least D/(1 + 5σ) dimensions. To see this, the lower bound for R absorbs the last summand of tr(F²) into a multiple of R²/D∗. The independent row count then gives

D tr(F²)/(tr F)² ≤ (1 + η₁)[1 + η₀ + σ(1 + a)²]/(1 − a)² ≤ 1 + 5σ.

For the last inequality, replace η₀, η₁ and a by σ/2 and multiply by (1 − σ/2)². Expanding, the right side exceeds the left by σ(16 − 52σ + 4σ² − σ³)/8, which is positive for 0 < σ ≤ 1/4. Finally let h be the rank of F. Its h positive eigenvalues sum to tr F and their squares sum to tr(F²). Cauchy–Schwarz gives (tr F)² ≤ h tr(F²), proving the claim.

For the two unit columns (1, 0) and (3/5, 4/5), each diagonal Gram entry is 1 and each mixed entry is 3/5. Thus tr F = 2 and tr(F²) = 2 + 2(3/5)² = 68/25. The trace bound gives h ≥ 25/17. An integer rank exceeding one in a two-dimensional space must be two. This illustrates the last inequality even when the two directions are oblique.

The family meets the lower bound on R by choosing ⌈C₀Γ²/σ⌉ words. Each contributes at least D∗/(C₀Γ²) columns. Multiplication gives R ≥ (C₀Γ²/σ) · D∗/(C₀Γ²) = D∗/σ.

To see where this hypothesis enters, consider a smaller family. Take one word consisting of a single unit column in ℂ100 and set D = D∗ = 100. Its Gram matrix is (1), so its diagonal error is zero. There are no distinct-word pairs and the row count is exact. Yet F is the projection onto that one column, with both traces and rank equal to 1. At σ = 1/100 the theorem requires at least 10,000 columns in total. Controlling the minor lists gives the error estimate. The independent count of columns allows the trace ratio to force a large span.

How much survives the ramification conditions?

For each word retain an ru-dimensional subspace, included by an isometry Vu. Suppose ∑u(du − ru) ≤ ρR, with 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1/4. The arithmetic column count supplies this loss. Set F′ = ∑u (AuVu)(AuVu)∗. Compression replaces each Gram block by Vu∗KuvVv. In orthonormal bases adapted to the retained subspaces, this keeps a submatrix, so tr((F′)²) ≤ tr(F²).

The first trace also decreases. In a word with mu = du − ru discarded columns, the trace of the identity on those columns is mu. The absolute trace of the error there is at most a√(mudu) by Cauchy–Schwarz. Summing and using ∑u√(mudu) ≤ √ρ R gives tr F′ ≥ (1 − a − ρ − a√ρ)R. For σ ≤ 1/20 the factor is positive. The compressed trace estimate then yields

rank F′ ≥ D/(1 + 5σ + 3√ρ).

The second-moment bound survives restriction. The smaller first trace increases the upper bound on the trace ratio by at most 3√ρ, as the calculation below shows.

For example, suppose the trace hypotheses hold with D = 100, σ = 1/100 and ρ = 1/10,000. The full span has dimension at least 100/1.05, hence at least 96. For the retained columns the denominator rises to 1.08. Their images still span at least 93 of the same 100 directions.

Where does the extra 3√ρ come from?

Put t = √ρ and L = 1 + 5σ + 3t. For the numerator, take the bound for tr(F²) before division by the first trace. Multiplying it by D, absorbing the term linear in R and using the same numerical inequality as above gives D tr((F′)²) ≤ (1 + 5σ)(1 − a)²R². For the denominator the discarded-column estimate gives tr F′ ≥ [1 − a − t(t + a)]R. Because t ≤ 1/2 and a ≤ σ/2 ≤ 1/40, one has 2L(t + a) ≤ 2(11/4)(21/40) ≤ 3(1 − a). Multiply this by t(1 − a) and expand the square to obtain (1 + 5σ)(1 − a)² ≤ L[1 − a − t(t + a)]². Applying the eigenvalue inequality to F′ gives the stated rank.

Restricting the columns changes the domain of the period map. Both ranks above are still measured in the space of all D rows. The map to the dual arithmetic lattice keeps only its Dar arithmetic rows. This projection has kernel of dimension D − Dar, so it can remove at most that many independent directions from any span. For example, let π project ℂ³ onto its first two coordinates. The planes spanned by (e₁, e₃) and by (e₁, e₂) both have dimension two before projection. Their images have dimensions one and two, respectively. In either case the exact loss for a plane W is dim(W ∩ ker π), by the dimension formula applied to π restricted to W.

Let V be the full row space, Var its arithmetic coordinate space, and W the span of the retained columns. Projection induces the following map of quotients.

V/W ↠ Var/π(W),   v + W ↦ π(v) + π(W).

Vectors differing by an element of W give the same target class. Every target class lifts by filling the omitted coordinates with zeros. Taking dimensions, the number of missing directions among the arithmetic rows is at most the number missing among all rows. If the latter number is at most ωD and Dar ≥ (1 − δ)D with δ < 1, the missing fraction among the arithmetic rows is at most ω/(1 − δ). This is the denominator in the slope argument, where the codimension bound at the slope threshold controls a further selection of columns.

5.17Why two auxiliary primes enter the counting floor

The lower bound for every prime level Tu contains m log(g0g1), where g0 and g1 are two fixed auxiliary primes. How can a term independent of the word u appear with just this coefficient? Compare the row level of rank r = k + m − 1 with the column level of rank k. Here m is even and at least two. We can calculate the part of their index ratio contributed by both primes.

Lean correspondence

5.18Counting matrices at one prime

Let q be either auxiliary prime. The number of invertible n-by-n matrices over the field of q elements is qn²Πn(q), where Πn(q) = ∏j=1n(1 − q−j). Choose the columns in order. Once i independent columns have been chosen, their span excludes precisely qi out of the qn choices for the next column. An index divides this count by the number of allowed level matrices. On the column side, these are upper triangular with diagonal entries 1. The strictly upper triangle has k(k − 1)/2 free entries.

The row has a central block of size k + 1 flanked by (m/2 − 1) singleton blocks on each side. Between different blocks all entries above the diagonal are free. Within the central block the first k positions have a free strictly upper triangle. Its final column has zeros in all k positions above its diagonal within that block. Thus the whole row matrix has r(r − 1)/2 − k free entries. Every choice has determinant one. Subtract the exponents of q in the two indices. The difference is r(r + 1)/2 + k − k(k + 1)/2 = A, where A = mk + m(m − 1)/2. The first k factors of Π cancel.

row index / column index = qA P(q),   P(q) = ∏j=k+1r(1 − q−j).

Check at q = 2, k = m = 2. The two invertible groups have orders (4 − 1)(4 − 2) = 6 and (8 − 1)(8 − 2)(8 − 4) = 168. Each level subgroup has one free binary entry, so its order is 2. The quotient of indices is 84/3 = 28, exactly 25(1 − 2−3). This checks the local identity in small ranks. The estimates for the full family use m ≥ 44.

5.19From local indices to a word’s level

Each auxiliary prime contributes f identical factors, where f counts the places in the construction. The logarithm of the real scale Xu divides the log ratio by fk. The part supplied by the two indices is therefore

(m + m(m − 1)/(2k)) log(g0g1) + (log P(g0) + log P(g1))/k.

How much can the last term cost? For 0 ≤ aj ≤ 1, successively multiplying by 1 − aj gives ∏(1 − aj) ≥ 1 − ∑ aj. The geometric series starting at k + 1 is at most 2q−(k+1) for q ≥ 2. Since k ≥ 1, this gives 1/2 ≤ P(q) ≤ 1. The error after dividing by k lies between −2 log(2)/k and zero. The proof uses the slightly weaker lower bound −2/k. The coefficient left after keeping m log(g0g1) is nonnegative.

To locate this term in the full count, write D★ for the row’s volume times its level index and its product of formal degrees, and du★ for the column’s genus mass times its level index and its product of representation dimensions. Genus mass weights each lattice class by the reciprocal of its number of automorphisms. The definition is Xufk = D★/du★. The volume identification replaces the row volume with the rank-r mass. Consecutive mass ratios then telescope from rank k to rank r. Each step M contributes ((M − 1)!)f. Across all steps these factors change the column’s Weyl factorial product ∏i=0k−1i! into its rank-r counterpart at each of the f places. The other factors carry the volume parameter, an Euler product and the placewise formal degrees.

For L = xε and positive weights wjρ, put S = ∑j=0m−1 (1/f)∑ρ log(wjρv/π), where v is half the host field’s root discriminant. The formal-degree bound at gap tolerance 1/3, the weight estimates, and the mass Euler-product bounds control the remaining factors. The term-by-term bound with the family’s spacing and size hypotheses gives S + m log(g0g1) − 11L ≤ log Xu. Finally, the prime selected in the word’s level window lies above Tu* = XuΓ−2/(fk). Taking its logarithm costs at most 2 because log Γ/(fk) ≤ 1. The family takes a common counting constant and threshold before the scale, index and word vary. The global floor follows with its larger error allowance. For the change between two words, return to the Vandermonde estimate.

5.20How a volume becomes a sum over lattice classes

The formula for the word scale uses the volume of a unitary group on the row side and a Hermitian genus mass on the column side. To compare ranks, we need both in the same units. A genus consists of lattices isometric at every finite place. Its mass is the sum of 1/|Aut(Λ)| over its global isometry classes. The proof starts in positive definite rank two, where the automorphism groups are finite.

Let Γ be the rational unitary group, G its adelic group and K the subgroup preserving the completed lattice at finite places and unrestricted at infinity. In the definite case the prescribed archimedean measures are probabilities. Applying the product normalization to the whole compact group at each infinite place gives μ(K) = 1. Pick representatives gi of the finite double quotient Γ∖G/K. In the class of gi, exactly |Γ ∩ giKgi−1| translates of a point by Γ land in giK. Weight that coset’s indicator by the reciprocal. Its sum over Γ is one on that class. Integrating the weighted indicators over G now gives the volume of a fundamental domain. The stabilizers are the lattice automorphism groups, so the result is the genus mass.

A finite model. Take G = S₃ and Γ = K = {1, (12)}. The two double cosets have representatives 1 and (13), with stabilizer orders 2 and 1. Their weights add to 3/2. Directly, μ(K) = 1 gives mass 1/2 to each element and a Γ-fundamental domain has three elements. This explains the inverse stabilizer in the formula. A deeper finite level K′ ⊂ K has measure 1/[K:K′]. Renormalizing that subgroup to measure one therefore multiplies the covolume by its index. In the word count the row uses its own index and the column uses its own, so their quotient is row index divided by column index.

5.21Why adjacent ranks have a predictable mass ratio

Write M for the new rank, f for the number of conjugate pairs of complex embeddings of the CM field, and v for half its root discriminant. The quadratic extension of its totally real subfield is unramified at every finite prime. For a totally positive definite integral Hermitian lattice Λ, count vectors whose squared lengths are at most j² at every embedding. Sum these counts over the genus using the reciprocal automorphism weights above. The zero vector contributes the mass μΛ. Grouping the other vectors by their represented value gives the same sum, now expressed through representation counts. Divide by j2fM and let j grow. The two ways of counting give

μΛ (πM/M!)f / (vfM δ) = (cM−1 λΛ/δ) M−f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

On the left, πM/M! is the volume of a unit ball in ℂM, and δ is the positive square root of the absolute norm of the lattice discriminant ideal. On the right, cM−1 is the mass constant for the preceding rank, λΛ is a product of local lattice corrections, and Lη(M) is the Euler product of the CM field. This second limit uses the representation-density formula and the asymptotic sum of its local factors. The zero vector’s separate contribution tends to zero after division. Cancel δ and use M!/M = (M − 1)!. For a lattice with an orthonormal integral basis every local lattice correction is one. The two standard masses consequently satisfy the following identity for the ranks M ≥ 3 used here.

massM / massM−1 = [((M − 1)!)(v/π)M]f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

For instance, take M = 3 and a finite prime of the totally real subfield of residue size 2. If it is inert, the unique prime above it has norm 4 and its Euler factor is (1 + 2−3)−1 = 8/9. If it splits, its two primes of norm 2 each contribute (1 − 2−3)−1/2, giving 8/7 together. These are factors at a single prime. Across the rank increments, the same positive rank-one constant occurs in both standard masses and cancels in their ratio.

To reach the indefinite row, the normalized unit-vector unfolding supplies the same ratio for a space and the orthogonal complement of a vector of norm +1 or −1. From definite rank two, use +1 to compare successive positive definite ranks. For a constant signature (P, Q) with P ≥ 2, induction on Q uses a −1 vector, whose complement has signature (P, Q − 1). The two inductions identify the row volume with the standard mass of its rank r. In the word-scale formula the column mass then cancels the common ranks, leaving exactly the increments M = k + 1, …, r. These are the factors estimated in the lower bound for each word.

5.22Why the mass comparison costs 11L

The mass identity tells us the scale Xu for each word u. How small can that scale be, even for the least favorable word? Put G = log(g0g1) and L = xε. There are f infinite places ρ and m positive weights wjρ at each. Their contribution is S = (1/f)∑ρ∑j log(wjρv/π), where v is half the root discriminant. We will bound how far log Xu can fall below S + mG.

Lean correspondence
  • The exact mass identity and its target

5.23What survives in the quotient of dimensions?

Fix a place. Write its row as λ = (c0, …, ck−2, −b0, …, −bm−1) of length r = k + m − 1. Its first block is nonnegative and decreases in steps of at least one. The bj are positive and increase in steps of at least one. The column u0 > ⋯ > uk−1 belonging to the word interlaces the first block, with ui > ci > ui+1. Write V(y) = ∏i<j(yi − yj). Each cross-block gap ci + bj is at least bj, and each gap within the negative block is at least one. This proves the first inequality below.

V(λ) ≥ V(c)∏j bjk−1,   V(u) ≤ D2k−3V(c),   D = 8xeL.

For the second inequality, the column has k − 1 gaps touching its first entry and another k − 2 touching its last. Each is at most D. Each remaining gap ui − uj is bounded by the distinct gap ci−1 − cj. The unused adjacent gaps of c are at least one. Dividing the inequalities now cancels the factor V(c). For a small check take c = (4, 0), u = (6, 2, −1) and b = (3, 5). The row has gap product 7,560, the column has gap product 84, and their ratio is 90. This example illustrates the interlacing calculation alone.

The local factor in the mass identity is dρFr/V(u), with formal degree dρ and Fr = ∏h=0r−1h!. At the required separation between parameters of opposite signature, the discrete-series estimate with tolerance 1/3 gives dρ ≥ (2/3)V(λ)/Fr by Weyl’s dimension formula. Thus the row factorials cancel as well. The source allows a logarithmic loss of 2k log D + 2k(1 + log k) in the Vandermonde comparison. At the family threshold, 2(log 8 + 1 + log x) ≤ L and log(2k) ≤ L, so this loss is at most 5kL.

5.24Adding the losses in the mass identity

The geometric weights satisfy 0 < bj < wjρ ≤ (1 + 1/x)bj and wjρ ≤ 2eL. Then k log w − (k − 1) log b = log w + (k − 1) log(w/b) ≤ 2L + k/x. Summing over m weights costs at most 2kL + k since m ≤ k and m ≤ x. Also log(2/3) ≥ −1. At each place the logarithm of the local factor is therefore at least k∑j log wjρ − (7kL + k + 1).

Each rank increment M = k + 1, …, r contributes a positive mass Euler product Lη(M). Group its local logarithms by the rational prime p. A prime ideal of residue degree d above p contributes at most (d/2)[−log(1 − p−M)] in absolute value. The residue degrees above p sum to at most the field degree 2f. Summing over p gives |log Lη(M)| ≤ f log ζ(M) ≤ f, since M ≥ 2. Averaging over the f places leaves a total cost at most m − 1 for the r − k rank increments.

Subtract S + mG from log Xu and multiply by k. In the mass identity the surplus m(m − 1)[log(v/π) + G]/2 is nonnegative. The two remaining discriminant terms cost at most kL + (m − 1)L/2, using 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and log(2v) ≤ L. The two auxiliary primes together cost at most 2. Add these amounts to the place and Euler losses.

8kL + (m − 1)L/2 + m + 2 + k ≤ 11kL,   log Xu ≥ S + mG − 11L.

Indeed, (m − 1)L/2 ≤ kL/2 and m + 2 + k ≤ 5kL/2 because 44 ≤ m ≤ k and L ≥ 1. For fixed family and constants ε > 0, C0, CY, a single threshold works for every admissible scale above it, every family index, every choice of spacing and weights satisfying the stated data, and every word. The later transfer from Xu to the chosen prime level in its short window has its own window loss.

5.25Why a real-place degree has the size of a Vandermonde product

The placewise mass estimate compares a row with the column belonging to a word. The row supplies a discrete series of the real unitary group U(p, q), an irreducible unitary representation σ with square-integrable matrix coefficients. For a nonzero vector w, its formal degree is ‖w‖4 divided by the integral of |⟨w, σ(g)w⟩|2. Multiplying the Haar measure by a positive number divides the degree by that number. The numerical comparison therefore requires a specific measure.

Let N = p + q with both signs present. The parameter λ has strictly decreasing entries indexed from 0, with λi − (N−1)/2 integral. Each index carries a sign, with p positive and q negative. Write Fn = ∏0≤a<na! and V(λ) = ∏i<j(λi − λj). On the normalized measure one has the following equality for the large-gap parameters used here.

d(λ) = V(λ)/FN,   FN = ∏i<j(j−i).
