5.26How an integral fixes the missing constant

Imagine moving λ by integer steps. When an admissible step raises one coordinate by one, the degree and the Vandermonde change by exactly the same ratio, as the embedding of a shifted model shows. Along λi(t) = λi + t(N−1−i), for integers t ≥ 0, the steps can be ordered so that decreasing order and the gap survive. Thus d(λ(t))/V(λ(t)) stays constant. To find its value, let Tt be the lowest compact type, the finite-dimensional representation of U(p) × U(q) selected by the weight λ(t). Form Yt = tpq dim(Tt)/d(λ(t)).

Put A = ∏(j−i) over opposite-sign pairs i<j. On the algebraic side the compact Weyl dimension formula cancels the same-sign factors of the moving Vandermonde up to ratios tending to one. Indeed, if the moving gap is g, its ratio is (g+b)/g, where b counts opposite signs strictly between the indices. Each opposite-sign pair leaves t/[λi−λj+t(j−i)], tending to 1/(j−i).

On the analytic side, polar coordinates use probability measure on the compact group and one complex coordinate per opposite-sign pair. The Haar density includes the constant c = FN/(πpqFpFq). Rescaling each complex coordinate by 1/√t absorbs tpq. The limiting squared coefficient has a Gaussian factor exp(−(j−i)|z|²) in each coordinate, whose plane integral is π/(j−i). The coefficient supplies a lower limit and an integrable upper bound supplies the matching upper limit. Comparing the two values of the same limit gives the stated degree.

V(λ)/[d(λ)FpFqA] = lim Yt = cπpq/A = FN/(FpFqA).

5.27The fraction retained in the word count

For exp(−N) ≤ η < 1/2 the family theorem asks that every opposite-sign gap be at least 8192 min(p, q)(pq)³ log(N)/η². This implies the large-gap hypotheses above. It then retains the lower bound (1−η)V(λ)/FN. For example, in signature (1,1) take λ = (30000.5, −29999.5) and η = 1/3. The required gap is 73728 log 2 ≈ 51104.36. The actual gap and normalized degree are both 60000. Here Tt has dimension one and Yt = t/(60000+t) tends to one. The lower comparison keeps 40000. In the full mass proof the same choice η = 1/3 gives dρFr ≥ (2/3)V(λρ) at each real place of row rank r. The factorial in the mass identity cancels the denominator of the Weyl product, leaving the row Vandermonde for the interlacing estimate.

5.28An upper bound for the scale of every word

Relative variation alone can leave all the words equally large. To bound their absolute scale, start again from the mass identity used for the lower bound. It gives fk log Xu as a sum of six terms. For an upper bound, a term of known negative sign can be discarded. The remaining positive contributions must be estimated even when the word and the family member vary. Assume 44 ≤ m ≤ k, r = k + m − 1, L ≥ 9 and log(2k) ≤ L. Write CY for the bound log gi ≤ CYL on each of the two auxiliary primes. The following budget is divided throughout by fkmL, so its sum bounds log Xu/(mL).

  • The coefficient of log(v/π) is f[(m − 1)k + m(m − 1)/2]. Since 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and m ≤ k, the normalized contribution is at most 3/2. The term in −log(2v) is nonpositive.
  • At most m Euler values enter. Each logarithm is at most f by the comparison with ζ(M) at integers M ≥ 2. Together they cost at most 1/(kL). The finite corrections log(1 − gi−j) are nonpositive.
  • The positive prime term has coefficient fm(2k + m − 1)/2. Since log(g0g1) ≤ 2CYL, it costs at most 3CY.
  • At each infinite place, separate the logarithm of the ratio of representation dimensions from the factorial products in Weyl’s formula. The gap estimate for the real-place degree and the column estimate bound the first by km(log 3 + 5 log(2k) + 5L + 10). For the factorials there are r − k additional factors j!. Each is at most rr. Since r ≤ 2k, their logarithms total at most 2kmL. Summing over f places costs at most 12/L + 12 after normalization.

These four bounds imply

log Xu/(mL) ≤ 3/2 + 1/(kL) + 3CY + 12/L + 12 ≤ 15 + 3CY.

For the last inequality even the looser k ≥ 5 suffices. The constants independent of CY sum to at most 3/2 + 1/45 + 4/3 + 12 = 1337/90, strictly below 15. Take the maximum of the thresholds for this estimate, the lower estimate, the real-place gap and the mass inputs. Thus the same threshold works for all words. To pass to the chosen prime Tu, its window has lower endpoint Tu* = XuΓ−2/(fk) and upper multiplicative factor 1 + 1/(fk). With Γ ≥ 1 this gives log Tu ≤ log Xu + 1. The construction absorbs the additive allowance into its common counting constant. The short-interval norm-prime selection supplies a prime in this window unconditionally.

5.29Where the logarithmic period comes from

The term Ωlog in the main-term calculation has a geometric meaning. At a single complex embedding, the norm of a generator of a differential line depends on the generator and the elliptic lattice. The proof first measures the line in a way that survives a change of generator. It then computes its mean using complex multiplication and carries that mean into the bounds for the columns of a theta kernel.

5.30Which changes of scale cancel?

Let K0 be the imaginary quadratic host field of discriminant −dK, and E the extension used in the host. Take a nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of K0 with norm prime to 2dK. If Δ is the discriminant of its embedded elliptic lattice and δ12 = Δ, the rescaled lattice Λ = δ·φ0(𝔠) has discriminant one. Take any number field M inside ℂ containing the specified images of E and the Weierstrass invariants g2(Λ), g3(Λ). For each embedding ρ of M, transport those two invariants and let Aρ > 0 be the area of the corresponding period lattice.

Fix a host embedding label τ. The source spans the vectors of conjugates of elements of the host fractional ideal and intersects the resulting module with the τ-coordinate line. Write ℓτ for the resulting module inside M and DM = [M : ℚ]. For a nonzero s in ℓτ, put I(s) = [ℓτ : 𝒪Ms]. The measured quantity is

mρ(s) = log(π |ρ(s)|² / Aρ),   Ω̄τ = (2 log I(s) − ∑ρ mρ(s)) / DM.

When ℓτ has generator a, every such s has form ca with 0 ≠ c ∈ 𝒪M. The index is |NM/ℚ(c)|. Meanwhile each local logarithm increases by 2 log |ρ(c)|. Their sum increases by twice the logarithm of precisely that index. Thus Ω̄τ equals the average of −mρ(a). For a small check, take the free line ℤ[i] and use the test element s = 1 + i. Its multiples form a sublattice of index 2. Each of the two embeddings contributes an extra log 2, cancelling the finite contribution 2 log 2. This example checks the normalization in a free line.

5.31Why the root discriminant appears

Write n = [E : ℚ], h = [E : K0] = n/2. Let b be the absolute norm of the product of the host fractional ideal with the relative different of E/K0. The ideal-index calculation gives I(s)n bDM = |NM/ℚ(s)|n. Taking logarithms and summing the local metrics eliminates the norm of s. Hence

Ω̄τ = (1/DM) ∑ρ log(Aρ/π) − (2/n) log b.

Set B equal to the absolute norm of the relative different. Its half-different identity gives b² = B. The discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = B(dK)h. Since rd(E) = |disc(E)|1/n, the correction (2/n) log b equals log rd(E) − log √dK.

For the area term the proof compares the conjugate lattices with a family indexed by ideal classes. Over a common extension their homotheties give 6 log Aoriginal = 6 log Afamily + log |ρ(u)|, with u a discriminant unit. The unit contributes zero to the sum over embeddings. Averaging over the extension gives the same mean as over M, because each embedding occurs with the same multiplicity. The Chowla–Selberg class-sum formula then evaluates the area mean as γ + log(2π/√dK) − dχ, where dχ = Re(L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ)) for the host quadratic character. This dχ is the scalar denoted d in the main-term calculation above. Subtracting the correction cancels log √dK. For every compatible M and every τ this gives

Ω̄τ = γ + log(2π/rd(E)) − dχ = Ωlog.

This identifies the scalar that occurs earlier with v = rd(E)/2. The calculation uses the CM family of period lattices, the Chowla–Selberg evaluation and the ideal-index formula as inputs.

Why does the class product give a derivative at one?

Let the imaginary quadratic host field have fundamental discriminant −d, with d > 4, class number h, and w roots of unity. Write χ for its primitive quadratic character of conductor d. For each ideal class choose its point z in the upper half-plane and rescale the period lattice to Weierstrass discriminant one. Write Az for the area of the resulting fundamental parallelogram. The class mean used in the period calculation is

(1/h) ∑classes log(Az/π) = γ + log(2π/√d) − L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ).

Fix the scale of the lattice. Write it as a(ℤ + zℤ), with y = Im z. Its area is |a|²y. The discriminant on ℤ + zℤ is (2π)¹²η(z)²⁴, and scaling the periods by a multiplies it by a−12. Setting the discriminant to one gives |a|² = 4π²|η(z)|⁴. Thus, for F(z) = √y |η(z)|², we get Az/π = 4π F(z)². The choice of twelfth root disappears upon taking absolute values. Barquero-Sanchez et al., (3.2) and the discriminant formula after (6.1)[67]

Take the logarithm of the class product. Put S = ∑1≤r≤d χ(r) log Γ(r/d). The Chowla–Selberg formula at conductor one gives (2/h) ∑ log F(z) = −log(4π√d) + wS/(2h). The evaluation of the Dirichlet logarithmic derivative at zero gives L′(0,χ)/L(0,χ) = −log d + wS/(2h). Substituting the second identity in the first cancels the gamma sum. Adding log(4π) from the area gives the following equality. Barquero-Sanchez et al., Theorem 5.1 and (5.13)[67]

(1/h) ∑classes log(Az/π) = ½ log d + L′(0,χ)/L(0,χ).

Reflect from zero to one. Write l(s) = L′(s,χ)/L(s,χ). Here L(0,χ) = 2h/w and L(1,χ) ≠ 0. Since χ is real and odd, its completed function is Λ(s) = (d/π)(s+1)/2 Γ((s+1)/2)L(s,χ). The functional equation identifies Λ(s) with a constant times Λ(1−s). The change of variable reverses the sign of the logarithmic derivative. At zero this gives l(0) + l(1) = −log(d/π) − (ψ(½)+ψ(1))/2, where ψ = Γ′/Γ. Inserting ψ(1) = −γ and ψ(½) = −γ − 2 log 2 gives l(0) = γ + log(2π/d) − l(1). The remaining ½ log d in the area mean changes the denominator to √d. Class number formula (5.8)[67] · Dirichlet functional equation and nonvanishing, (25.15.5) and (25.15.9)[68] · Digamma values, (5.4.12) and (5.4.13)[69]

Check the constants at discriminant −7

Here z = (1+i√7)/2 represents the principal class. The ring ℤ + zℤ is norm Euclidean. Given any complex quotient, first subtract an integer multiple of z to leave imaginary part at most √7/4 in magnitude, then an integer to leave real part at most ½. The squared error is at most 7/16 + 1/4 < 1. Euclidean division makes every ideal principal. Thus this single point gives the whole class mean. The eta product gives log(4πF(z)²) ≈ 1.426502. The logarithmic derivatives are l(0) ≈ 0.453547 and l(1) ≈ 0.015636. Substituting either into the corresponding area formula gives 1.426502.

5.32From embeddings to column heights

The coefficient embeddings ρ and the infinite places w of the field of the column matrices index different lists. The kernel estimate chooses one field M containing the coefficients and the generators aτ, and nonnegative weights Wwρ. For each w the weights sum to one. For each ρ their average over w equals 1/DM. Define the period at a matrix place by pτ(w) = ∑ρ Wwρ[−mρ(aτ)]. Interchanging two finite sums gives

meanw pτ(w) = ∑ρ (meanw Wwρ)[−mρ(aτ)] = Ωlog.

Each place can have its own period. Only its mean is prescribed. The kernel theorem inserts these local numbers into its logarithmic bounds for the matrix factors. It treats the vacuum theta norm separately by an upper bound on its mean. The construction also needs the character and weight identifications, the field of definition, the trivial twist and the sharp local data of the selected column. An independent estimate for the final evaluation map and positive definite row metrics then turn the bounds into framed rows with an invertible ramified frame at every infinite place.

The version used in the every-character argument inserts these rows into its definite-side condition and carries that condition into the family hypotheses. At the final assembly the row bounds enter divisibility. The separate global estimate constructs the matrix rank bounds that accompany divisibility. The proof combines the two at the chosen family. The positive definite metrics, evaluation bounds, class counts and individual matrix-factor norm estimates remain inputs to the derivation above.

A construction with compatible generators identifies the stored Ω-values with exp(−mρ(aτ)) and reindexes the embeddings to obtain this comparison. Given both inputs, theta_norm_family_of_linked derives a family norm condition. The selected global theorem calls link_gl, which constructs its rank and slope input from the real-place conditions.
